section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to our course on business communication!

In these five weeks we’ll be learning all about why effective communication is a key to your success in business. We’ll see that business communication is much more than just emailing your boss or speaking up at a meeting—in fact, principles of good communication can improve your performance in many aspects of your professional life. Our goal will be to understand those principles and put them into practice.

That means we’ll be covering things like emotional intelligence, social media, accessibility, business presentations, technology, and problems with communication across cultures, along with many other subjects. We’ll see lots of interesting examples and connections to real-life issues you may face at work, and we’ll have some fascinating discussions about how individuals and groups get along.
It’s going to be fun! Let’s get started.

section.title: Communication: Justin and Kaya’s Story
section.para: To see the sorts of things we’ll be talking about, let’s begin with a story. The story features two coworkers, Justin and Kaya, who exchanged emails over the weekend. Their exchange wasn’t exactly pleasant, and so they’re meeting to talk about what went wrong. Justin and Kaya’s story will illustrate many aspects of communication in business that we’ll be exploring.
As you read, you might ask yourself the following questions:

listitem.para: What aspects of business communication does the story illustrate?
Which parts of Justin and Kaya’s communication went well, and which could be improved?
Have I been in a situation like this before?
Have I acted like Justin before? Have I acted like Kaya before? Why?

important.title: Justin and Kaya
important.para: Justin scrambled through the office on his way to see Kaya, dropping his phone twice. He was worried he’d be late because the office kitchen had been a mess when he went to make lunch, and eating took a lot longer than he thought it would. But he skidded to Kaya’s door at 1:30, right when they said they’d meet. He knocked.
“Who is it?” said a muffled voice from inside.
“Hey Kaya, it’s Justin. Stopping by to chat, like we said.”
“Hey, Justin,” Kaya said. “Come on in.”
Justin rattled the doorknob. “I think it’s locked.”

“Oh, sorry. Let me get it…there.” Kaya opened the door and led Justin into the room. She pushed a chair toward him and rolled her chair from behind her desk to a circular table in the corner. Justin went over to the table and they both sat.

“So, I don’t think this needs to take long,” said Justin. “First, I want to apologize for what happened over the weekend. I misunderstood what you wanted at first and so we were talking about different things. I was already upset because of some things my kids were doing, and I let that get into what I wrote to you. I shouldn’t have said what I did and I’m sorry.”
“Yeah, you aren’t normally like that,” Kaya said. “I wondered if something was wrong. It didn’t seem like you.”
“It wasn’t. You aren’t responsible for my feelings, and you were just doing what Ariel asked you to do with the Penske file. So I apologize.”
“Apology accepted.”
Justin looked at Kaya, and she looked back. For a moment neither spoke.
“Uh . . . do you want to say anything to me?” said Justin.
“Like what?”
“Well—I mean, I was rude and I shouldn’t have been. But you said some rude things too.”
“You think so?”
“I mean, yeah, I do think so. Do you not?”
“Well, you’d made me upset. I was just reacting.”
“But you reacted rudely.”
“That isn’t how I see it, Justin.”
“Uh-huh,” he said, folding his arms. “Well, I guess you’ve made your stance pretty clear on that, then.”
“I’m hoping our email exchange will go a lot more smoothly next time,” said Kaya.
“Yeah . . . yeah, I am too.”
“Great work on the Penske stuff, by the way. The firm’s going to love it. You saw the predictions for the account, but I think even those numbers are conservative.”
“What? Yeah, the numbers,” said Justin, still annoyed. “I’m sure they’ll be fine. It is what it is.”
“What it is is a great account! I’m so glad we get to work together. You’re a great colleague.”
“You are too, Kaya,” Justin said without looking up. He was gathering the things he’d brought. “Good meeting. I’m glad we had it.”
“It feels nice to clear the air, doesn’t it?”
“Definitely,” said Justin, almost running out the door. “See you later.”
“Have a great afternoon!” said Kaya.
Justin was grumbling to himself on the way back to his cubicle. “First the kids, then lunch, now this,” he said, shaking his head.
“Hi, Justin!” said a coworker from a nearby cube, waving and smiling.
“Shup up, Jerry!” said Justin, sitting down at his desk. His phone clattered on the floor.

section.title: What Is Communication?
section.para: The story of Justin and Kaya is an example of communication in a business environment. They’re work colleagues, assigned to the same projects, and they see each other frequently. They’ve been working a lot and are both sending emails on Saturdays while expecting fast responses. Other things in their lives are forcing them to add the weekend work on top of everything else, which isn’t always easy.
So Justin and Kaya are communicating—or at least trying to. But what is communication, exactly? Let’s look at a few ways to understand it.

One way is that communication is languageA set of symbols used to share meanings.. Language is a set of symbols used to share meanings. Some symbols are sounds, like when we say words, while others are written, like when we write a message. Languages are also governed by sets of rules. The rules tell us lots of things, like how to form the symbols (“i before e except after c”), how to connect symbols to each other (sentences always have verbs), and how to receive symbols (the word “compress” means one thing if someone emphasizes the first syllable, and another thing if they emphasize the second).

Different languages have different sets of rules, and rules can differ even within a language. English is very different from Chinese, but American English is different even from British English, and English of the West Virginia backcountry isn’t the same as the English of the California coast. Different communities make their own rules.

So there’s no doubt we use language to communicate. Justin and Kaya do it a lot in their story—they used written language in their emails and spoken language in their meeting. But communication must go far beyond spoken and written languages. Think of everything Justin communicates to Kaya with his apology, and everything she communicates back to him by refusing to apologize herself. None of that content is in the words they say or write, but it’s there all the same, and it has a massive impact on how they experience their interaction.

A second way to understand communication, then, is as the sending and receiving of informationAny meaning sent or received by someone.. In human interactions, information is any meaning sent or received by someone. We sometimes call a bit of information a messageA piece of information.. During their meeting, Justin and Kaya both send and receive a great deal of information—they share their meanings with each other in what they say but also in things like where they sit and how fast they speak. Even Kaya’s locked door sends a message, communicating a particular piece of information to anyone who wants to enter.

One of the most important things we’ll learn in this course is that we are all constantly sending messages—everything we do communicates something to the people around us, even when we don’t intend to be communicating. In other words, Kaya’s locked door sends a message to her coworkers, even if she locks it just because it makes her feel comfortable. She has a reason for her action, but the action still communicates information, and that information may not have the meaning Kaya hopes.

We should also pay attention to how people receive our meaning. In fact, instead of “receive,” it might be better to say that we “interpret” messages. Receiving something can be a passive action, requiring no thought or effort on our part. But interpreting is an active process—we, as receivers of information, help to construct the meaning. When someone communicates with us, we use our background knowledge, our relationships, and our goals to understand what they mean. Communication is never just a one-way street—it’s always an exchange in which two people create meaning together. We’ll talk about this point a lot, including when we learn about giving effective business presentations.

We’re still not quite finished with defining communication, though. It’s the sending and interpreting of information, but since everyone does that all the time, we need to restrict our definition a bit more. In this course, therefore, we’ll define communicationSending and interpreting information in a particular context. as sending and interpreting information in a particular context. The contextThe circumstances in which people communicate. is the circumstances in which people communicate. A context might include a place, like Kaya’s office—but it always includes the purposes and goals people have in communicating, the rules governing their social interactions, the relationships they have, and everything else that might affect how they send and interpret information.

A context gives us many of the rules we use to interpret messages. For example, in Justin and Kaya’s story, Kaya works in an office while Justin has a cubicle. We don’t know for sure, but from those facts it seems that Kaya outranks Justin or has some managerial role over him. That part of their relationship is essential to the context, and may help explain why Justin kept his frustration to himself during their meeting.

Communication—the sending and interpreting of information in a particular context—is everywhere. It seems simple at first, but things get complicated fast when we realize just how many factors influence the messages we send and what we mean.

For some people, many of those factors come from their workplace and professional environments, and that’s why we can study business communication in the first place. We’ll focus on those aspects of communication next.

section.title: What Is Business Communication?
section.para: We’ve defined communication as the sending and interpreting of information in a particular context. With only a slight modification we can also define business communication. Business communicationThe sending and interpreting of information in a business-related context. is the sending and interpreting of information in a business-related context. There are many business-related contexts, so that category is pretty broad. We won’t include things like how customers react to advertisements on social media, because our focus is on how business professionals themselves can communicate successfully. But that’s still a broad category, and that’s how we want it. As this course will show, all of our actions as professionals can count as communication, and making sure we’re communicating the right messages is essential to success in any role in our organizations.

Business communication is about learning and mastering the rules that lead to successful communication in a business context. What makes for a great job interview, for example? That will require communication of a very particular kind. What about a good presentation at a board meeting? A successful salary negotiation? A positive instance of conflict resolution? All these circumstances and many others call for expertise and skill with communicating in a business context. We’ll be gaining that expertise and developing that skill in this course.

section.title: The Purpose of Business Communication
section.para: Every case of communication has a particular purpose. The immediate purpose is to send or interpret a message, but since all communication takes place within a larger context, each case of communication supports larger purposes as well. Justin and Kaya have the immediate purpose of resolving their misunderstanding from the weekend, but they also want to help their team grow their account, which in the end will make their firm more successful.

Or imagine another business communication task: informing your organization’s employees about a harassment training seminar. Suppose the organization has contracted with an outside company to run the seminars. You work in human resources, and your job is to tell the employees about the seminars and sign them up for one of three seminar times. Your direct purpose is to put their names on a list and get them into a room at a specific time, but the real goal of your communication is to improve your workplace culture and make people feel safer and more comfortable at work. That purpose, in turn, contributes to still other purposes.

The larger purposes behind our communication activities come from our job descriptions, our industry, our company, and so on. There is something that unites all these purposes, however: they all contribute both to our own success, and to the success of our organizations. In fact, it isn’t an exaggeration to say that the ultimate purpose of business communication is to drive the success of individual professionals as well as of companies. Modern business practices are more collaborative than ever—in most fields and in most positions, the days of being able to show up to an office and work a full day mostly by yourself are long gone.

Instead, employers demand the ability to work in teams and to flexibly adapt strategies to fast-changing market conditions. More than anything, these skills require communication: can you grasp the essential features of a new product or new customer base to share with your firm’s marketing team? Can you persuade operations that the lighting on the showroom floor isn’t just a facilities issue, but also makes a difference to sales? Can you deliver a graceful and engaging presentation, custom built for a new potential client, to explain why the greater cost—which you have no control over—is worth the money? And after you’ve done all this, can you ask your manager for a well-deserved raise as a reward for your communication skills?

If you can, the benefits to you and your organization will be enormous. You’ll accomplish not only the more immediate purposes of your communications but the larger ones as well, and you’ll refine skills that are constantly in demand and that, thanks now to the internet and other facts of the contemporary business world, will never lose their relevance.

As we learn how to carry out these purposes, we’ll discover that our success in business communication depends primarily on how well we are able to select a communication method appropriate to a particular circumstance. With so many ways to share information, we can’t expect one way to be the best all the time. The best method is not the one we like the most or are most proficient at, but the one that best carries our intended meaning and best delivers it to an audience whose needs and preferences we’re already familiar with.

Since audiences and needs can change, we’ll focus much of our course on how to discern the factors that help us select the correct communication method, given what we know about our situation. We’ll then be able to clearly define the purpose of our communication and understand why the method we’ve chosen, rather than some other one, is right for our task.
The purpose of business communication is business success. So how do we get there? What are our tools? Let’s take a look at those next.

section.title: The Means of Business Communication
section.para: If the purpose of business communication is what we want to accomplish when we communicate, then the means are how we do it. And we’ve never had more ways to send messages: social media, internet ads, billboards, press releases, intraoffice memos, Slack channels, and meetings are all now totally viable ways of sharing information; and that’s not even close to a complete list. The means and methods seem boundless.

In this course we’ll look at the most common and useful means to master for business communication. In the next section, for example, we’ll examine some common business documents and how they’re used, with advice about when they’re the right choice for what you want to share. But among those details we should take care not to lose the overarching point, perhaps the most important thing we could learn about business communication: that everything is communication.

Everything is communication. This saying doesn’t mean that every activity we perform is a communication activity, or that communication is the only thing that matters in business. What the saying means is that everything we do sends a message, whether we intend to or not. In life and certainly in business, we’re always communicating information; we’re always sending signals, and other people may always be interpreting those signals. Even when the message we’re sending is as simple as “I’m choosing to work on this task, rather than that one,” we cannot help but communicate to others something about our priorities and goals.

Let’s elaborate on the idea that everything is communication by returning to the example of Justin and Kaya, from the start of this topic. The obvious examples of communication in that story come from what Justin and Kaya say to each other. Less obvious but still clear examples of communication include Kaya’s refusal to apologize, her compliments about the Justin’s work after her refusal, and Justin’s body language when he leaves Kaya’s office. With all of these actions Justin and Kaya are sending unmistakable messages to each other, and most people won’t have any trouble picking them up. Everything is communication—and with everything they’re doing, they’re communicating information to others.

The story also contains much less noticeable cases of communication, however, and it’s in those cases that we see the value of the idea that everything is communication. Consider the following parts of the story, and think about what message each would be sending, positive or negative, if they took place in a real office:

listitem.para: The messy kitchen. The office kitchen was a mess when Justin went to prepare lunch, so whoever ate before him left it that way and didn’t clean up.
The locked door. Justin arrived to Kaya’s office on time and tried to go on, but she had locked the door.
The circular table. Kaya chose to meet with Justin at a circular table in the corner of her office, rather than from behind her desk, so that they’d both be sitting at the same table.
The cubicles. Justin works at a cubicle in a large office, and has at least one other coworker, Jerry, who works in one too.

section.para: Each of these parts of the story occurs within a certain context and tells us about that context and the people working in it. Take Kaya’s locked door. She’s got an office and so can shut her door, and leaving the door closed is one thing, since she might be trying to concentrate or have a video call. But what is she telling people by locking her door? The message is something like, “I’ll see you when I’m ready, and not before.” Anyone trying to speak to her in person about something would receive this message loud and clear, and they would understand that she doesn’t wish to be bothered for almost anything.

The locked door sends a fairly negative message. But now take the circular table in Kaya’s office. She could meet with Justin while sitting behind her desk, and that would send a message—of her superiority, almost as though she sits in judgment. But Kaya doesn’t do that. Instead she meets at a table where they both sit together without a massive barrier between them. Although Kaya may make some mistakes in the resulting conversation, she sends a positive, welcoming message in the way she arranges the space in which communication will happen.

From this short story, we were able to extract four examples of business communication that have nothing at all to do with spoken or written language. And we may not have covered them all! Factors like these are often in the background, but they’re still there; and without words they communicate just as clearly as if we’d printed the messages and hung them on posters over the doorway.

In this course we’ll have many chances to examine particular means of business communication, like emails, job interviews, and all-hands meetings. We’ll study the rules that govern their use and that can lead to success. But these particular means are only part of a much wider network of human communication where everything, at least potentially, can become a means to deliver a message. Everything—from how we talk, to who sits where, to the furniture, to the free drinks in the fridge—communicates a message about our relationships, values, and priorities.

Everything is communication. It might scare us at first, but we’ll learn that the idea can become empowering when we take control of how we communicate and what information we’re choosing to send. With business communication, we’re in the driver’s seat, and we get to make all the most important choices for what our actions say about us and how they do it.

section.title: Common Business Documents and Their Uses
section.para: “Communication” is related to the word “community,” and different business communities set the standards for how they approach communication. This includes business documents. We’ll finish our first topic with a discussion of some common business documents and their use. Depending on when and where you’ve worked in the past, some of these will be familiar, while others may not. We’ll talk about the basics here to get you familiar enough that you can recognize and use them without any trouble. These points will be helpful for many circumstances, but it’s up to us to learn to recognize exactly when and how they apply, and when they don’t.

First, some words of advice about business documents. In previous generations—and by that we mean prior to the widespread adoption of computers and the internet—business documents used to have much more standard formats and well-defined uses. This isn’t really the case any longer. Depending on the employer, for example, we wouldn’t now consider it unusual to receive a job offer via text message, when in the past an organization would have communicated that same offer in a mailed letter on official stationery. The ease of creating and modifying documents by computer, along with the general informalization of work practices brought about by the internet, have caused rapid changes in how business documents are used and which ones are thought to be acceptable for certain purposes.

For that reason, all the guidance in this section comes with the following warning: it depends on where you are, and who you’re communicating with. An email is by far the most common business document, but it’s only possible to give very general instructions about appropriate ways to write and use that document. Beyond those general instructions, everything you need to know about email will be determined by how people in your organization and in your field use email. We’ve all received emails written so formally that it’s like the English royal family is coming to visit; on the other hand, who hasn’t gotten an email whose subject line is blank and all it says is “metting in 5”? Both documents are emails, but they serve such different audiences and purposes that they really have nothing in common besides being emails.

A key skill we’ll develop in this course is the ability to discern the conventions, or rules, that people around you are following in their communications. Once we understand those conventions, we can mold our behavior to fit them and do things the way other people are doing them, rather than trying to enforce the “correct” rules we learned in previous careers or in a business communication course. There are very few universally correct rules for business communication, and apart from things like be clear, avoid offense or harassment, and keep your audience in mind, there might be none. The correct rules are the ones that a situation calls for—and so, while there are general principles of successful communication, the rules you use depend on where you are and who you’re communicating with.

section.title: Résumés and CVs
section.para: The first business document is the résuméA summary of your work experience and qualifications for particular positions.. Sometimes spelled “resume,” a résumé is a summary of your work experience and qualifications for particular positions. In some places outside the US the term “CV” may be more common. CVCurriculum vitae, a Latin phrase meaning “course or span of life; a document similar to a résumé.” stands for curriculum vitae, a Latin phrase meaning “course or span of life.” Some fields inside the US, such as many areas of academia, also call this document a CV.

A résumé or CV gives a brief summary of your education, your professional positions, your qualifications, and relevant skills. The most common practice is to list your most recent position or educational attainment first, along with a brief description of job duties or projects completed. Previous positions then follow, again with the more recent listed first.

The precise format your résumé takes is up to you, but remember that everything is communication. The words on your résumé communicate your experience, but the résumé’s format communicates something about your own personal style and can even indicate whether you understand norms within your field, such as whether résumés are usually short or long.

If you need to create a résumé or are looking to update a current one, the safest bet is to ask a few successful colleagues for copies of theirs to see what they have done. If one strikes you as interesting or attention-grabbing, ask yourself why, and then add that feature to your own. You can also use someone’s résumé to create a templateA skeleton document that you can add your own information and experience to. , or a skeleton of the document, to which you would add your own information and experience. Résumés are generally considered to be public documents, and it isn’t unethical to copy the format of someone’s résumé in order to create your own.

You should never try to pass off someone else’s experience as your own, however, nor should you ever make up experience or education you don’t have. It’s common to describe past work projects in fanciful terms to make your background seem more exciting than it actually is, but dreaming up a college degree you didn’t earn or a management position you didn’t have will likely end in you getting discovered and possibly fired.
Here are some other guidelines for successful résumés:

listitem.para: Don’t be afraid of white space. A résumé chock-full of text from top to bottom suggests that its author isn’t confident enough in their own experience to let a simple description of that experience speak for itself. Boldly state your qualifications and achievements in direct language, and be brave enough to leave it alone after that. In addition, a well-organized résumé with appropriate spacing between lines and sections has more visual appeal and is much easier to read.

The more specific, the better, including numbers. Did you grow your company’s customer base by 50%? Then write that, instead of just that you grew the company’s customer base. Particular facts, project titles, coding languages, dollar values, and other numbers give concrete evidence of your ability. Name them, and avoid vague descriptions that could be true of any other job candidate.

Brag. Your résumé is your professional profile, and it should tell people exactly how much value you will deliver—a lot! A résumé isn’t the time for modesty. Own your accomplishments and communicate them to your audience.

The shorter, the better. If you can clearly and appealingly communicate your most valuable contributions in a single page, then do it. Filling a position requires many employers to sift through hundreds of résumés, and a brief, compelling document will have the widest appeal.

Do what others are doing. Don’t copy others’ experience, but learn from the way they describe it. Do people in your field tend to create résumés with a particular format? Learn that format, and learn to work within those constraints to make yourself stand out.
Don’t lie. We mentioned this above, but it’s worth repeating. Exaggerated descriptions of boring work might be expected, but lying could have serious consequences.

section.para: As before, we should take all these guidelines in the context of our particular organization, field, or profession. Long CVs are the norm in academia, for example, and tech- or code-oriented résumés might include things like links to GitHub repositories or other projects. The exact content and format of your résumé depends on where you are and who you’re communicating with. Audience expectations regarding these documents will trump almost any general guideline given here or elsewhere.

section.title: Email
section.para: Without question, the most common document in contemporary business practice is the email. Emails are easy and quick to write, they cost nothing to send, they transmit fast, and they leave a permanent record. Almost everything about them is customizable—besides having a recipient, a subject line, and a place for the rest of the text, everything about them can be changed. Fonts, colors, images, videos, links, and other things are all whatever you want them to be in an email.

This almost infinite flexibility means, however, that rules for email use are even more discipline- and community-dependent than those for résumés. What’s more, the relationship you have to an organization or to the recipient of the email matters a great deal, and might even be the only relevant factor in determining the format and formality of your email communication: when you know someone well, an email can be just a few words, all misspelled; when you don’t know someone at all, you have to take a completely different approach.

As for résumés, there is a safe and worry-free way to handle email communication, regardless of the circumstances. The first step is to use the template below, which strikes a middle ground between too informal and excessively formal:

imagedata.alt: An email template: the font is a standard sans serif typeface; the opening line is a greeting of Dear Mr/Mrs. Smith. After the greeting there are four paragraphs. The first introduces the writer of the email. The second says why you are writing. The third contains any request for action or follow-up on the part of the recipient. The fourth thanks the recipient for their time and points to something in the future. Following those four paragraphs is a farewell.

section.para: Don’t worry about the content of this email—the important thing is how it’s set up and what each part accomplishes. First, the font is a standard sans serif typeface that’s easy to read. The default font setting on Gmail is similar to this one, and it works well in many circumstances. Second, a greeting of “Dear ______” is a neutral, all-purpose way of beginning an email to any recipient.

After the greeting there are four paragraphs. The first introduces you, the writer of the email. The second says why you’re writing. The third contains any request for action or follow-up on the part of the recipient. The fourth thanks the recipient for their time and points to something in the future.
Following those four paragraphs is a farewell. “Sincerely” is a good neutral way to finish, and so are “Best” or “All the best.”

So the first step in our safe and worry-free way to communicate via email is to open an email communication with this template. Assuming the recipient responds, the second step is then to modify the tone or structure of future emails based on their reply. Are they more informal when writing back? Then feel free to be a little more informal. Do they maintain or even raise the level of formality? You can follow along. The beauty of this template is that it won’t be considered too laid-back for someone who prefers formality, but it won’t seem stilted to someone who’s more relaxed.

Generally speaking, in email communications, it is the recipient that sets the tone of the exchange. Most of the time it’s the recipient that is being asked to read, reply, or do something as a result of an email, and so it’s good to follow their lead. But be sure to maintain appropriate professional distance—if you don’t already have a relationship with someone, keeping your tone and format one step more formal than your recipient’s is a safe practice too.

Note also that all four of these paragraphs are short. In general, email is a bad medium for communicating large amounts of important information—not because the medium itself is ill-suited for it, but because people just aren’t used to having large amounts of important information arrive via email. Most people scan and filter emails quickly, looking for only the highest-priority items and skimming or ignoring everything else. Our email communications will be more successful when we remember how people interact with their inboxes: fast and without paying too much attention.
You’ll pretty much never go wrong by starting with this template, modifying it for your particular situation, and then following your recipient’s lead in your future communication.

When you have a spare moment, glance through your inbox and see what emails you’ve received lately. Which ones were most successful in getting you to read and respond, and why? Which were the easiest to understand? Which annoyed or angered you? Imitate the good practices, and avoid the bad ones.

section.title: Office Memos and Reports
section.para: The final documents we’ll cover are office memos, or “memoranda,” and reports. Our discussion will be short because the landscape for these business documents has changed so much in the past two decades. There are thousands of organizations that have never sent a memo and multiple generations of employees who have never received one, much less read one. For the most part, the memo, as well as its longer counterpart, the report, have been replaced by emails and email attachments.

Memos and reports, where they still exist, tend to be written in more formal, official language, since for many years they were considered to be the official form of communication within offices. Memos often have the word “MEMORANDUM” at the top, followed by the name of the recipient, the name of the sender, and the date. The current interface for email communication is a deliberate imitation of this common memo format.

One clear indication of the long-term destiny of the memo is the space allotted to it in business communication textbooks. Hartley and Bruckmann’s 2002 Business Communication devotes four pages to the memo and gives example structures. Hartley, Knapton, and Marriott’s 2023 Professional and Business Communication, on the other hand, gives one-third of a page.

If it becomes necessary for you to write a memo or other official report, find out as much as you can from your organization about the format you should follow. If you aren’t sure, you could work with the following template as a base.

section.title: The Simple Memo Framework
section.para: In business environments, you will probably encounter many different templates for internal communication. Some organizations, for example, have rigid forms for project updates, while others just use open-ended email formats. But relying on a pre-formatted template is not enough to guarantee effective communication. Whether you are writing a memo from scratch or working with existing text, you need a mental framework to organize your thoughts.

Though formatting can change from company to company, the core of a strong business memo remains constant. The following three-part framework will help your message stay on track, and it’s flexible enough to fit into many other formats.

listitem.para: Purpose (The “why”): Never force your audience to guess why they received a document. The very first section of your memo should state the context and the reason for writing. Are you requesting authorization for a new expenditure? Are you summarizing the results of a client meeting, or clarifying a change in HR policy? By clearly stating the purpose at the beginning, you allow the reader to understand why they’re being contacted in the first place.

Key Message (The “what”): Business writing front-loads the main point—that is, it gives the most important point right away, with no buildup. Think of it this way: If your audience reads only the first paragraph of what you send, they should still walk away knowing the most important information. Don’t bury the results of a report or the final decision of a meeting in the last paragraph. Put the bottom line up front.

Action Required (The “next steps”): Effective business communication drives action. Conclude your memo by stating what needs to happen next. Avoid vague phrases like “Thoughts?” or “Just let me know.” Instead, be specific about who needs to do what, and by when. For example, you might say, “Please review the attached budget and reply with your approval by 5:00 p.m. on Friday.” On the other hand, if no action is required, you can make that clear by saying that the memo is “for informational purposes only.”

section.title: A Note on Tone
section.para: The clear structure of a simple memo framework will make it more likely that your message gets read, but the tone determines much more than that. Memos are often official records of business decisions, and so they may be referenced months or years later. Their tone should therefore be professional, objective, and direct.
We’ll talk about tone a great deal later on in this course. For now, we’ll just note that achieving the right tone is often a balancing act. Consider the following guidance:
Professional, not stiff: You want to sound competent and serious, but not robotic or archaic. Avoid using fancy buzzwords, “legalese,” or overly complex words where simple ones will do.

Objective, not emotional: Business memos should focus on facts and outcomes, not personal feelings. Avoid using highly charged adjectives (like “disastrous” instead of “unsuccessful,” “appalling” instead of “unsatisfactory,” or “shocking” instead of “unexpected”), and stay away from things like multiple exclamation points or conversational slang.
Direct, not rude: In business, being concise is a virtue. Getting straight to the point respects your audience’s time. But brevity should not come at the cost of politeness.

As we will see next, finding this balance can be difficult for generative AI tools, which can sometimes veer into being too casual or, conversely, into sounding uncomfortably robotic. Let’s take a look at some examples.

important.title: AI Skills Development
important.para: To illustrate the difference between a raw AI draft and a polished professional document, let’s look at a common workplace scenario. A manager needs to announce that the team will be starting to use new time-tracking software next week. The team has never tracked hours before, so for some this may be a sensitive issue.

Below are two versions of a memo to make this announcement. The first was generated by an AI tool with the prompt, “Write a memo telling the team they need to use the new TimeKeeper software starting Monday.” The second is a human-refined version using the guidelines of the simple memo framework we just discussed. As you read them, compare them in terms of purpose, key message, action, and tone, as well as any other features you notice.

sidebar.para: To: All Staff
From: Management
Date: October 8
Subject: Implementation of TimeKeeper Software

We are absolutely thrilled to announce that starting this Monday, the company will be undergoing a digital transformation by implementing the incredible TimeKeeper software! This is a fascinating opportunity for everyone to log their minutes with extreme precision.

It is imperative that all employees cease their current habits and strictly adhere to the new logging protocols immediately. Failure to utilize the system will result in disastrous data gaps. We hope you are as excited as we are to track every moment of your productivity! We strive to be a data-driven company, after all. Please ensure you have an account created soon.
To: All Staff
From: Management
Date: October 8
Subject: Action Required—New Time-Tracking Process Begins Monday

To make our client billing more accurate, we are moving to a new time-tracking system, TimeKeeper, effective Monday, October 15. We know that this is a big change for our team, and we want to make the transition as reasonable and as seamless as possible.

Starting next week, all staff members should create their accounts and log their hours in TimeKeeper. The previous manual spreadsheet system will be retired on Friday. Management will be available for training all this week, so stop by for help.
Download the TimeKeeper app to your desktop by 5:00 p.m. this Friday.
Watch the 5-minute tutorial video (link attached).
Log your first entry by 10:00 a.m. on Monday, October 15.

section.title: Comparing the AI- and Human-Written Memos
section.para: Using our simple memo framework, we can clearly see why the AI draft fails and the human version succeeds. Here are some specifics:

Tone alignment. The AI draft is tone-deaf. It describes a mandatory administrative chore as “fascinating” and talks about being “thrilled.” This false enthusiasm will come across as insincere to most people. The tone then swings wildly to being aggressive (“strictly adhere,” “disastrous”). The human version stays objective while recognizing possible difficulties.

Clarity of action. The AI draft says “ensure you have an account created soon” (AI-written text loves to “ensure” things). This is vague. Does “soon” mean today or next week? The human version gives a specific deadline, 5:00 p.m. Friday, which is much easier to work with.
Purpose. The AI buried the reason for the change in buzzwords about “digital transformation.” The human version stated the purpose clearly up front: “To make our client billing more accurate.”

From these comparisons and others you might have made, we can see that AI is a powerful tool for generating text quickly—but it lacks the social intelligence to understand how a message will be received by a real audience. AI can provide a useful start on many projects, but make sure that you’re always using your own judgment to refine the details and to communicate on a human level.
We’ll speak more about many of these issues later in the course.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: In the opening topic of our course we introduced the idea that everything is communication. This idea tells us that every part of our behavior communicates information to other people, including when we don’t intend it and even when we don’t want it. Far from being something scary, however, the knowledge that everything is communication puts the power in our hands to make choices about what and how we want to communicate. The purpose of this course is to give you the tools to use that power successfully in your professional life.

Before that, though, we need more knowledge and more experience, and that’s what we’ll get in this topic. Each section is a primer on some of the foundational things we need to know for successful communication. You’ll notice that a lot of the things we cover have nothing to do with writing, speaking, or other behaviors we normally associate with communication. That’s because so many of the most important factors of communication are not the messages nor even the means to send the messages, but instead belong to the context of communication or the emotions and beliefs of the audience. Our success requires understanding those factors.

And although we’ll focus on their application to business, the subjects in this topic could appear in any book about communication in any field, because they’re so broad. The general principles of successful communication apply to all areas of human interaction. Here and in later topics we’ll be refining and specifying those principles for business contexts.
The basic principles of interpersonal communication stem from basic parts of our human nature, so let’s take a look at that nature and its relation to communication next.

section.title: Emotional Intelligence
section.para: Humans are emotional creatures. We mark the highest moments of our lives as the times of most exquisite joy, and the lowest moments as those of deepest sorrow. In between we daily navigate a forest of other emotions, ranging from those that excite and energize to those that depress and discourage. Powerful emotions can drive us to do things we’d never do otherwise, and a lack of emotion sucks the flavor from life. At any given moment we’re feeling something, even an absence of other feelings, and we can usually say whether we want that feeling to continue or we’d like to feel something else instead.

Given these facts of human nature, two major factors in interpersonal communication are reading and reacting to the emotions of others, and managing our own emotions. An emotionA feeling usually accompanied by characteristic thoughts and tendencies to act. is a feeling usually accompanied by characteristic thoughts and tendencies to act.Goleman defines emotion very similarly: “A feeling and its distinctive thoughts, psychological and biological states, and range of propensities to act.” Goleman, D. (2006). Emotional intelligence. Bantam Books, p. 289. There are many emotions, and our language is full of words to describe them, like rage, shock, guilt, and love. We do sometimes experience these feelings totally by themselves. But as our definition suggests, emotions often carry with them certain thoughts, like “I want to spend more time with this person” (love), or certain tendencies to act, like avoiding talking to someone after you’ve offended them (guilt).

Based on how we understand facial cues, we sometimes say there are four basic emotionsThe four emotions that most if not all other emotions stem from: fear, anger, sadness, and enjoyment.: fear, anger, sadness, and enjoyment. Perhaps every other emotion does come from one of those four, but even if not, some emotions tend to appear with others, like happiness and excitement or sadness and lethargy. We understand the relationships between emotions because of our own experience.

Many emotions involve our relationships with other people: we love someone, get angry at what they’ve done, feel comfort when they console us, and become annoyed when they don’t listen. Often, maintaining successful relationships comes down to our ability to understand the emotions of others and share and manage our own. In other words, it comes down to communicating about emotions, and for that reason we need a framework to help us think about how.

That framework is emotional intelligence Defined by Peter Salovey and John D. Mayer as "the ability to monitor one’s own and others’ feelings and emotions, to discriminate among them and to use this information to guide one’s thinking and actions.". The term, often abbreviated EI, entered the language of business communication in 1990 and has since spread into many fields and professions. Salovey, P., & Mayer, J. D. (1990, March). Emotional intelligence. Imagination, Cognition, and Personality, 9(3), p. 185–211. . EI is “the ability to monitor one’s own and others’ feelings and emotions, to discriminate among them and to use this information to guide one’s thinking and actions.”Salovey, P. & Mayer, J. D. (1989). Emotional intelligence. Imagination, Cognition and Personality, 9(3), 185–211. EI isn’t just about recognizing the emotions we and others are feeling; it’s about using that information within a larger context to communicate and act successfully.
Later developments of EI divide it into five domains:Goleman, D. (2006). Emotional Intelligence. Bantam Books.

listitem.para: Knowing one’s emotions
Managing emotions
Motivating oneself
Recognizing emotions in others
Handling relationships

section.para: Skill in each domain is important for communication. If we don’t realize we’re angry, then we may begin a conversation that’s guaranteed to end badly because we’re not emotionally prepared for it; not understanding our own bodily rhythms throughout the day may lead us to procrastinate important projects, because we never end up working on them when we have the most energy. Likewise, failing to recognize the emotions of others means we’re flying blind in our interactions with them, since we’ll have no way to predict how our words and actions might affect them.

Emotions are an inescapable part of any context for communication. The better we perceive them, the better we can tailor our reactions to meet the needs of those we’re communicating with. The information we gather about emotion, from other people and from the context, is called affective informationInformation we gather about emotion from other people and from context.. Since everything is communication, we send the world messages full of affective information all the time: facial expressions are obvious sources, but more subtle sources like clothing, posture, and steady eye contact also send messages.

Our ability to understand and use affective information is called emotional literacyOur ability to understand and use affective information. , and we can build toward mastery of emotional intelligence by developing emotional literacy in the five domains listed above.

So what actions can help us achieve emotional literacy in an area where we’re deficient? By far the most significant change we can make to our behavior is to start to pay attention. Most people are so wrapped up in what they are feeling that they forget that other people are currently experiencing emotions just as important as their own. Have you ever taken a moment to think about that? Consider how much your emotions affect what you do and say—then consider that, in this way at least, everyone else is just the same as you are. Their emotions have the same weight in their life that your emotions do in yours. Wouldn’t it therefore be important to take those emotions into account in communicating with them?

Since they’re so often turned inward, most people miss the abundance of affective information other people are offering. That information gives us a window into someone’s mind, but only if we pay enough attention to notice it. Slow down. Watch, and notice the signals others are sending.

The first step toward emotional literacy and mastery of EI, then, is to pay attention to affective information. We discover this information not only in the words someone is saying, but in how their face and body convey those words; we can also learn to draw out greater amounts of it by the way we engage with a person in conversation. The following five techniques are especially useful and can be used in any interaction with anyone:

listitem.para: Maintain eye contact while staying aware of body language. An intense, blinkless stare is perhaps too much, but you’ll miss key information if you often look away. Learn to interpret how someone’s body changes when they say certain things.
Avoid cutting off someone’s speech or even preparing a response as they talk. Both these actions draw our attention away from the information they’re giving us.

Learn to mirror, or restate, the most important parts of what someone said or how it made them feel. MirroringRestating the most important parts of what someone said or how it made them feel. reflects our investment in their words and emotions and discourages us from crafting a response or reacting emotionally ourselves.
Learn to ask follow-up questions about how an idea or experience makes someone feel. These questions invite them to elaborate on their emotions and yield additional affective information.

Remember that most conversations are not competitions. Successful communication, in business or anywhere else, implies that both people feel heard and understood. That success is shared by both people, and conversations aren’t zero-sum games.

section.para: In our next section we’ll discuss how to be a good listener, and the short version is that good listeners pay attention to affective information by doing the five things listed above. They learn how to draw out more information, and they can respond based on what they learn.

While it’s true that some people are naturally better at emotional literacy than others, everyone can develop these skills and reach mastery in each domain of EI. They are skills, which means we improve by practice. Practice cultivating the ability to pay attention to affective information by having conversations while using the five techniques listed above. Learn to view conversations as opportunities to become better communicators.

The next step in developing our emotional literacy is to pay attention to our own emotions, and to begin to notice the patterns of our emotional life. In many moments of the day we can pause to ask ourselves, What am I feeling, and why? Don’t judge your emotions or punish yourself for them; just experience and understand. What place are you in emotionally, and what has led you to that place? Where would you like to go next, and how might you get there?

If you have trouble answering these questions, consider keeping a journal of your emotions and your reflections on them. If you do, you’ll begin to notice patterns in how you feel and in the things that make you feel those ways. Those patterns are affective information about yourself, which is no less valuable in developing emotional literacy. Remember that human interaction is an interplay between two people and their emotions. Learning to understand your emotions and how they lead to certain patterns of action will make you better able to communicate successfully.

The EI framework is a way of thinking about emotions and how they influence our lives. Each emotion is a feeling accompanied by characteristic thoughts and actions, and many necessarily involve other people. Emotions drive our actions and decision-making far more than reasoning or argument do. With mindful attention to the affective information others are offering, you can become more emotionally literate and excel in each domain of emotional intelligence.

section.title: Fundamentals of Interpersonal Communication
section.para: In this section we’ll discuss the fundamentals of interpersonal communication. We can’t treat every aspect of the subject here, but using what we know about communication, context, and emotional intelligence, we can get into many of the most important issues.

The fundamentals we’ll discuss apply to all interpersonal interactions, which means that they apply to any example of communication with other people. We’ll make some specific applications to business contexts here, but future topics will take these fundamentals further and give detailed, business-focused discussions.

Human communication is an ongoing flow of information and other signals between two or more people. The fundamentals of interpersonal communication help us to demonstrate our emotional literacy and take control of that flow. The information flow is always happening, even if we aren’t aware of it. Everything we do affects it, at least potentially. What information will we choose to send, whether verbal, affective, or otherwise? Will we be in control of the information we’re sending? Will we read and react to the information we receive?
We can do all those things, and well, by learning these communication skills.

We’ll organize these fundamentals in a manner developed by communication expert Owen Hargie. We’ve modified Hargie’s system to include additional items specific to business communication. We’ll cover the following ten:

listitem.para: Context
Nonverbal communication
Reinforcing
Reflecting
Questioning
Listening
Explaining
Self-disclosure
Opening and closing
Assertiveness

section.para: Let’s start with context.

section.title: Context
section.para: The first fundamental of interpersonal communication is context. As defined in the previous topic, a context is the set of circumstances in which people communicate. These circumstances will have many features, from things like temperature to the amount of ambient light. But for interpersonal communication, especially in business, the following four aspects of a context are the most important:

listitem.para: Who is the audience. What are the expectations of the person you’re communicating with? What are their needs, and what do they hope to receive from the interaction? What style of communication do they prefer?

What is your relationship to the audience. The three most important relationships are superior-subordinate, coworker-coworker, and customer-client. Because each industry and organization handles these relationships differently, we’ll discuss them in detail later.
What are your purposes and goals. What is the larger purpose of your communication? How do those purposes fit into your own larger goals and the goals of your organization?
Where are you. How does the physical environment determine what communication techniques are most appropriate? How should you modify your approach to take that environment into account?

section.para: Most of the time, contextual factors like these determine what communication approaches will be appropriate for a given interaction. Never forget that communication always happens in a context; there is always more going on than there appears to be.
In addition, these contextual factors can affect some or all of the other fundamentals on our list.

section.title: Nonverbal Communication
section.para: The second fundamental is nonverbal communication. Nonverbal communicationAny aspect of a message that isn’t spoken or written. is any aspect of a message that isn’t spoken or written. Nonverbal communication carries a great deal of affective information, and as we’ve said before, the nonverbal parts of a message are frequently more important than the associated words.
We’ll discuss five parts of nonverbal communication below. For each, ask a trusted mentor or coworker for advice about the information you send with these aspects of your nonverbal communication.

ToneManner of expressing vocal communication. is a crucial part of nonverbal communication. When said with different tones of voice, the same words can have vastly different meanings: imagine someone laughing and sarcastically saying, “I don’t want that” when offered a donut, versus someone screaming those exact words into another person’s face. The words are the same, but the tone is entirely different, and so is the message.

Maintaining a calm tone and adding appropriate emphasis to different parts of a message communicates confidence and reliability. Speaking too quietly, too loudly, or too harshly or gently can all be off-putting.

Eye contactThe stable exchange of looks between two people during an interaction. is the stable exchange of looks between two people during an interaction. For the most part, consistent eye contact communicates attention and interest. Occasional glances away are appropriate, but look away too often and your eyes will be saying “I don’t care” to the person you’re talking to.

Personal spaceThe distance between you and the person or group you are talking to. refers to the distance between you and the person or group you are talking to. Too close and you make people feel uncomfortable; too far and you have to shout. While conventions around personal space may vary by local custom, a distance of three feet or so is a good baseline. If you notice other people backing up when you speak to them, they may be communicating a need for greater personal space.

TouchPhysical contact with someone; the use of physical contact to communicate affection, friendship, support, or other messages. is physical contact with someone, and in interpersonal communication, touch is the use of physical contact to communicate affection, friendship, support, or other messages. Touching at work, however, can also make people feel uncomfortable or even constitute sexual harassment. The safest course of action is to avoid all forms of physical touch beyond a handshake, where that greeting is appropriate.

Many other body movements can communicate affective information—for example, gesturing with your hands can be an important part of effective presentations. We’ll cover some of these other behaviors in later topics.

Other areas of behavior beyond these five belong to nonverbal communication as well. Learning appropriate conventions and practicing appropriate behavior in the areas listed here will fix the most obvious problems with nonverbal communication.

section.title: Reinforcing
section.para: The third fundamental is reinforcing. Reinforcing, or reinforcementThe feedback we give to our communication partners as they speak., is the feedback we give to our communication partners as they speak. This feedback may be verbal, as when we say “I see,” or “Uh-huh,” to communicate that we are listening and to encourage someone to continue; or it may be nonverbal, as when we maintain eye contact and nod as they speak to communicate the same things.

Reinforcement is less about a response to someone’s remark and more about your reaction as they are making the remark. The most appropriate places for reinforcement are in short breaks in someone’s speech, when they pause but haven’t finished speaking. The most common reinforcements are “Uh-huh” and “I see,” but there are many others, including “That makes sense,” “I see what you’re saying,” “Interesting,” and so on. Choose the ones that best fit a particular context, and allow yourself some variation.

The fundamental of reinforcement reminds us that conversation is a flow, an exchange, between two or more people. When we reinforce properly, we participate in that flow and demonstrate to our partners that they’re not just talking to a wall or a robot. Proper reinforcement lets someone else know that we are listening and are invested in what they’re saying.

section.title: Reflecting
section.para: ReflectingResponding to a conversation partner with statements that don’t just acknowledge what the partner has said, but actually restate that content and present it again. is more than reinforcing. Reinforcement requires a stock set of words or phrases to maintain the ongoing communication flow. Reflecting goes beyond reinforcing to include statements that don’t just acknowledge what someone has said, but actually restate that content and present it again to a conversation partner.

The purpose of reflecting is to demonstrate not just that you are listening, but that you’ve actually understood the most important parts of what someone has said. Reflecting is therefore part of mirroring, which we discussed as part of emotional intelligence. Mirroring and reflecting demonstrate our investment in someone’s words and emotions and discourages us from crafting a response or reacting emotionally ourselves. By doing these things, we show our understanding and thereby communicate that we are someone who cares. We thus encourage our conversation partner to continue communicating and being open by sharing verbal, affective, and other kinds of information.

Reflecting also has the benefit of drawing our attention away from responding immediately to what is said. By focusing on reflecting, we remain mindful of what someone is saying, rather than what we wish to add in reply.

section.title: Questioning
section.para: The fifth fundamental of interpersonal communication is questioningAsking topical, sensitive, and thoughtful questions to probe a communication partner for more information.. Questioning is our ability to ask topical, sensitive, and thoughtful questions to probe a communication partner for more information. Some general questions, such as “And how do you feel about that?” or “What can I do to help?” can serve more of a reinforcing or reflecting role, but they can also prompt the deeper sharing of information; other more specific questions, like “And what specific needs do you feel your accounting office is currently facing?” help direct the conversation toward the fulfillment of some larger purpose.

Of all the fundamentals of interpersonal interaction, questioning is one of the only ones that we can’t immediately improve by making small, consistent changes to our behavior. Learning to ask, “How do you feel about that?” can add significant depth to any communication; but good questions usually require much more specificity and will reveal not only that you are listening but that you are thinking through the implications of what someone is saying.

You can improve this skill by noticing questions that seem good to you, either ones you’re asked or ones you hear. Ask yourself, what makes that question a good one? How could someone know to ask it? Can you modify a version of the question to ask in other contexts?

Especially in business, there are some topics we should refrain from asking about—particularly questions about private matters. Questions we’ll want to avoid include “Are you pregnant?”, “I heard you arguing with your spouse on the phone at lunch, is everything all right?”, and “Are you alone a lot at home?” Questions like these can make someone feel immediately uncomfortable and communicate an inappropriate level of interest in someone else, or an interest in things that have nothing to do with a business context.

The wrong question can torpedo an otherwise promising interaction, while the right one can take it to new heights. Learn to understand the context and purpose of each interaction to develop the skill of asking useful, appropriate questions.

section.title: Listening
section.para: All five of the previous fundamentals for interpersonal communication rely on the sixth, which is listeningThe hearing and attention you give to what someone else is saying.. In communication, listening is the hearing and attention you give to what someone else is saying. It is more than passively receiving information; to listen effectively, you must actively participate in the flow of communication.

Since listening underlies the previous fundamentals, we can become better listeners by becoming more proficient at handling issues of context and nonverbal communication, and at reinforcing, reflecting, and questioning. In addition to those skills, we can become better listeners by avoiding the tendency to craft a reply to someone while they are still talking. The other fundamentals will help get rid of that tendency, but it’s difficult when we believe someone is wrong or they are otherwise provoking an emotional reaction in us, either intentionally or unintentionally.

Managing those tendencies in ourselves, however, is part of the challenge of interpersonal communication. The more we can practice and improve, the better we’ll be, and we’ll cultivate listening skills that will make others seek us out as experienced and valuable communicators.

section.title: Explaining
section.para: We’ve now reached the seventh of our ten fundamentals of interpersonal communication. That seventh is explainingClearly communicating of our own opinions, knowledge, and feelings., or the clear communication of our own opinions, knowledge, and feelings.

You may have noticed that explaining is also the first of the fundamentals that requires us to speak at length about our own views. This is intentional. A significant part of our success as business communicators lies in the ability to override our natural tendency to make ourselves the focus of an interaction. By focusing on the needs of others and practicing these fundamentals, we’ll spend most of our time listening and reinforcing and reflecting and questioning, which will yield more information and mark us as skilled communicators that others wish to be around.

When the flow of some communication requires us to explain what we believe or feel, we should do so in clear statements, without hyperbole or unnecessary repetition. We need not apologize for sincere, informed beliefs or appropriate emotional reactions, and we have a right to expect that others will be reasonable listeners when we explain.

Along with questioning, explaining is another fundamental that we can only improve substantially with significant and sometimes challenging practice. Styles of explanation vary greatly from person to person, and our capacity to understand what we think and feel is determined by our family background, previous experience with explaining, and the care with which we believe others will receive what we communicate.
The same is true for the next fundamental, which builds on explaining: self-disclosure.

section.title: Self-disclosure
section.para: The eighth of our ten fundamentals is self-disclosureThe gradual revealing of personal information across time to initiate, deepen, or maintain a relationship.. Self-disclosure is the gradual revealing of personal information across time to initiate, deepen, or maintain a relationship. Self-disclosure occurs in intimate family relationships, as when we come to know our romantic partners better by spending time with them and learning what they have to say about themselves. But it occurs in other kinds of relationships as well, including business relationships.

Self-disclosure allows us to express thoughts and feelings about ourselves that are important to us and allows others to come to know us better. This disclosure is common in an interview environment, for example, where you may describe yourself and your career goals in order for an interviewer to assess whether you fit in a particular position. Certain kinds of work and professional projects require spending a lot of time with people, and by self-disclosure those people can come to know each other better. The professional benefits are significant, as they begin to understand how best to use the resources available to resolve specific problems. There are also personal benefits, such as a more enjoyable experience at work.

Self-disclosure involves explaining but differs from it in two main ways. First, explaining usually has a much more limited scope and usually concerns the communication of specific pieces of information, such as a particular idea or feeling. Self-disclosure is broader and takes place over a longer period. Second, the primary purpose of explaining is to send a certain message or communicate a certain meaning to someone. Self-disclosure, on the other hand, is more about coming to know who a person is.

The proper use of self-disclosure, including in our reception of the self-disclosure of others, requires a high degree of emotional intelligence. To do it well, we need emotional literacy and an awareness of how we are sending and receiving affective information.

section.title: Opening and Closing
section.para: As fundamentals of interpersonal communication, openingThe way we begin interactions. and closingThe way we end interactions. refer to the ways we begin and end interactions, respectively. A clear beginning to an interaction signals your interest and suggests you have a clear purpose in speaking to someone. A clear ending is a show of respect for your conversation partner and suggests that your own time is valuable as well.

On the other hand, think about how quickly an interaction can sour when it’s gone on too long. We start to feel awkward and self-conscious, and our opinion of the person we’re interacting with may change as well. We feel uncomfortable and want the interaction to stop but may not know how to make it happen. It’s not a fun experience.

Learn to develop a sense for how interactions flow through different stages: an opening, an initial exchange of greetings, the exchange of more significant information, and a natural end. When the natural end comes, it is best to close the interaction. You will not make a better impression or change someone’s mind by overstaying your welcome.

Of all the ten fundamentals of interpersonal communication, opening and closing are some of those we can most easily improve by learning stock techniques for initiating conversations and finishing them. Memorizing a few openers along with ways of gracefully exiting an interaction will allow you to make the time you do spend with others more powerful.

section.title: Assertiveness
section.para: The tenth and final fundamental is assertivenessThe attitude with which we engage in the other nine fundamentals of communication.. Assertiveness is the attitude with which we engage in the other nine fundamentals. To be assertive is to have a strong sense of self and to be willing to present your needs and desires as legitimate without apologizing for them. It involves a respect for yourself and an expectation of respectful treatment by others.

Assertiveness is not being overbearing, disrespectful, or rude—there is a difference between owning your opinions, which is assertive, and shoving them down someone’s throat, which is overbearing and rude.
You are a person and a member of a professional community, and you deserve respect for both. Carry that respect with you in your interactions with others, and they will respect you back.

section.title: Fundamentals of Interpersonal Communication Wrap-up
section.para: In this section we’ve covered ten fundamentals of interpersonal communication. These aren’t necessarily the only ten, but they’re ten of the most important, and improvement in any of these areas will make a tangible difference in your professional life.

While the fundamentals vary in the level of effort it takes to improve them—from opening and closing, which takes little, to self-disclosure, which can take a lifetime—they are all identical in that we improve on them through practice. It may sound funny to “practice” something like nonverbal communication or listening, but it’s no different from developing any other skill, like playing basketball or sewing. There are things we start out not being aware of or not knowing how to do. Once we become aware of them and learn a process, we begin to understand what improvement in a certain area requires. We can then let the amount of practice dictate how skilled we’ll become in a certain area.

These fundamentals of interpersonal communication, along with almost everything else in this book, are skillsAcquired abilities used to perform certain tasks well.. Skills are acquired abilities used to perform certain tasks well, and successful business communication requires us to cultivate skills. We improve our skills through practice, and at least with communication, how good we become is up to us. Practice will make the difference, and we should always remember that we aren’t stuck in a particular place in our communication skills. We can always get better through practice.

section.title: Credibility
section.para: The final section in this topic is about credibility. We treat it last because credibility is the culmination of the knowledge and skills we’ve discussed in this chapter. Credibilinity as a communicator is the product of wisely developing and using emotional intelligence and the fundamentals of interpersonal communication.

In general, credibilityThe trust others place in someone as a communicator. Credibility has two parts: credibility as reliability or truthfulness in sharing information, and credibility as commitment to one’s word. is the trust others place in someone as a communicator. There are two aspects to credibility, however, and while they usually go together, they don’t have to. Let’s look at each.

The first part of credibility is credibility as reliability or truthfulness in sharing information. This is the kind of credibility a journalist looks for in anonymous sources—what the journalist looks for is reliability, so that she can go to press with a story and trust that the anonymous source is telling the truth.

The second part of credibility is credibility as commitment to one’s word. This kind of credibility we often name integrityA person’s internal commitment to honest, upright, and principled behavior, even when others are not around or when abandoning those principles would offer some an advantage.. Integrity is a person’s internal commitment to honest, upright, and principled behavior, even when others are not around or when abandoning those principles would seem to offer some sort of advantage. We demonstrate credibility as integrity when we tell the truth and try to conform our actions to ethical principles.

Both aspects of credibility are important for communication. In order for interpersonal interactions to succeed, those communicating must begin by assuming that they will be reasonably honest and that the information they share is true, according to their understanding. They must assume that they are sharing information in good faith. Communication can’t happen without these assumptions. If you believe someone is lying to you, for example, how much do you pay attention to the specifics of what they say? They aren’t sending useful messages, nor are they contributing to any larger purposes your communication might accomplish. They violate the basic assumptions that make communication possible.

Likewise, both aspects of credibility are also important for business communication. In most circumstances, however, credibility as integrity or commitment to one’s word is more important than credibility as a reliable source. Credibility as a reliable source is just a matter of whether you are telling the truth. Credibility as integrity is a matter of whether you intend to tell the truth, and that intention tells others something about you as a communicator.

Reliability is good, but most professionals aren’t evaluated on whether they can be considered a trusted source about something that most people don’t know. Instead, in the business world we are usually evaluated on whether we try to tell the truth and do what’s right, given our limited knowledge and ability. That trying is integrity. Given enough time, those we communicate with will notice our integrity, and it will become part of how others perceive and communicate with us.

Depending on who you are and what your reputation is, people will grant you a certain amount of credibility to begin with. After that, what you do with that amount is up to you—to either increase or squander it.

Choose now to commit yourself to credibility and integrity in communication. You can decide in favor of honesty and principles, even in challenging situations. While you don’t have complete control over your reputation—people can always distrust you, even when you haven’t done anything wrong—you do control most of it.
Choose to build your credibility and integrity. Your long-term success as a communicator, in business and in other areas of your life, depends on it.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 2: Context, Culture, and Internet Communication for Business. This week, we will cover the following topics:

listitem.para: : Context and Group Communication
: Culture and Communication within Organizations
: Internet and Social Media Communication

section.title: Introduction
