section.para: In business communication, nothing happens in a vacuum; there’s always a context with larger purposes and goals for our communication. Sometimes we know a lot about the context, while other times we know only a little. The more we know about it the better off we’ll be, but at the very least we must remember that the context is always there. There is no such thing as a free lunch—or, in words more fitting here, there’s never any meaningless communication. It only seems meaningless from a particular point of view.

GroupsA set of more than one person we’re communicating with. are important parts of the contexts in which we communicate. In business communication, a group is just a set of more than one person we’re communicating with. Sometimes it’s obvious we’re dealing with a group, as when we go to a job interview and a panel of four people asks the questions. Other times it isn’t so obvious.

For example, suppose that Maura sends an email to her supervisor, Helen, complaining about the behavior of a coworker. The information in the email is sensitive, and Maura expects that Helen will keep it private. Maura is happy to see that Helen sent her response only to Maura. Maura responds again, and the two carry on an email communication about the coworker’s behavior, with Maura believing that she’s communicating about the issue with just a single person.

But now suppose that, without Maura’s knowledge, Helen has been blind-copying some of her colleagues on her responses, including the coworker whose behavior is being discussed. In other words, Maura has, without realizing it, actually been communicating with an entire group of people. They can all see her complaints and monitor the entire communication.

How might Maura change her behavior if she knew the true group context of her communication? She might soften her descriptions of her coworker’s behavior, or she might take responsibility for provoking some of it; maybe she would mention some of the other group members and their possible involvement. She might also, of course, choose not to begin the communication at all!

Communicating with groups is an important part of business success, but there’s more to this type of communication than just being aware of the group. The fundamentals of interpersonal communication all apply to groups, but in many cases we’ll have to modify how we apply them.

Consider, for example, how listening changes when you’re in a group—you’ve got more than one person to listen to, and you must determine who in the group is the person you ought to listen to. Whose comments are the ones you should take seriously and respond to, and how can you tell? Who has the power to make decisions, and what are their needs? Others in the group may not share those needs, but your success may hinge on understanding what the essential needs are while ignoring everything else.

Similarly, credibility changes in groups as well, simply because so many more relationships are in play. If you’re meeting with a group of five people, then each may have a different perception of your credibility and so a different perception of both the trust they should place in you and your integrity. In addition, a group of six people means there are fifteen distinct one-on-one relationships among those individuals. Your success may hinge on figuring out which relationships carry the most weight and how to orient your message to those relationships while ignoring the others.

In this topic, we’ll use what we’ve learned about business communication to develop a model for it, and then we’ll add to the model in order to understand group communication. We’ll then use our model to navigate some of the ins and outs of group communication in business.

section.title: Communication: A Model Built for Two
section.para: In we defined communication as sending and interpreting information in a particular context. We then built on that definition to understand business communication as sending and interpreting information in a business-related context. then deepened our understanding by exploring emotional intelligence, the fundamentals of interpersonal communication, and the way these factors affect our credibility.
By combining material from both topics, we can now offer the following diagram as a model for business communication between two people. Let’s take a look.

imagedata.alt: A model illustrating communication between two people. On one side is communicator 1 (the sender). In green are the fundamentals of interpersonal communication that apply to the sender. These include (within the person sending the message) an understanding of audience needs and the sender's own beliefs, desires, and needs; and (within the message itself) the spoken words or written language that compose the surface message, and the tone, body language, eye contact, space, touch, etc. that compose the affective information. The surface message + the affective information = the complete message. On the other side of the model is communicator 2 (the receiver). In red are the fundamentals of interpersonal communication that apply to the receiver. These include (within the person receiving the message) an understanding of audience needs and the receiver's own beliefs, desires, and needs. On the sender side of the model are additional factors affecting the communication, including emotional intelligence, emotional literacy, explaining, self-disclosue, opening & closing, and assertiveness. On the receiver side of the model are additional factors including emotional intelligence, emotional literacy, reinforcing, reflecting, questioning, and listening. Affecting the communication are the history, relationship, and credibility shared between the two communicators. The message is also affected by niose: any factor that interferes with the correct interpretation of the message. And the entire communication is surrounded and influenced by the context: the larger purposes of communication, goals, environment, relationships, etc.

section.para: This diagram models communication between two people. Although it assumes that only one of them is sending a message, we must remember that both people are always sending messages all the time.

On the left we see the person creating a message to send to a recipient. On the right we see that recipient, who will not only receive the message but also interpret it. With a sender sending a message to a receiver who interprets it, we have an instance of communication. In green we see the parts of the communication that are controlled or mostly controlled by the person sending the message. In red are the parts of the communication controlled or mostly controlled by the person receiving it. And this communication, as noted by the large blue box, is occurring in a particular context.

Note that we can communicate a message in various ways, such as email, text, or actual conversation. We called these the means of communication in , but they may also be called the channelsThe mediums by which messages are transmitted. of communication. A channel of communication is the medium by which a message is transmitted. For business communication, talking in terms of means is preferable because it suggests that everything could be a way to transmit a message, beyond the established channels we’re familiar with. For example, in the story of Justin and Kaya, the channels of communication are email and conversation. But many other means in their environment are sending important messages, including things like Kaya’s locked door and Justin’s cubicle.

The diagram reflects many aspects of context as we’ve discussed them so far in our course. Context involves things like the larger purposes of a communication—maybe these two are coworkers, for example, deciding which marketing team to hire for a new product. That larger purpose sets certain goals that become part of the context as well, in addition to the context of the physical and business environment. As always, the purposes and goals for communicating are themselves up for discussion and revision, and shifting goals may end a communication or render it unnecessary.

One of the most important parts of the context for communication is the relationship between the two people communicating. We see that relationship at the bottom of our model, along with two of its most important components: the history between them and the resulting credibility. In communication, a historyThe sum of all past interactions between two individuals. between two individuals is the sum of their past interactions, whether few or many, harmful or uplifting. These past experiences, negative or positive, become a source that people draw from in their communication. The history also helps determine the credibility they attribute to each other, or the trust they place in each other as communicators. Like the larger purposes of the communication, credibility has a major impact on how people navigate communication.

Finally, in green next to the person sending the message is a list of the fundamentals of interpersonal communication that apply to the sender. These will be the practical skills the communicator uses to fashion the most appropriate message, tailored to the audience’s needs. Similarly, the person receiving the message uses other skills in interpreting it. Exercising many of these skills requires the other communicator to give feedback, which creates a feedback loop between both people. Because they are so important to each side of communication, emotional intelligence and emotional literacy appear on both lists.

This model includes references to material we haven’t discussed yet, especially in the stages of creating, customizing, and interpreting messages. Creating the message and putting it into a medium someone else can receive, like spoken words or an email, is called encodingCreating a message and putting it into a medium someone else can receive, like spoken words or an email.. DecodingThe process a receiver performs when interpreting a message. is the process the receiver performs when interpreting the message. NoiseAny factor, contextual or otherwise, that interferes with the correct interpretation of the message. refers to any factor, contextual or otherwise, that interferes with the correct interpretation of the message. Successful business communication requires careful attention to strategies for encoding, decoding, and mitigating noise. We’ll learn more about these stages in later topics.

To be clear, in the majority of cases where two people are communicating, not everything mentioned in this diagram is being indicated overtly—only rarely do we explicitly note that we’re creating a message or using a particular skill of interpersonal communication. In short, virtually everything here happens beneath the surface of a communication, often without the participants being aware that it’s taking place at all.

The purpose of this model, then, is to take all that activity happening under the surface and bring it to our conscious awareness. We can only practice and improve on what we’re aware of, after all, and so if we never get to know business communication at this level, then we’ll be ignorant of the many ways we could change our behavior to be more successful. The model turns person-to-person communication inside out so that we can see the gears turning and decide how acting differently would make the gears turn better.

The model we’ve proposed here accounts only for a communication interaction between two people. While group communication builds on the same fundamentals of interpersonal communication and includes many parts of the same basic model, it’s different enough that it’s worth studying on its own. Group communication will thus be our subject in the next section.

section.title: Communication: A Model Built for Groups
section.para: Our model for communication, represented in the figure in the previous section, describes a communication interaction between two people. Many of our day-to-day interactions take place between just two people, and of course this type of interaction is common in business as well. But in many business environments, group communication is the norm. Joining a call, hosting a videoconference, having lunch with clients, giving a presentation, hitting “reply all” in an email—all of these are basic business interactions that happen regularly, and all are types of group business communication.

Our model for group communication builds on the basic two-person model. Many aspects of that model remain the same as we move from communicating with a single other person to communicating with more than one. Other aspects become more complex, and there are several new things to look at as well.

Let’s begin with the most obvious change: by introducing at least one other person into our communication, we introduce at least two other relationships and, therefore, two other histories and measures of credibility. Suppose that Joanna is speaking with Franklin, for example. Our two-person model accounts for their history, the trust they place in each other, and other parts of their relationship that will affect how they communicate. But suppose that Vanessa enters the conversation as well. Joanna will have some kind of relationship with Vanessa, and so the pair will have their own history, but Vanessa also has a relationship with Franklin. This relationship may be entirely independent of Joanna—she may have had nothing to do with it in the past and perhaps doesn’t know anything about it. Nevertheless, the relationship between Vanessa and Franklin is still a factor in Joanna’s communication with both of them, and it may affect whether she’s able to accomplish what she hoped by speaking to Franklin in the first place.

To see this effect, we may imagine a situation where Joanna hopes to receive a significant new work responsibility from Franklin. Her goal in speaking to him is to sell herself and her abilities in hopes of getting that responsibility. But once Vanessa arrives, Joanna must consider this new communication partner and how she has changed the dynamic of the conversation. Think to yourself about how Joanna’s actions might change, for instance, depending on which of the following roles Vanessa plays in the group, along with her corresponding relationships with both Joanna and Franklin:

listitem.para: Vanessa and Joanna are casual friends, but they’re competing to receive the same assignment, and their friendship has cooled since the competition began.
Vanessa is Franklin’s trusted adviser—for him Vanessa has enormous credibility, and a recommendation from her would carry great weight in his mind.
Vanessa is widely thought to be the most annoying and incompetent person in the office and only got a job because her grandfather founded the company.
Vanessa is the HR director for the organization and knows confidential information about both Joanna and Franklin.

section.para: Imagine Vanessa taking up each of these roles when she runs into Joanna and Franklin in the hallway—the resulting conversations will be very different! Her presence, along with the presence of any other person, adds more than just a new set of relationships. She may also change the context, the environment, or even the achievable goals of the original communication.

That’s the first point to make about group communication: we must remember not only that additional people bring new relationships, but that new relationships may change any other aspect of the context of communication. If Vanessa loves hockey and never stops talking about it, then from Joanna’s point of view she may derail the communication and even take it from a business communication to a personal one. New relationships introduce more variables to a communication, so it’s important to see how they change the context and affect communication at any spot in the model, from the creation of the message to how it’s decoded to how it’s delivered.

A related challenge of group communication arises when we consider who the interpreters of the message are. Technically, anyone who receives the message is an interpreter, since every recipient of every message is an interpreter. But not all interpreters are created equal—in most instances of group communication in business, one interpreter or a small number of them are far more important than the others and may be the only ones that matter at all. In our example, perhaps Vanessa is part of a search committee that Franklin belongs to as well, and so she has some of the responsibility for filling the new role Joanna hopes to receive. It sounds cynical, but the reality is that in this case, whether Joanna ought to take Vanessa into account in her communication depends on whether Vanessa has any real voice on the search committee.

Joanna thus faces the problem of tailoring her message to the people that matter. She faces the problem of defining what the message actually is—what is she trying to communicate, and to whom? And how much can she ignore the people, relationships, and other aspects of the context that don’t matter as much for her goals?

The problem of defining the message in communication isn’t new, since it comes up outside of group communication as well. The task of fixing the content of a message and its means for delivery faces several challenges, ranging from poor encoding—such as poor word choice or inappropriate nonverbal communication—to unwilling interpreters—such as people who will not fairly interpret what we say or do, no matter how kind or obsequious we are.

This problem becomes more acute, however, as the group with which we’re communicating becomes larger, because the number of beliefs, desires, and needs goes up, as does the number of different opinions about the purpose of the communication and what its goals are. Our model represents these aspects of communication inside the head of communicator #2. They’re colored red to show that they are outside the control of the person sending the message: no matter the effort the sender takes to customize a communication for a particular person or audience, it’s always possible to be misunderstood. And since communicator #2 is just a stand-in for any member of the group with whom we’re communicating, the possibilities for misinterpretation grow as the group becomes larger.

As a result, defining a message and customizing it based on relationships and goals is more difficult in group communication, and groups may cause even more significant difficulties in determining whether we’re staying on messageBeing guided by your original goals and purposes; holding to what you believe is the most appropriate message in a conversation. or not throughout a communication. To stay on message in a communication means to continue to be guided by your original goals and purposes and to hold to what you believe is the most appropriate message, despite the communicative noise and other factors that might otherwise push you off course.

Group communication is especially susceptible to wandering off messageDiscussing topics that have nothing to do with the original message or are irrelevant to the original purposes and goals of the communication., or getting into territory that has nothing to do with the original message or is irrelevant to the original purposes and goals of the communication. It can happen in hallway conversations like the one between Joanna, Franklin, and Vanessa, but larger groups are even more at risk. How many meetings have you been in where it felt like different communicators had lost the thread of the discussion? Or where you can’t remember how the group arrived at a particular subject and so can’t tell whether it’s relevant? Even worse, how many meetings have you been in where the message and purpose were never defined in the first place, and so the entire thing is a waste of time?

In future topics we will cover strategies for avoiding these problems. The most important thing to remember, though, is that we should begin important group communications with a clear purpose in mind and a message tailored for our audience, according to the best knowledge we have at the time. As an interaction progresses, we get more information and can adjust as needed. But in general, departing from the original message and goals is probably a mistake, because without those things the conversation would have had no purpose in the first place.

For all these reasons, context takes on an even more important role in group communication, as does our control over a context. If we can control the context and control how relationships, histories, beliefs, desires, needs, and other factors are influencing the message and its delivery, then we can control the communication.

This is a somewhat paradoxical phenomenon of group communication: as the group becomes larger, the beliefs, desires, needs, and other possibly relevant contextual factors balloon. But they also become easier to control as long as we understand which of those factors matter and maintain an assertive grip on them, thus keeping them at the forefront of the group’s mind. In short, every group wants to have a leader, and the leader isn’t necessarily the one who has the final say over a decision or who has the most power; the leader in a group communication is the one who best manages the contextual aspects of the interaction and therefore plays the strongest role in shaping the message.

The basic model of two-person communication serves as the basis for understanding group communication in business. Groups still rely on relationships, credibility, and other aspects of one-on-one communication, but individual roles, relationships, and goals can have a powerful impact on how group interactions play out.
In the end, the person who controls the context controls the message.

section.title: Power and the Unwritten Rules of Group Communication
section.para: In the previous section we applied our model of communication to group communication. Many important parts of business communication involve groups, and we focused on how the many relationships, beliefs, and goals involved in groups can change the context of communication. We suggested various strategies for success in those situations, including defining the message clearly and controlling the context. We’ll discuss those strategies further in future topics on crafting messages, creating persuasive communications, and delivering effective presentations.

Our model of group communication accounts well for the many overt or observable aspects of interaction between three or more people. We can broaden our understanding of these aspects by discussing them in terms of another important part of group interaction: power.

In general, powerSomeone’s ability to do something or make something happen. refers to someone’s ability to do something or make something happen—like if I have the power to vote or the power to kick a ball into a goal. If I have the power to do either of those things, I’m able to do them, perhaps because I have a legal right or because I know how. In interpersonal relationships, power is the ability to make things happen with other people. In communication, then, power is that same ability. Power is not the same as persuasion, though persuasion may be a part of how someone exercises power.

The idea of power in communication and relationships has acquired a negative connotation in recent years, as more people become aware of both how common and how subtle abuses of power can be. An abuse of powerAn unethical or otherwise inappropriate exercise of power done to harm someone or get a person to act in a way that they may not to want or agree with. is an unethical or otherwise inappropriate exercise of power, done to harm someone or just to get a person to act in a way that they may not to want or agree with. Abuses of power are often the result of power imbalancesAlso known as unequal power dynamics; the disparity in power between two people., or unequal power dynamics. Those two terms, as well as others, refer to the disparity in power between two people. In some ways, the person with less power is at the mercy of the more powerful, although principle-based leaders will be sensitive to such disparities and will not exploit them.

In most cases of group communication, power and power imbalances may be innocuous in that they aren’t generally used to manipulate. Instead, the significance of power is in managing group dynamics: who is in charge—not in name only, but in reality? Who controls the flow of a communication? Who decides what is relevant and what isn’t? In the previous section we said that the person with authority over these matters is the one directing the communication, even if they aren’t saying anything or even being spoken to. These facts lead us to what we can call the unwritten rules of group communicationThe unspoken or unacknowledged ways that power influences a communication..

The unwritten rules of group communication are the unspoken or unacknowledged ways that power influences your communication. The rules can be more prominent and obvious, such as the assumption that the person with the most power will have the final say. Or they can be subtle and difficult to discern, such as the ways members of a group feel like they have to speak in order to defer to other members of the group.

A model of power may help in understanding how we ought to communicate with these rules in mind. In 1959, sociologists John French and Bertram Raven proposed a way of thinking about social power that included five elements, to which Raven later added a sixth. They called these six elements the six bases of power. A basis of powerThe source of the power that someone has over another. is the source of the power that someone has over another. Because the six power bases have to do with many different aspects of individual and group communication, we have not represented them explicitly in our model in the previous section. We could locate them, however, in the relationship and history, the understanding of needs and desires, and the creation and interpretation stages of the message transmission process.
Here are the six bases of power, along with the definitions given by French and Raven. In the definitions, we should understand “O” and “P” to be two communicators:

listitem.para: Reward power. “Reward power is defined as power whose basis is the ability to reward.”
Coercive power. “Coercive power of O/P stems from the expectation on the part of P that he will be punished by O if he fails to conform to the influence attempt.”

Legitimate power. “Legitimate power of O/P is here defined as that power which stems from internalized values in P which dictate that O has a legitimate right to influence P and that P has an obligation to accept this influence.”

Referent power. “The referent power of O/P has its basis in the identification of P with O. By identification, we mean a feeling of oneness of P with O, or a desire for such an identity. . . . P’s identification with O can be established or maintained if P behaves, believes, and perceives as O does. Accordingly O has the ability to influence P, even though P may be unaware of this referent power.”
Expert power. “The strength of the expert power of O/P varies with the extent of the knowledge or perception which P attributes to O within a given area.”
Informational power. Informational power is the control O has over the information P may need to reach a goal.

section.para: These six bases are the source of the power that exists in both individual and group relationships. The power dynamics in a relationship are an ebb and flow of these sources, as some become important in certain circumstances while receding into the background in others. These sources are also significant contributors to the respect one is granted by others, and the credibility that one therefore enjoys.

For example, suppose that Ophelia is a project manager and Patrick is the member of the project team with specialized knowledge in software development. Consider the following ways that these sources of power may play out in their relationship and their communications:

listitem.para: Reward power. Ophelia has the ability to reward Patrick with a bonus or greater salary for his work on the project.
Coercive power. By threatening Patrick, Ophelia may be able to get him to work longer hours or take ethical or professional shortcuts that he otherwise might not want to take.
Legitimate power. Ophelia is the project manager, given oversight of the project by an executive. Patrick understands that relationship and doesn’t mind deferring decisions to her.

Referent power. Ophelia may occupy a role in the organization that Patrick wishes one day to have. Patrick feels that if he behaves like Ophelia, he will have a better chance at obtaining that position.
Expert power. Ophelia doesn’t know much about coding or software development, and so here Patrick has the power, since Ophelia recognizes he has essential expert knowledge.
Informational power. Both Ophelia and Patrick have informational power: Ophelia from the organizational side and Patrick from the side of his expertise.

section.para: It’s easy to imagine how each of these power sources would impact how Ophelia and Patrick communicate. In addition, as the flow of an individual interaction moves Ophelia and Patrick from topic to topic, different sources of power become more and less important and are given attention when necessary before being set aside for a time.

And for groups, these six sources of power exist as facets of the many relationships between individuals in the group. That’s a lot of relationships, and a lot of sources of power! And yet, successful group communication, especially in difficult or high-stakes circumstances, depends on discerning the important aspects of power and correctly reacting to these dynamics.

Our models of individual and group interaction, together with the other information and techniques in this book, will help you learn to correctly discern those power dynamics and react to them. But there is no substitute for practice. As we’ve said, business communication is a skill. We improve at it when we learn what’s best to do, then try to put that learning into practice. There’s no question that we’ll fail, but over time we’ll fail less, and we’ll create a reputation of ourselves as skilled communicators whose input is valuable no matter the circumstances.

People express power in all parts of their communication and the context they create: how they talk, how they look at each other, how and where they sit, and so on. It may be distasteful and even a little uncomfortable to think about how these unwritten rules factor into communication, but we ignore them at our own risk. Our model of group communication tells us as much—all of the nonverbal and contextual aspects of communication can make a difference, and sometimes they make all the difference.
The question is, who will pay attention to all this? Who will gather affective and other information to adjust their behavior and shape the message and the eventual outcome of the communication?
And the answer is, the one with the power.

section.title: Managing Group Dynamics
section.para: The fact is that, depending on our role in a group, we may have little control over group dynamics or little power to push a communication in a particular direction. Unfortunately, group dynamics are managed according to the unwritten rules of group communication, or the unwritten rules of power—if you have little power, then a knowledge of the rules doesn’t help much.

However, it would be a mistake to disregard the points in this topic purely because you may not be in a position of power or leadership. Good leaders will exemplify skills of effective group communication, and they will understand the sources of power and manage power dynamics equitably. But only some people are leaders in any given interaction. And for good reason, because when everyone tries to lead a communication, it’s like having too many cooks in the kitchen—getting anything useful done becomes much harder. Since our focus is group communication, we’ll provide tools to help you participate in the group’s interactions and communications, even when you aren’t a leader or don’t have much power within the group.

The goal is to become an effective communicator so that you can achieve the goals you wanted to achieve by communicating in the first place. Sometimes this will require you to direct a conversation or take the lead on a pressure-packed presentation to a client. Other times you’ll find it’s necessary to take a back seat and stay silent through an entire communication. An effective communicator is someone with the wisdom to recognize what is needed in different situations and with the self-control to do what is necessary to succeed in them.

As you learn techniques and practice skills to develop this wisdom in yourself, remember that each person in a group communication is part of their group. There’s a history, relationship, and sources of power for each pair of relationships. This means that getting agreement and buy-in from different group members may demand careful thought and attention to individual needs. Focus on each relationship, when necessary, so that a group communication can be a sum of successful individual communications. For each group member, we could fill out a model of individual communication—what would we include in it, and why? What would we need to know to cut through context and noise and deliver an effective message?

As in every part of communication, the more information we have, the better. When we have more information, much of the power in a communication and control over its context sways in our direction. We also improve our group communications as we become better able to discern what is important and react accordingly. We might sum it up with the slogan, “Read and adjust.” We read the information we are being given—we pay attention to all sources of information, verbal and nonverbal, in accordance with our emotional literacy and communication skills. We then adjust our message and means of delivering it to respond to that information, in light of our original goals. Read the information and feedback, then adjust the message. Read and adjust.

section.title: Communication in Modern Organizations
section.para: In the first topic of our course we discussed business documents. One of these was the memo, and though we offered some guidance about memos, we also said, “There are thousands of organizations that have never sent a memo and multiple generations of employees who have never received one, much less read one.”

This point applies beyond office memos as well. It is striking to note, but with the exception of email and websites, virtually none of the most important forms of business communication even existed 20 years ago. Texting, social media, Slack, video calls—all of these and more are relatively recent innovations in the business communications landscape. And if we turn back the clock 10 more years, then widespread email and website use is gone, too.

Thus, the past 30 years have seen technologies and messaging strategies that have not just created new options for business communication but fundamentally changed the most basic ways that communication operates. Someone with communications experience in a particular industry could find that experience obsolete in as few as three or four years, as new ways of messaging and persuading rise to the surface and swamp the old methods. On the other hand, learning new communication systems can offer immediate advantages.

For many people trying to get a lay of the land from the outside, it can be difficult to see what channels of communication are carrying the most important information and why. The purpose of this topic is, therefore, to orient ourselves toward the channels that will make the most difference within an organization. How might we be expected to communicate with our groups, teams, and companies? How do the channels available to us influence the way we design, customize, and transmit our messages? We’ll answer those questions and others here.

Because each organization is different, not everything we say here will apply to every team or every company. Nevertheless, we can still make the discussion relevant by framing it in terms of organizational culture. Organizations have personalities and ways of working, which are often so tangible that you can sense them as soon as you enter a building or an office. The values and principles that compose an organization’s culture determine how communication will best take place within it. So to understand communication within an organization, we must first understand how its organizational culture develops and spreads among its members.
Let’s look at that next.

section.title: Organizational Culture
section.para: Without taking time to think, answer the following questions:

listitem.para: Who is your loudest, most obnoxious friend?
Who is your shiest, quietest friend?

section.para: The two people who came to your mind when you answered these questions are probably pretty different from each other. One might speak with a loud voice, tell a lot of jokes, and love to be the center of attention at parties. The other might keep to him or herself, not share a lot of personal details, and prefer to stay in the background at social gatherings, if attending them at all. Such different personalities make these two people different, but their personalities also impact you. Your interactions with each will depend on what you know about their respective personalities and what kind of communications they like. Someone who’s always up for a good time might not mind getting a phone call from you late at night with an invitation to go out, while another friend might get angry or even offended by the same call. Your friends’ ways of being make them who they are and determine the best ways to interact and communicate with them.

In this respect at least, companies are no different from people. A company will have a personality and a style—it will have a way of doing things that permeates the organization as well as the interactions its members have with each other and with others on the outside. Think about different stores, businesses, or companies you associate with. Which are fun to go inside or be around? Do some play energetic music? Do some greet you more enthusiastically, while others ignore you? Are some quick to forgive mistakes by employees and customers, while others won’t let anything go? What do you imagine it’s like to work at these different places? What would it be like to communicate with representatives of these organizations, or to be a member and communicate with those on the inside?

All these questions strike at different parts of an organization’s culture. A culture, or organizational cultureAn organization’s ways of being and doing things, together with the values and principles supposedly behind those ways., gives rise to different styles of interacting and communicating. An organization’s ways of being and doing things, together with the values and principles supposedly behind those ways, are its culture. Organizational cultures determine what it’s like to be a member in an organization, what it’s like to associate with them, and what channels of communication are likely to be most successful.

Our definition of organizational culture includes the word “supposedly.” This is because the values and principles a company claims to affirm are not always the ones it actually affirms in practice. Think of groups or companies you’ve been a part of in the past that said one thing and did another. Which did you believe: the group’s words, or its actions? The reality of organizational culture, then, comes not from fancy mission statements or the latest buzzwords a company adopts to project an image. A group’s true culture shows more in how it acts than in what it says, and the mismatch between stated values and true values is itself a part of organizational culture wherever it exists. Members of such organizations would be wise to keep the mismatch in mind.

At the beginning of this topic we noted recent changes in channels of business communication. One way to understand these changes is to take them as changes to an organization’s culture. A company that opts to have many traditional in-person meetings with a traditional management and office structure shows its commitment to a certain set of values by those choices. Likewise, a company that styles itself as light on its feet may want to change communication methods frequently in order to eke out whatever advantage they can from new technologies.

Along with business communication, changes in organizational culture tend to accelerate over time—there have always been changes, but now the rate of change is increasing. Many causes contribute to this acceleration, including rapid executive turnover at some companies or union efforts at others. The COVID-19 pandemic in particular forced massive changes in many organizational cultures, since it was impossible for most office workers to appear in person at all.

Pandemic-related culture changes are still echoing throughout many industries. Perhaps the most prominent ongoing issue, which also happens to be crucial for communication, is that of remote versus in-person work. According to a 2022 Microsoft survey conducted anonymously with employees of many organizations and fields, 87% of employees report that they are productive at work.Microsoft. (2022). 2022 work trend index. That percentage includes many remote workers. In contrast, the same data indicated that only 12% of leaders have full confidence that their team is productive. This enormous gap represents a significant disagreement in organizational culture that, for many companies, has yet to be resolved. Even remote workers, pressured by an attitude of busyness, can be victims of what marketing expert Randy Murray calls “productivity theater”—appearing to work in order to placate the boss.Stillman, J. (2013, August 27). Is your staff always busy? You have a problem. Inc.
We’ll explore the implications that these and other aspects of organizational culture have for business communication in the next section.
Despite these faster changes, however, organizational cultures still tend to coalesce around a small number of broad values, thereby producing one of just a few general culture types.

The competing values frameworkA framework that says that organizational cultures form as companies seek a balance between values that compete, or are in tension with each other. of Kim Cameron and Robert Quinn is one way to model these types. Cameron, K. S., & Quinn, R. E. (2011). Diagnosing and changing organizational culture (3rd ed.). Jossey-Bass. The competing values framework says that organizational cultures form as companies seek a balance between values that compete, or are in tension with each other. Pushing the company further toward one value requires moving away from another, and so how a company manages competing values determines what kind of culture they promote. As we’ll see, these culture types then impact how communication can best take place both inside and outside the organization.
For Cameron and Quinn, the two pairs of competing values are as follows:

listitem.para: Pair #1: Stability and control compete with flexibility and discretion.
Pair #2: Internal focus and integration compete with external focus and differentiation.

section.para: The values of pair #1 involve how fast an organization can change and who makes the decisions about the change. Does it only change slowly, driven by a deliberate, top-down decision-making process? Or is it more nimble, giving each employee autonomy to do what she thinks best? The values in pair #2 involve what an organization focuses on and how it relates to potential competitors. Does it ignore competitors and develop its own processes to realize a certain vision of itself? Or does it encourage employees to compete with each other in an internal marketplace to produce the best outcomes and stand out from other companies?
The way a company balances these values creates an organizational culture of a certain type. The following figure represents the four general organizational types:

imagedata.alt: A framework that shows the four potential organizational types on a quadrant. The vertical continuum has flexibility and discretion at the top and stability and control at the bottom. The horizontal continuum has internal focus and integration on the left and external focus and differentiation on the right. In the top-left quadrant is the clan organization (collaborate). In the top-right quadrant is the adhocracy organization (create). In the bottom-left quadrant is the hierarchy organization (control). And in the bottom-right quadrant is the market organization (compete).

section.para: The first pair of values, stability/control and flexibility/discretion, is on the vertical axis. The second pair, internal focus/integration and external focus/differentiation, is on the horizontal axis. Choosing a location on the two axes sets a company in one of the figure’s four quadrants, which are the four culture types.

A hierarchy cultureThe culture that focuses on control; its goal is the creation and maintenance of formal processes and authority structures. focuses on control. Its goal is the creation and maintenance of formal processes and authority structures that it sees as essential to success, and it creates an environment of control. The market cultureThe culture that acts as a marketplace unto itself, prizing competitiveness and productivity as individual employees work within their areas of specialty. is a culture that acts as a marketplace unto itself, prizing competitiveness and productivity as individual employees work within their areas of specialty.

A clan cultureThe culture characterized by a strong collaboration among employees, instead of competition, with much looser or even absent top-down guidance. embraces the values opposite a market culture on both axes. It is characterized by a strong collaboration among employees, rather than competition, with much looser or even absent top-down guidance. The result is an environment where employees have more autonomy and are expected to work in teams; clan cultures may even call themselves a “family.” The culture opposite a hierarchy culture is an adhocracy cultureThe culture that acts flexibly to create solutions to specific problems while avoiding fixed procedures or hierarchical decision-making processes.. The term “ad hoc” is a Latin phrase meaning “for a particular purpose,” and refers to a decision or action taken in response to a specific, one-off occurrence. An adhocracy is therefore a culture that acts flexibly to create solutions to specific problems while avoiding fixed procedures or hierarchical decision-making processes.

In our discussion of organizational culture so far, we’ve had in mind more office-oriented companies and other traditional business groups. But the model of culture types applies to all organizations. Think about a night club, for example, which is a very different kind of organization. Even though it’s different, a night club must still find a balance between the pairs of competing values, and as a result may have one of various cultures. An overbearing night club owner might require employees to do things the same way all the time, in order to provide each customer with the exact same experience every time they attend. A less controlling owner might give more authority to employees to interact with customers in other ways, which might create a more spontaneous experience that’s always different.

Night clubs, wealth management firms, fast food restaurants, and video game developers are all very different kinds of businesses. But they may still select the same underlying values and balance them in the same ways—leading these organizations, which most of the time would never have anything to do with each other, to have similar cultures. In at least some broad ways, working at a night club with an adhocracy culture would be like working at a video game developer with the same culture. The companies do different things and have different goals, but the ways they express their underlying values could be similar.

In this section we’ve given a few examples of how different organizational cultures give rise to different ways of interacting and communicating, and you’re probably already thinking of others. The type of culture a business has determines what forms of communication will be most important to it, so we’ll explore the relationship between culture and communication in the next section.

section.title: Organizational Culture, Communication, and Employee Engagement
section.para: In the previous section we saw a model of organizational culture that defined a culture based on pairs of competing values. One of the model’s advantages is that it allows us to think about business communication in terms of culture for a wide variety of organizations. Regardless of their product, service, or industry, businesses with similar cultures are likely to use similar communication styles.

In fact, it isn’t a stretch to say that organizational culture not only affects communication within an organization, but actually determines to a large extent how that communication will happen. Let’s consider why.

We already know that business communication is the sending and interpreting of information in a business context. We also know that contexts can include many different factors, from the relationships and histories we have with others to the actual physical circumstances we’re communicating in. But context also includes organizational culture, and at least for business communication, organizational culture will often be the single most important part of the larger context in our communications.

Let’s see some examples, starting with a hierarchy culture. A hierarchy culture emphasizes formal lines of authority, top-down decision-making, and fixed reporting relationships. Think about how those features of a culture might affect the way you communicate within it. If you worked in a hierarchy culture and had an idea for a new product or process, who would you speak to about it? Your organizational culture would dictate that you speak to your immediate supervisor, and it would be uncommon or even unacceptable to go over that person’s head to speak to their boss or their boss’s boss. In a company with a rigid enough hierarchy, it might even be impossible for a low-level employee to offer new ideas or critique existing processes. This culture focuses on fixed areas of responsibility, and stepping outside the hierarchy might not be a realistic option. In this case, the hierarchy culture would determine a lot about how you could expect communication to take place: many announcements from senior leadership, many company-wide standards and protocols, many formal procedures to follow for sharing information.

In contrast, consider your experience of communication in an adhocracy culture, where procedures get invented as you go along and only exist as long as they’re useful. Would it be appropriate to go over your boss’s head with an idea to innovate a certain product? It might be—if you have a boss at all. There might even be meetings whose purpose is to field ideas from people who aren’t the typical decision-makers, since fixed reporting relationships and formal lines of authority will be rare in an adhocracy. Communication in such an organization is going to be more of a free-for-all as people make decisions with an eye toward what needs to be done now and how best to do it.

We’d expect to find a similar free-for-all in the communications of a market culture. Management may institutionalize the ways that ideas compete against each other within the organization, but there will still be competition, along with the more open-ended and democratic decision-making that often accompanies it. The opposite of a market culture would be a clan culture, and there we could expect communication to be more respectful of closer working and collaborative relationships that people have with each other.

Organizations will always differ from each other, and things work differently across industries; but an organization’s culture determines context, and therefore that culture determines communication. For within-organization communication, no other single factor will impact means and styles of communication more than organizational culture.
Culture determines context, and therefore culture determines communication.

So far we’ve been thinking about how organizational culture determines communication at an organizational level. But it also does so for the actions and interactions of individual employees, primarily by means of employee engagementThe extent to which employees are empowered, energized, and invested to contribute to organizational success.. We will define employee engagement as “the extent to which employees are empowered, energized, and invested to contribute to organizational success.” Bisson, S. (2023, June 2). Microsoft’s work trend index: Employee engagement pays off in productivity, stock price. TechRepublic. An engaged employee is one who cares about an organization and makes sure that what they do builds on what others are doing. Someone who’s engaged is much more likely to do meaningful work, and meaningful work then creates more engagement.

In a recent survey of millions of employees at many different companies, Microsoft found that at the least engaged organizations, almost one-quarter of employees don’t even know what they should be focusing on at work. That’s a clear failure of communication, which then creates a negative loop: employees who don’t know what to focus on aren’t engaged, and care less and less about what they ought to focus on. In addition, employees at highly engaged organizations are 46 percent more likely to see their organizations as strong communicators. In other words, those employees are much more likely to look at their own companies and their own organizational cultures and see them as communicating effectively. As a result, employees at engaged organizations are 37 percent more likely to be confident in their organization’s leadership. Microsoft. (2023). Work trend index special report.

Highly engaged organizations are ones where leaders work with employees to figure out how best to communicate with them, rather than fixing the “best” communication practices in advance. Engaged organizations communicate openly and clearly with their employees, modeling the best practices we’ve seen in other topics. And organizations’ communications and cultures impact the bottom line: according to Microsoft’s data, the most engaged companies outperformed the S&P 500, sometimes performing twice as well as other companies. Microsoft. (2023). Work trend index special report.

Let’s not get the causes and effects mixed up here, though. While employee engagement is a key, only engaging organizations and strong, engaging communicators can create employee engagement. It doesn’t come about by magic nor by accident. An organization must expend deliberate, mindful effort to carry out a program of open and clear communication, with the awareness that open communication in one direction requires receiving open communication in the other direction as well. We’ll explore this feedback loop in the next section.

Above, we said that culture determines context, and it therefore determines communication. This is true, but we must remember that the best way to improve context and communication within our organizations is not necessarily by starting with culture. Instead, we should begin by having in mind what kind of communications we want to prevail in our organizations, so that we can then consider what kind of culture is most likely to lead that direction. In other words, we begin with the end in mind, realizing that an organizational culture is not an end in itself. Rather, it’s a means to many ends: communication, profit, innovation, and growth. We first need to set our goals on those long-term markers of success, and then build the culture that will take us there.
Culture determines communication, but the way we want to communicate should determine culture.

section.title: Communication, Teams, and Psychological Safety
section.para: Communication within organizations can take place at many different levels. Horizontal communication Communication that takes place between individuals at the same level, such as colleague to colleague or manager to manager. takes place between individuals at the same level, such as colleague to colleague or manager to manager. Vertical communicationCommunication across levels, such as a company-wide announcement or an employee having lunch with an executive to give feedback on a review. is communication across levels, such as a company-wide announcement or an employee having lunch with an executive to give feedback on a review. Vertical communication isn’t uncommon, of course, but most employees find that the majority of their communications are horizontal.

Horizontal communications most often take place within teamsA group of people who most often communicate with each other, regardless of whether they’re working together on a particular project or assignment.. The term “team” in a business context has many different meanings, and could refer to an actual team of five basketball players who meet to play at lunch, or to a group of marketers convened to address concerns about a particular account. Rather than attempt to define a team for many organizations, we’ll instead give a working definition for our purposes here: a team is a group of people who most often communicate with each other, regardless of whether they’re working together on a particular project or assignment.

Defining teams in terms of frequently-communicating groups puts the attention on why and how we’re communicating with our teams. What are the goals of our communications? What information needs to be shared, and why? What are the best ways to communicate to achieve those goals? How can we match our means of communication to the needs of those we communicate with? The success of team-based communication depends on how attentively we’re able to answer these questions.
According to organizational behavior expert Michael West, the effectiveness of any team depends on five different components:

listitem.para: Task-related objectives: teams actually do the things they were created to do.
Team member well-being: team members grow and develop, and manage challenges and stress together.
Team viability: teams are set up in a way that makes it likely they’ll function and continue to function well.
Team innovation: teams develop and use new processes and procedures.
Inter-team cooperation: teams work well with other teams in an organization. West, M. A. (2012). Effective teamwork: Practical lessons from organizational research (3rd ed.). Blackwell.

section.para: The most successful teams will include all five of these components. And while the components are quite different from each other, and sometimes don’t affect each other much—whether a team innovates may have nothing to do with whether it works well with other teams—all five components have an important element in common: in each case, excellence requires strong communication.

Teams will do the things they are made to do—if someone has communicated those things to the teams in the first place. Teams can grow and develop together—if they’ve communicated about what their weaknesses are and how they feel about them. Viable teams are viable because they’re filled with people who trust each other enough to communicate and continue to communicate. Teams naturally innovate when they openly share ideas and perspectives. And effective teamwork across teams is really just effective communication.

Teams form and re-form fluidly across modern organizations and in different organizational cultures. But it remains true that effective teams are filled with effective communicators, and effective teams are those that best understand the communication process and work to follow the principles of effective business communication. Those principles, found in this topic and elsewhere, make the strongest teams.

To make this sort of collaboration possible, new software systems such as Slack and Discord are built with team communication specifically in mind. They therefore allow teams to think deliberately about how they will develop West’s five components of team effectiveness. Slack, Discord, and comparable programs such as Microsoft Teams, allow small groups to quickly organize and communicate the most important information they need to fulfill their responsibilities. These programs may also be part of an organizational culture or even the institutionalized communication systems within a company. They go far beyond email in allowing much wider-reaching communications to take place instantly, and for teams to organize their efforts while rarely, if ever, needing to meet in person.

One striking feature of these and other next-generation communications systems is that they allow anyone to say anything to anyone at almost any time. The very use of these systems constitutes a strong commitment to a certain organizational culture, since they tend to democratize communication within organizations and open up message channels that may have traditionally been closed. For this reason, the context of this more egalitarian environment must allow for honest and vulnerable sharing of information. An environment that does this is said to be psychologically safe.

Social scientist Timothy Clark defines psychological safetyA condition in which you feel (1) included, (2) safe to learn, (3) safe to contribute, and (4) safe to challenge the status quo—all without fear of being embarrassed, marginalized, or punished in some way. as “a condition in which you feel (1) included, (2) safe to learn, (3) safe to contribute, and (4) safe to challenge the status quo—all without fear of being embarrassed, marginalized, or punished in some way.”Clark, T. R. (2020). The 4 stages of psychological safety: Defining the path to inclusion and innovation. Berrett-Koehler. 2. All four parts of psychological safety—what Clark calls inclusion safety, learner safety, contributor safety, and challenger safety—refer to people’s perceived ability and willingness to be a part of a group and share from themselves in order to benefit both themselves and the group. People who don’t feel inclusion safety, for example, won’t feel like they belong or are wanted, while people who don’t feel challenger safety may have important ideas about how an organization functions but be unwilling to share them. The four aspects of psychological safety build on each other, with inclusion safety coming first and challenger safety last.

At its core, psychological safety is about the way people communicate. People who don’t feel psychologically safe won’t be willing to communicate openly—or, more likely, they’ll communicate just those things they believe want to be heard, and they’ll occupy the role they feel most comfortable and safe in, whether or not that’s the best role for them. Because these people fear rejection or punishment, they shut down their own tendencies to communicate and share what would be best for the team, focusing instead on what is best for themselves. Who could blame them? They’re scared of doing anything else.

Teams that fail to create a psychologically safe environment make it impossible to communicate honestly and vulnerably, making it far less likely that they’ll be able to develop the components of effective teams. Those components flourish in environments of psychological safety, where emotionally literate people use the best communication practices to include each other, support each other, and even challenge each other as they learn to do things better.

Microsoft’s survey of employee engagement describes the resulting loop of open communication as a “feedback flywheel.”Microsoft. (2023). Work trend index special report. A flywheel is a large wheel in a machine that stores energy so that the machine can continue to operate as intended even when its power source is disrupted. A feedback flywheel is a communications loop in which people share ideas and then take each other’s ideas seriously, leading to continuous, reciprocal feedback across an organization. This loop then becomes a source of “energy,” or inspiration and innovation, felt by engaged employees as their confidence in themselves and their teams and organizations grows. The components of effective teams become natural for those teams as their freedom to communicate unleashes their most significant contributions.

A feedback flywheel can’t exist in just any team. Only those that are psychologically safe, with team members who understand what it means to be strong communicators, can establish them. Effective team communication grows out of effective organizations, which set out to establish certain means and channels of communication by designing the right culture. Teams in those environments will communicate best, produce most, and bring the greatest satisfaction to their members.

section.title: Meetings
section.para: One of the most common settings of important communication within organizations is the meeting. With that in mind, we’ll conclude this topic with a brief discussion of meetings.

Because meetings vary so much based on who attends them and what they’re for, it’s difficult to give general guidance about running them effectively. Meetings continue to be an important part of business communication, however, and so we offer the following points to consider.

listitem.para: Is a meeting necessary? With internal communication tools like Slack, the reality is that a meeting may no longer be the best way to share information or hold discussions, at least in some circumstances. It is simply not necessary to gather staff together to speak in person about matters that could be treated in an email or group chat. If you are thinking of convening a meeting, ask yourself, is what you might gain by gathering in person worth whatever you give up by drawing your team away from their other tasks? Remember, though, that meetings can serve purposes beyond sharing information, solving problems, or brainstorming—they can build camaraderie among individuals, create group unity, and produce other benefits as well.

Define the meeting’s purpose. A meeting without a purpose is like watching a turtle crawl across a highway: you hold your breath until it’s over, and then hope you never have to see it again. If a meeting is necessary, be sure you can state its specific purpose in a single sentence. Remember, “We usually get together on Wednesdays” is not a purpose for a meeting, it’s a description of what people normally do. A purpose is something else you intend to do or hope to accomplish by meeting. What is the point of the meeting, and how will you know whether it addressed that point? How will you be able to tell the meeting has been successful?

Begin and end on time. Starting late penalizes those who arrive when it was supposed to start and communicates the message that you do not value the time of those who are attending. Keeping to a tight schedule tells your participants that you respect them and their other activities.

Create and follow an agenda. An agendaA plan for a meeting, showing what will be discussed, in what order, and approximately what amount of time will be given to each item. is a plan for a meeting, showing what will be discussed, in what order, and approximately what amount of time will be given to each item. A clear agenda communicates the purpose and content of a meeting. Prepare it in advance and distribute it to each attendee.

Put the most important things second. Many meetings put the most important agenda items last, as though all the small things need to be resolved before addressing the big one. But doing things this way makes it likely that you won’t be able to give enough time to the most important agenda items, and even if you reach them, some participants will be tired and others may have to leave before they can contribute. Put the most important things second on the agenda, after a brief opening and welcome, to ensure you’re able to deal with them adequately.

Avoid decision deferral. Decision deferralThe tendency to procrastinate by delaying important decisions until a later time. is the tendency individuals and groups have to procrastinate by delaying important decisions “until next time.” When there is enough information to make a decision and the issue has been discussed, make a decision and move forward.

Make clear assignments with a timeline, communicate them, and follow up. End the meeting with a brief summary of what has been discussed, and a rundown of action items and who they’ve been assigned to. Use deadlines and be clear about them. Make sure those individuals receive and know about their assignment, and follow up with them to see what they’ve been able to do.

section.para: While many meetings do make attendees feel as though boredom is the force that shall slay the world, it doesn’t have to be like that. Thoughtful preparation, respectful planning, and a commitment to meaningful action can rescue some meetings, though perhaps not all. All meetings, no matter how well planned, run the risk of committing what meeting expert John Tropman has called “time wasting in cold blood.”Tropman, J. E. (2014). Effective meetings: Improving group decision making (3rd ed.). Sage. 30.

If a meeting is necessary, then prepare and plan it, and execute the plan with all the haste and expediency of a new parent whose infant is crying in the next room but can’t help the baby until the meeting ends. You’ll get more done, and everyone else in the meeting will thank you.

section.title: Communication Inside and Outside an Organization
section.para: In the previous topic we focused on communication within business organizations. Because companies can control the way people communicate inside them, at least for the most part, we centered our discussion on organizational culture. As part of the context in which business takes place, organizational culture determines much of what within-company communication ends up being like.

When we turn around and consider communication outside an organization, we find that things aren’t so simple. There’s still a context for communication, but it’s far broader; and depending on who we’re communicating with, it could be as broad as the entire world! No amount of corporate planning or image management will allow us to control that context, and so an organization’s industry- and public-facing communication will necessarily be very different from its internal communication. Whatever it says and however it says it, the organization is sending messages to an outside audience, and when that happens, all bets are off. The game has changed.

The primary difference, then, between business communication inside and outside an organization is the loss of control. Internal communications can influence or even govern the context by specifying who the senders and interpreters of a message will be and what the rules for interpretation are. And, while people can be fickle, communications inside an organization can usually rely on a fixed set of assumptions and beliefs about the company: that it’s succeeding, that it has a bright future, that it has good intentions, that it is culturally relevant, and so on. Those assumptions, together with the established rules for creating and interpreting messages, mean that internal communication is far more predictable. There’s more control.

Compare that situation to the one we face in trying to communicate with people outside our business. For one, the audiences are far more varied—they’re customers, clients, vendors, people with no relationship to our company, people who have never heard of our company, and everything in between. Those people will carry many different assumptions about our organization—some of those assumptions might be true and fair, while others might be false and biased. But whether they’re false and biased is almost beside the point, since those assumptions will influence how the audience receives and interprets our communications all the same.

The idea of home-court advantage is helpful here. Communicating within an organization is like playing a basketball game at your own arena, giving you home-court advantage. Playing at your home court means that you know exactly what all the idiosyncrasies of the court are like—you know the building and the hoops and the noise levels, and you can use that insider information to your advantage. Even more importantly, the majority of people in the arena are there to cheer for you! They’re your fans and they want you to succeed, and so are going to give you the benefit of the doubt whenever possible. At your home court, everything is balanced in your favor. But when you go on the road, you can’t count on any of that. You don’t know the place or even the equipment; there may be house rules you’re not familiar with, and most people at the game are against you. They’d love to see you fail, and might even want to help make it happen.

Keep this idea in mind as you read this chapter: communication outside your organization is like playing on the road. You’re in unfamiliar territory, you might not have any insider knowledge, and you can’t count on anyone to treat you well or even fairly. You must proceed accordingly.

And so, since business communication is so different inside and outside an organization, it’s worth taking time to sort out techniques and strategies for communication outside our organizations. That’s what we’ll do in this chapter.

Before getting started, though, a brief caution: of all the subjects in this book, this is the one we’re able to cover least well. The reason is that the areas of external communication range from advertising to branding to hiring to public outreach. As we’ve said before, everything is communication, and each public-facing activity a business performs is, in one way or another, a message sent to outside audiences.

We’ll thus restrict ourselves to considering internet and social media communication, but even with that narrow focus, our subject matter could still include digital branding, digital marketing, website and image development, and many other things. We will need to leave some things out.

Nevertheless, there’s still much to say. We’ll focus on extending our model of communication to the internet and social media, with attention to the parts of the model we retain control over in those communications. We’ll discuss relationships and trust, principles for social media interaction for businesses, and how different media platforms affect the way we should develop our communications strategies for each.

section.title: The Iron Laws of Internet Communication for Business
section.para: To begin, we offer the following four Iron Laws of Internet Communication for Business:

listitem.para: Law #1: Everything is permanent (and accessible).
Law #2: You will be misunderstood, often willfully.
Law #3: Some publicity is bad publicity.
Law #4: You are who you are thought to be—at least online.

section.para: Since social media platforms are internet-based forms of interaction, these laws apply to them and to anything else you do online. Let’s discuss each in turn.

section.title: Law #1: Everything Is Permanent (and Accessible)
section.para: Every medium for sending messages has some level of permanence: handwritten letters can be saved, smoke signals could be videotaped, and even face-to-face conversations can be recorded. There’s always a way to make a particular message last.

The permanence of the internet is different from these traditional channels in two ways, however. The first is that no special effort is required to make it permanent. Online chats are saved by default; social media posts get saved; vigilant keyboard warriors screengrab offensive or surprising posts to call someone out later. When all else fails, the Wayback Machine, a website that automatically archives time-indexed versions of other websites, can show us what the internet looked like in the past.

The second difference with the permanence of the internet is that what remains permanent becomes immediately accessible to anyone who wants to find it. Once something gets saved online and search engines discover it, it’s forever available with just a few keystrokes. Engraving an offhand, foolish remark on a stone monument in the town square would not make it more lasting or more known.

That’s why the first law of internet communication for business isn’t just that everything is permanent—it’s that everything is permanent, and accessible. You should assume that any internet-based communication—any email, instant message, social media update, blog post, image, or anything else—will last forever, because it will. You should also assume that any interested people, no matter how far removed, will eventually see it, because they will.
What you communicate online will likely never die and never be forgotten. The internet has a short attention span, but whatever you say will always be there.

section.title: Law #2: You Will Be Misunderstood, Often Willfully
section.para: With face-to-face communications, and in other channels as well, it’s usually safe to assume that the people receiving and interpreting our messages want to treat our meaning at least somewhat fairly. That is, we can usually count on them to interpret the message charitably: to make an effort to understand our perspective and to give us the benefit of the doubt if we haven’t been perfectly clear about something. Charitable interpretationMaking an effort to understand a certain perspective and to give others the benefit of the doubt when interpreting a message. takes place in the decoding stage, when the person receiving our message uses their emotional literacy and other techniques of communication to grasp our meaning.

In the wild west of internet communication, however, and especially on social media, we have no promise of charitable interpretation and cannot even reasonably hope for it. Our messages will be received by too many people with too many motives: most won’t care, but others will want us to be embarrassed or to fail and will actively work to bring about one or both of those outcomes. Some will ignore an obvious interpretation in order to mine our words for anything that can be twisted in another direction.

There is a reason why so many online corporate communications sound as if they were vetted by the world’s least fun team of lawyers before release to the public. Some in our audience will misunderstand us on purpose. We must expect this willful misinterpretation and take it into account in our communication.

section.title: Law #3: Some Publicity Is Bad Publicity
