section.para: You’ve probably heard the adage that “no publicity is bad publicity.” The idea would be that any amount of attention a business receives is good in the long run, since even negative attention exposes more people to the business’s existence or to its particular goods and services. It’s not clear whether this adage has ever been true, but the idea behind it isn’t necessarily unreasonable.

On the internet, however, the adage is absolutely false—some online publicity is definitely bad publicity, and it can materially harm a business or even destroy it. For example, in 2018 the customer service Twitter account for T-Mobile Austria accidentally revealed that the company stored user passwords without basic cybersecurity protections.Brandom, R. (2018, April 10). T-Mobile Austria is working to implement a basic security measure “as quickly as possible.” The Verge. The public blowback was both immediate and significant, and the company scrambled to assure its customers that it would soon implement updated protections. Here, the company’s actions brought attention that permanently changed its reputation.

Careless communication online may bring negative attention, and in most cases it’s unlikely that the attention will be for a company’s good in the end. Some publicity definitely is bad publicity, and businesses must clearly define their online and social media strategies to avoid it. We’ll discuss this issue more later in the topic.

section.title: Law #4: You Are Who You Are Thought to Be—At Least Online
section.para: In our model of communication, the decoding or interpretation stage takes place after we’ve sent a message and it’s been received by someone else. We might have done our best to make our meaning clear and appropriate for the context, but at that point it’s out of our hands. The meaning that is received and understood depends on our audience. In a sense, what we communicate is what our audience decides we communicate—the message is what it’s thought to be.

This is even more true for online communication, which most of the time lacks the contextual and nonverbal cues that otherwise signal important aspects of our meaning. We can do our best to be clear and manifest virtues like kindness and honesty, but whether our intentions are recognized or honored is not up to us.

Poor online reputations are extremely easy to create and almost impossible to expunge once they spread. That reputation will determine who we are seen to be; and who we’re seen to be might as well be who we are, since it will have that kind of power over the ways that customers and other audiences interact with us.

section.title: Why the Iron Laws Matter
section.para: Let’s be honest—the iron laws of internet communication for business are a bit of a downer. Four downers, to be exact. The laws are primarily negative, in that they focus on warnings about the uglier side of online communications. They’re sort of like a map whose goal is to walk us through a field of land mines, where one wrong move can have disastrous consequences.

The fact is, however, that online and social media communication are new worlds that are being created and explored as we speak. In addition, the parts that already exist change quickly, as new businesses, new technologies, and new audiences join the conversation.

As this new world evolves and the rules for successful internet communication change, however, some things do remain constant—and those are the things to be cautious about, or the things we ought not do. The four laws are intended to capture the parts of internet communication that are most important, but also most constant.

As we work on our strategy for a positive online presence , we can keep these laws in mind. We can also remember them as we craft individual communication and build relationships through communication. The rules might be a bit dour, but success in online communication requires the same deftness that it would take to make it through a minefield unscathed.

section.title: Relationships and Trust in Internet Communication
section.para: One of the most important parts of our communication model is the relationship between the two people communicating. As part of the context for communication, a relationship includes many things that extend beyond a particular moment, such as the history between the two and how that history has shaped the credibility that each gives to the other. In turn, two communicators may trust each other to different extents, which impacts what they’ll share and how they’ll share it.

The part of our model that sees the most drastic changes for internet communication is the context, and in no aspect of the context do we see more significant differences than in the relationship and trust that underlie an instance of communication. For the most part, internet communication still takes place between two individuals (though artificial intelligence is becoming more common, as we discuss later in this section and in a later topic). But the rules of the game online are very different.

We see some of this difference in the very idea of a “relationship” online. Virtually anything can count as a relationship, and I don’t even need to have a relationship with someone to initiate an online communication. Right now, for example, I could go on X or Instagram and send a direct message to Taylor Swift—she and I have never met, but that’s no problem. I can still message her. She won’t receive it, of course, and even if she did, she wouldn’t respond. But that isn’t the point. The point is, without a relationship at all, I’m still able to open a channel of communication that could succeed, at least potentially. That kind of access to communication was impossible before the internet.

Thus the idea of a relationship online is a much more fleeting thing, able to be created and vanish much faster than normal relationships. The trust corresponding to a relationship is also much more fleeting: it can pop into and out of existence quickly, depending on who is talking to whom and about what. Since so many of the information sources we draw on for normal communication are absent over the internet, we cannot use things like affective information or a comfortable, inviting storefront to generate and maintain trust. What we have is most often a text box, waiting to be filled with whatever seems like the most important thing we could say.

For this reason, managing relationships and trust online is a job that can quickly spiral out of hand if we’re focused on the wrong things. Chasing down trolls on Facebook probably isn’t the right thing. But what is? And how do we know it?

Here’s a way of organizing our thinking about these issues. Since online communication is in a constant state of change—the audience is changing, the content is changing, and even the means for communication are changing—it becomes even more important than usual to establish something fixed, something known and understood and well-defined. If online communication is a turbulent world, we can make it less so by sinking an anchor into a place of our choosing to hold us there, securing and making firm at least half of the components in our communication model.

For businesses online, this anchor is a constant online identity. Let’s look at some of the components from the model: on the side of communicator #1 (that’s us), we have things like our understanding of audience needs, our beliefs and desires, our emotional literacy and assertiveness, and so on. If we, as a business, understand those things about ourselves—if we know what our needs and desires are and understand the kinds of messages we want to send—then we establish ourselves as an organization with clear objectives to accomplish and clear methods to accomplish them. That identity becomes a fixed anchor that other people, when the circumstances are right, will wish to communicate with—because they’ll see our consistency, and consistency in online communication is the currency of trust.

In other words, we ought to resolve to perpetuate a well-chosen online identity, because that very perpetuation is what will create credibility and a reputation of trust—so that, when the time comes for people to communicate with us, we’ve already done a great deal of the work. We’ve already become a trusted entity online, even if we haven’t communicated with this specific client or customer before. We’ll be able to draw on a reservoir of credibility that anyone could verify, which then becomes the currency with which we develop relationships online. We’ll return to the issue of online identity later in this topic, when we discuss how to develop strategy for social media communication. For now we should note two caveats.

First, what counts as a fixed or anchored online identity will vary by organizational culture. In the previous topic we said that some organizations are more interested in and better suited for change. Such groups will often design an organizational culture whose leadership and working styles reflect this interest. If that culture ends up emphasizing flexibility, then a perfectly fixed identity online may not be possible or even desirable. That’s fine. Flexibility in itself may be an identity, and so might adaptation. A big part of creating that identity is in how it’s explained to others, which is mostly within our control.

Second, everything we’ve said about relationships, trust, and a stable online presence must be taken in light of the iron laws of online communication. Our presentation here makes the job of creating and maintaining relationships online seem easier than it actually is. Yes, we can choose our online communications, and we can design a powerful and interesting profile for our organization on the internet. But as the iron laws suggest, you will be misunderstood, often willfully, and you are who you are thought to be. The person receiving our communications is the final arbiter over what our messages will mean for them.
Nevertheless, a stable presence is still far more likely to generate and preserve trust than anything else. Consistency in online communication is the currency of trust.

section.title: Artificial Intelligence
section.para: We previously pointed out that communication online is still most likely to take place between human beings, such as in email exchanges, message board forums, or private chats. There have always been automated responses for things like customer service, but for the most part, the internet merely opens new channels for two people to communicate.

Recent years have seen a significant change here, however, and it’s one with important implications for online communication. This change is the introduction of powerful artificial intelligence (AI)Technology that mimics human intelligence. systems to the internet in general. The most well-known of these is ChatGPT, but there are others. ChatGPT is a language processing system capable not only of holding conversations but of writing other original communications as well, including things like press releases, technical manuals, employee handbooks, and other business documents. In fact, for all you know, an AI wrote this paragraph, or even this entire topic. But it didn’t, since a human wrote it. Really. No, really, a human wrote it. I promise.

Artificial intelligence seems ready to impact internet communication even more significantly in the future. However, the only honest thing we can say about that impact at this time is that we don’t yet know what it will be. There are still no accepted norms for the use of AI-generated communications and content, and individual industries and professional fields are making up the rules as they go. In academia, for example, ChatGPT seemed like an immediate threat, since students would be able to use it to write whole papers with no real effort. But in other fields it was a godsend, automating tedious work or just providing new inspiration and new connections where none would have been noticed before.

Because there are still no accepted norms for using AI in business communication, we’ll have only two things to say about it here, before returning to the issue in a later topic. The first is that, with the AI cat out of the bag, there’s no putting it back in: artificial intelligence communication is here to stay, and it’s most likely to become more prevalent. With no hope to eliminate it, then, we have a choice: will we try to work against it, or with it? Depending on your industry and role, AI may be a powerful tool.

The second is that each person using AI ought to pay attention to the rules for its use in a particular field. There is no governing body of AI ethics who tells us what is and isn’t right to do in computer-generated communication. We ourselves must be sensitive to the ways we can communicate with AI, and ought to choose those methods that seem most likely to benefit our organizations and those we communicate with. Investigate your field to determine what rules, if any, people are following in their use of AI, then follow suit.

One day AI may become common in all areas of business communication, and it may not. In the meantime, it’s one tool among many for sending messages: sometimes it might be the right one, and other times it won’t be.

section.title: Developing Strategy for Social Media Communication
Audience Demographics
section.para: The first thing to keep in mind when developing strategy for social media communication is the different audiences on different platforms. For example, in 2023 the largest demographic of Facebook users was 25–34-year-olds, making up 23.6 percent of the platform’s users in the United States. Another 18.4 percent were between 18 and 24, meaning that more than 40 percent of Facebook users in that year were 34 years old or younger.Statista. (20203, August 2). Share of Facebook Users in the United States as of August 2023, by age group. That seems like a lot, until we realize that almost 60 percent of users were therefore 35 or older.
Compare that audience to TikTok, where more than 70 percent of users in the United States are below 35. That’s a huge spread, and other services will have user bases of very different ages as well.

Platforms also differ on the kinds of people they attract. A teenage female who uses TikTok to share dance videos is probably not the kind of person who spends lots of time dissecting political controversies on Reddit.

The first part of developing social media strategy, then, is to study your audience. Where are they spending time online, and what are they doing when they get there? Age can help, as we’ve seen, but different platforms offer very different online experiences.

section.title: Brand Strategy and Content Strategy
section.para: The next step in developing strategy is to understand the difference between brand strategy and content strategy. Brand strategyA brand’s general presence associated with particular words, images, and idea. is what your online presence is like—what words, images, and ideas do people associate you with online? What sort of impression do you give off? While brand strategy is very general, content strategySpecific messages (advertisements, posts, shares) a brand will send across communication channels. is much narrower, referring to what specific messages (advertisements, posts, shares) you will send. You may have different content strategies for different communication channels or different social platforms.

It’s easy to remember the relationship between the two strategies: content follows brand. Brand strategy is more fundamental to a business’s identity and core values, and ideally will demonstrate those online. Content strategy consists of specific tactics designed to further a business’s interest by taking up specific communication plans for different segments of an online market.

Brand strategy must come before content strategy. In fact, brand strategy is the anchor we spoke about in the previous section on relationships and trust. It’s the constant identity we maintain online, and it fixes us in a place from which we then determine our more specific strategies. We can try to design content strategy without a brand strategy, but doing so would be like coming up with menu items for a restaurant whose food style you haven’t determined yet. You wouldn’t offer cheeseburgers at a fancy French restaurant, but how can you know that hamburgers are out until you decide you’re going to serve French food?

Online brand strategy must cohere with your business. CoherenceThe fit between what you do as a business and how you communicate online. refers to the fit between what you do as a business and how you communicate online. A lack of coherence is usually the result of missing or misunderstood brand strategy and often leads to ineffective or even detrimental social media use by a business.

For example, suppose you run a funeral home, which is a serious, respectful, and often formal business. Then imagine finding out that your online content manager made the following post from your business account:
section.blockquote: Lit graveside service🔥for Rosa Garcia of Denver today, who tragically suffocated in a house fire after the Nuggets game the other night. Tons of people & tears. Check out the drip on that departed!💦Still killin’ it, Ms. G! 💀💀💀
section.para: The message isn’t at all coherent with the business. It reflects a total lack of brand strategy, or perhaps a failure to translate brand strategy into effective content strategy. In short, a business of this kind just shouldn’t be sending messages like that. In addition, we’ve all seen tone-deaf corporate messages about touchy social issues, most of which feel as though they’re trying to ride a bandwagon to good publicity but doing it very poorly.
Clear and coherent brand strategy leads to effective social media communications by drawing on the relationships and trust from a consistent online identity.

section.title: Clear Objectives and Metrics
section.para: As we deploy different items of content on social media platforms, we should remember to set clear objectivesGoals for a specific content strategy, e.g. ten thousand impressions, five thousand retweets, and so on. and metricsValues that can be measured to determine whether an objective has been accomplished. . An objective is a goal for a specific content strategy: ten thousand impressions, five thousand retweets, and so on. A metric is a value we can measure to determine whether we have accomplished an objective. Most of the time we state objectives in terms of one or more metrics, but that may not always be the case.
Without objectives and metrics, it will be difficult to determine whether our content strategies are bringing the results we want.

section.title: Responsiveness
section.para: Another crucial part of our strategy will be our responsivenessThe time and effort someone spends engaging with content they didn’t create. . In social media communication, responsiveness refers to the time and effort we spend engaging with content we didn’t create. In other words, how responsive will we be as a participant in the global conversation of social media?

Our level of responsiveness should follow from our brand strategy and reflect the frequency of our content strategy. Organizations like fast-food restaurants, soft drink companies, clothing companies, and others will probably be highly responsive, since everyone is a potential customer and they want to remain at the forefront of daily online conversations. A fine arts dealer like Sotheby’s probably won’t be nearly as responsive and will be far more careful in how it curates its messages across different channels.

section.title: Cultural Sensitivity
section.para: Another issue to consider is cultural sensitivityThe extent to which we will follow prevailing norms of online interaction for things like cultural debates, cultural appropriation, and other aspects of identity differences. , or the extent to which we will follow prevailing norms of online interaction for things like cultural debates, cultural appropriation, and other aspects of identity differences.

Most people have strong feelings about cultural sensitivity and the social and political disputes it involves. Whatever your views, be reminded: social media doesn’t care what you think, and the internet doesn’t care what you think. Don’t forget the iron laws of internet communication for business. Choose brand and content strategies that allow you the greatest possible flexibility in communicating online, while making wise choices about what should and shouldn’t be said.

section.title: Crisis Contingency Plans
section.para: If we’re communicating online, and on social media in particular, mistakes are inevitable and challenges will come. How will we handle them?

Our procedure for handling mistakes and other problems in social media communication is called our crisis contingency planA procedure for handling mistakes and other problems in social media communication. .

There are two important advantages to creating a crisis contingency plan. The first is that, since we create it before everything goes wrong, we can take the time to think through the best ways to handle negative attention online. Sometimes it’s best to respond to problems with formal statements or press releases, and sometimes it’s best to ignore them. Which we ought to do depends on our business, our brand strategy, and the type of crisis we’re dealing with; but if things have hit the fan and we’re scrambling, we may not have time to think carefully about our course of action.

The second advantage of a contingency plan is that it gives us steps to follow when things go badly. When they do, we just follow the plan, trusting that we’ve already thought of what’s most important.
And don’t worry; the internet has a tendency to make mountains out of fractions of molehills. Social media won’t forget—but it will move on.

section.title: Social Media Strategy
section.para: In this section we’ve covered the basics of developing a strategy for social media communication. While it’s not an exaggeration to say that this area of business communication changes almost daily, there are still underlying principles we can apply in many situations.

Internet communication in general, and social media in particular, are volatile fields. They have the potential to make powerful impacts on our business, both positive and negative. Our model of communication applies to these fields, but we have to adapt it in various ways based on the features of internet communication. If we use these features to our advantage and build a trustworthy brand strategy, the internet can be a powerful tool for external business communications.

chapter.title: Research and Persuasion for Business Audiences

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 3: Research and Persuasion for Business Audiences. This week we will cover the following topics:

listitem.para: : Research and Crafting Effective Business Messages
: Persuasive Business Communication across Channels
: Audience, Diversity in Communication, and Accessibility

chapter.label: Topic 6
chapter.title: Research and Crafting Effective Business Messages

section.title: Research and Writing
section.para: Throughout our previous five topics, we’ve discussed many contexts for communication and the channels appropriate to them. Some of them are more formal, like a business email to a prospective client, while others are less so, like a Slack message telling someone to grab you a coffee.

While this evolving world will continue to produce new contexts and channels for business messages and interpretation, business communication at its heart will always be a part of human communication. This means that the two basic kinds of messages are those that are written and those that are spoken—and effective business communication requires competence in both.
We’ll begin to develop that competence here. The second half of this topic will discuss strategies for effective writing, and we’ll address spoken communication and business presentations later.

What these core competencies have in common, however, is researchThe process of gathering, organizing, and interpreting information in order to communicate it to others.. Research is the process of gathering, organizing, and interpreting information in order to communicate it to others. Research is a necessary part of communication in many fields and plays a crucial role in business communication in particular. Since so many business messages—think any advertisement, for example, or any pitch to potential clients—rely on our ability to package and deliver information persuasively, we must learn how to access that information in the first place.
Research, therefore, will be our subject in this topic.

Before getting started, it will help to say a word about research in general. Many books, including this one, speak of a research “process,” or a series of steps we can follow to generate and organize information. A step-by-step model can be useful for thinking about the research process, especially for those who don’t have much experience with research.

Here we would warn about thinking of the research process as something overly linear. By “linear” we mean following a series of steps in order, without looking back—when we complete one, we leave it behind and don’t worry about it again. If research were a linear process in this sense, then we could follow the same series of steps in every situation, and what might happen in the later steps wouldn’t affect the earlier ones. As long as we followed the process then we’d reach the goal.

As we'll see, though, research isn’t actually like that, and later steps can and should affect how we see the earlier ones. Rather than linear, then, a better term for the research process is iterativeRepeated one or more times, changing the process each time in response to new information or new goals.. To call a process iterative is a fancy way of saying we repeat that process one or more times, changing the process each time in response to new information or new goals. We iterate our research by gathering information, evaluating our process, redoing what’s necessary, and then gathering more information. Sometimes the iteration may take just twenty or thirty minutes, while other times it could take months or even longer. Regardless of the time, the iteration stays constant: we do things again with new information to make our output as effective as possible.

We’ll soon see a model of the research process with iteration built in. Before the process, though, we have to talk about the most important part of research and crafting effective business messages: the audience.

section.title: The Bottom Line: The Audience
section.para: By far the most important part of researching, crafting, and writing effective business messages is the audienceThe intended recipients of your message.. The audience is just the intended recipients of your message—in a conversation the audience is whoever you’re talking to, in a presentation it’s whoever is sitting in the room. No matter who it is, there is nothing more important to research and writing as tools for business communication than the audience.

On the surface this might seem a bit strange, that the most important part of the research process isn’t really a part of the research itself. After all, audience members aren’t going to help you look for reliable sources or organize your notes. So why should the audience matter?

The answer is that each business communication has a specific purpose. We’ve talked about that purpose as belonging to the context of communication, since we’re trying to send messages in order to accomplish something. And since people composing an audience are the ones we’re trying to accomplish that thing with, the beliefs, interests, and needs of our audience are absolutely essential to successful research and message crafting. In most situations, audience members, not you, will determine whether you’ve been successful. You can have the world’s snappiest business presentation, but unless it’s snappy to your audience, then your work is for nothing.

Many of these points will seem obvious—and yet, countless audiences everywhere, every day, are irritated by communications that don’t take them into account. Think about it: when were you last bored in a conversation, a meeting, or another instance of communication where you were the intended audience? Why were you so bored? The answer is probably that those communicating with you didn’t give any thought to what you were interested in or wished to hear.

Both inside and outside business, the most common way of preparing a written communication or spoken presentation goes like this: We receive an assignment to create a message. We do some research to find a few talking points, and then we stick them into a document or PowerPoint. We add more material to fill out walls of text, and then, if we’re feeling merciful, we add a few images or bad jokes to lighten the mood. Then we send our communication or give our presentation.

And even though we worked hard on it, and even though it’s important to us and might be relevant for others, our audience dislikes it. They’re unmoved and we fail to accomplish the purpose for the communication. And the reason is simple: at no point in the process did we give any real thought to the audience’s experience of our communication, or how their beliefs, interests, and needs should affect how we communicate.

In reality, the audience—along with their beliefs, interests, and needs—ought to determine not only what we say but how we say it. The audience even determines whether we need research in the first place! If throwing facts and figures at a group isn’t going to persuade them of something, then why do it? Why spend time developing a technical document when the audience doesn’t care about technical details? Why stack the deck against yourself by taking an approach the audience is likely to be antagonistic toward?

The bottom line is that we must always, always, always think of the audience first, before we start even planning our communications, much less researching. We must ask what they will want to see, what will interest them, and how the messages we could share can meet their needs. Again, this may all seem obvious in the abstract, but in practice it’s much harder to remember and commit to.

We might put it this way: one of the greatest challenges to effective business communication is overcoming our fundamental self-centeredness. Here we don’t mean self-centeredness in the sense of being selfish or narcissistic. What we mean is, in planning, researching, and delivering business communications, our tendency is to do so as though we were the audience. We therefore tend to assume that our audience knows all the background we do, wants more or less the same things as us, and understands, without much explanation, why what we’re saying should appeal to them. We know and understand all of those things, after all. So why shouldn’t they? If only they were us, they’d totally get it!

Effective research, writing, and communication require us to become aware of this self-centeredness and take action to offset it. We ask ourselves not what we want to say, but what the audience wants to hear; not what would be useful for us, but what would be useful for them. Most importantly we ask: how can we take the information we want to give, and deliver it in a form that will be appealing to them? Keep in mind, our task isn’t just to entertain—it’s to accomplish the goals behind our communication. If we’re going to do that, we have to think beyond ourselves.

In short, we must think audience first. An audience-first approachAn approach to communication that focuses on asking, who is my audience, and what do they believe, want, and need? to business communication begins by asking, who is my audience, and what do they believe, want, and need? The answers to those questions then determine what kind of communication will be best, including the channel and format. They’ll also determine what we should say and how to say it. Once we’ve made those choices, we plan and research and craft and write, but we never lose sight of those we’ll be communicating with. With an audience-first approach we’re mindful of them throughout the process, and most of our iteration, or repetition, occurs to meet their needs.

imagedata.alt: A diagram illustrating the audience-first approach. First is the audience: What are their beliefs? What are their interests? What are their needs? These questions lead to the delivery method, format & style, research, writing, and content creation. These lead back to the audience: Who are they? What is the context? What is the purpose? These questions lead to the information, which leads back to the delivery method, forma & style, research, writing, and content creation. These can lead back to the audience, or to the final message.

section.para: We’ll have a chance to develop this audience-first approach in greater detail in later topics, including in one dedicated to successful business presentations. For now we have enough of a framework to outline the research process with the audience in mind, so we’ll discuss that next.

section.title: The Research Process for Business Communication
section.para: One of the most important parts of an audience-first approach is research. Research is the process of gathering, organizing, and interpreting information in order to communicate it with others. Those “others” are our audience, and because we undertake a research project with their needs in mind, their expectations help us determine what research to do.

Remember, the audience-first approach to research we’ll discuss here isn’t set in stone. There are other ways of doing things, and with practice you’ll discover what works best for you. Departures from this approach won’t change the fundamentals, like how the audience’s expectations affect the information we need. But beyond those fundamentals, research is a flexible process and there is more than one way to do it successfully. This all-purpose model can be adapted and expanded in many directions.

section.title: The Research Process: ASOEC
section.para: This model of the research process is built around the acronym ASOECAn acronym for analyze audience, search, organize, evaluate, and craft; ASOEC is an all-purpose model for audience-first research processes.:

listitem.para: Analyze audience
Search
Organize
Evaluate
Craft

section.para: In this section we’ll elaborate on the first four parts, and we’ll save the “C,”craft, for the next section.

imagedata.alt: The ASOEC research process. Audience: What information does the audience need? In what format does the audience need the information? What is the expected level of rigor? Search: What sources do I need? Where will I find them? How many details do I need? Organize: What have I discovered? What patterns, interconnections, and meanings have I noticed? What is the logical order for presenting my findings? Evaluate: Are my sources reasonably free from bias? Would a reasonable outside observer find my sources believable and relevant? Craft: How do I frame my findings? How do I use my findings to accomplish my goal? How do my findings augment my message?

section.title: A: Audience

listitem.para: What information does the audience need?
In what format does the audience need the information?
What is the audience’s expected level of rigor?

section.para: The “A” in ASOEC stands for “audience,” or “analyze audience.” In line with our audience-first approach, our research begins with the audience.

Suppose we’re preparing an environmental impact report as part of deciding whether our business should construct a new building outside of town. A report like this one will require research, since we need details about what the construction and operation of the building will do to the area and its wildlife. So we know we need information. But what specific information we need depends on our audience.

Imagine the difference, for example, between delivering the impact report to the biology faculty at a local university, delivering it to the city council, and delivering it to Ms. Jenkins’s third-grade class. The biology faculty will mostly be PhD-holders who have spent many years doing research of their own, and will expect to see a requisite level of detail. They may not care at all about other things, though, like costs or the long-term profit viability of the location. On the other hand, the city council probably won’t want every biological detail, perhaps preferring an overview of our research findings with a mix of financial information and other points. Finally, Ms. Jenkins’s third grade class won’t care much about any of those things, and will be more interested in hearing about how all the ducks quacked when you slipped on the riverbank.

With each audience so different, each also creates very different research needs. If we aren’t attentive to those needs, we’ll miss the target in our report. Biologists really will want details—if we don’t have them, we aren’t going to seem credible or serious. The city council may not care about all the details but they probably won’t be satisfied with vague generalizations, either.

Considering the audience and their needs is the first step in the research process. It doesn’t make sense to begin any other way. Our research will be both more efficient and more effective when we take an audience-first approach. The key questions we’ll ask ourselves include, What information does the audience need? In what format does it need that information? And what is the expected level of rigor?

RigorThe exactness with which one gathers, uses, and cites information. refers to the exactness with which we gather, use, and cite information. The proper level of rigor is whatever will best accomplish the purpose at hand. We’ll have more to say about rigor later as well.

section.title: S: Search

listitem.para: What sources do I need?
Where will I find them?
How many details do I need?

section.para: The next step is “S,” to search for the information we need. The kind of information we need, along with where we need to look and the appropriate number of sources, is determined by the audience’s needs. The purpose of your communication with them is to inform and persuade. Not every document we produce needs to look like a master’s thesis. The right number of sources is however many you need to serve your purpose and no more. Some people might be impressed when you throw around superfluous bits of information, but many people will not.

The best way to begin searching is on Google or another internet search engine. If you need academic or other more rigorous sources, Google Scholar is a good place to start. Copy and paste important pieces of information along with the web addresses so you can properly cite your sources later. In the initial stages you’re looking for anything that might be relevant to what you need, so you don’t have to be too particular.

As you continue searching, though, you’ll start to see which pieces of information are more relevant to your audience and purpose, so you’ll be able to narrow your search. More focused searches will yield more focused information, which is more useful for narrower questions.

The number of details you need is part of the rigor of your research. If you need specific answers to specific questions, then you might have to look several times using different searches. Again, the level of rigor and detail required comes from the audience. If you don’t need many details, then don’t waste the effort.

The key questions to ask while searching are, What sources do I need? Where will I find them? And how many details do I need? As you answer these questions, always remember that the audience comes first.

section.title: O: Organize

listitem.para: What have I discovered?
What patterns, interconnections, and meanings have I noticed?
What is the logical order for presenting the information?

section.para: “O” is the next letter in our acronym, and that means the next step in the research process is to organize the information we’ve found. In this context, to organizeTo find themes, patterns, and interconnections among search results. information means to find themes, patterns, and interconnections among the results of your searching. What ideas or claims come up again and again? What are the most crucial points? What are the most important questions to ask about this body of knowledge?

As you organize, it can be helpful to move things around on a page so that similar pieces of information are together. Spatial organization in a document—that is, where things are located—is a huge help in organizing our thoughts.

Organizing our research and grasping patterns will help us understand the meaning of what we’ve discovered. The ability to distill a wide body of information into basic points is important for many fields, but especially for business communication.

Another important part of organization is to consider which pieces of information are more fundamental than others. One idea is more fundamentalA concept important to the process of organization; a fundamental idea is a primary idea or claim upon which everything else is based. than another if you’d have to understand the first in order to understand the second. As you organize the results of your search, keep an eye out for what is most fundamental: what is the first thing to know about this issue, or what is the idea or claim that everything else is based on?

Asking questions about what is fundamental helps us keep a focus on our audience, because in presenting information later, we’ll usually want to lead with the most fundamental points. Ask yourself, if you were to present your research to someone who knew nothing at all about it, what would you need to tell them first, and why? What points would help them frame and understand everything else? And what would come after that?

A few key questions to ask when organizing information are, What have I discovered? What patterns, interconnections, and meanings have I noticed? And what is the logical order for presenting this information?

section.title: E: Evaluate

listitem.para: Are my sources reliable?
Are my sources reasonably free from bias?
Would a reasonable outside observer think that my sources are believable and relevant?

section.para: As the research process moves forward, we get closer to deciding what pieces of information we’ll actually use to craft an effective message or presentation. Part of that decision is the “E” in our process: evaluate. In the evaluation stage, we focus on the sources: which sources of information can we expect to be most reliable? Well-known news organizations, for example, usually hold themselves to high standards of accuracy and reporting, and so they usually make for reliable sources. Random Instagram stories or Facebook posts, on the other hand, are not usually the stuff rigor is made of.

An element of reliability stems from possible biasIn the context of business communication, bias is the selective gathering or reporting of information, such that the resulting communication doesn’t tell the whole story or doesn’t tell the story fairly.. In the context of business communication, bias is the selective gathering or reporting of information, such that the resulting communication doesn’t tell the whole story or doesn’t tell the story fairly. There are at least two kinds of bias we ought to be aware of. The first is that our sources may be biased, depending on where we are drawing information. The second is that we ourselves may be biased, in that we’ve only searched for or selected information that supports our point of view while excluding everything else. This kind of searching is an instance of the confirmation biasSearching for or selecting information that supports our point of view while excluding everything else., or the tendency to seek only sources that already agree with what we think. We can avoid the confirmation bias by making a conscious effort to look for points that disagree with our view, in order to understand, if possible, the whole story.

It’s difficult to do, but as we evaluate we can try to imagine what a reasonable outside observer might say about our sources. Have we looked at all sides of the issue? Are we treating the topic fairly? We can’t answer these questions perfectly, and the very idea of a reasonable outside observer is a fiction. But we can imagine presenting our sources to someone who doesn’t have a stake in the issue—what would they say? Would the information we’ve found make the right kind of impact?
Key questions for evaluation include, Are my sources are reliable? Are my sources are reasonably free from bias? Would a reasonable outside observer think that my sources are believable and relevant?

section.title: C: Craft

listitem.para: How do I frame my findings?
How do I use my findings to accomplish my goals?
How do my findings augment my message?

section.para: The “C” is the final stage in our research process: craft. We’ll discuss the details of crafting a message with our research in the next section.

section.title: General Guidelines for Business-Oriented Research
section.para: There are a few more guidelines to add beyond the principles in ASOEC.

The first has to do with rigor. As we discussed, rigor is the exactness with which we gather, use, and cite information. The level of rigor required in our research depends on our audience, but one important distinction here is between academic research and business research.

Academic researchResearch intended for publication in academic journals by degree-holding specialists in a particular field. is research intended for publication in academic journals by degree-holding specialists in a particular field. In general, academic research requires a much higher degree of rigor, both because those involved are usually specialists, and because publication happens only after a process of peer reviewThe process in which specialists review a piece of research, like a scientific article, to check whether it is correct and exact enough to merit publication.. Peer review is the process in which specialists review a piece of research, like a scientific article, to check whether it is correct and exact enough to merit publication. Peer review is often demanding and requires careful attention to detail and sources.

In general, business researchInformation acquired to inform business decisions; the conclusions of this type of research aren't usually published in public venues, and the results of its research process are usually intended as supplements to other claims rather than the focal point of a presentation. doesn’t require the same level of rigor—not because business research is not serious work, but just because the information and conclusions usually aren’t published in public venues, and the results of the research process are usually intended as supplements to other claims rather than as the focal point of a presentation.
As always, the audience is what matters. Most academic audiences will expect a higher level of rigor than most business audiences, but that may not always be true.

The second guideline has to do with citations. In research, a citationA reference to the original source for some piece of information. is a reference to the original source for some piece of information. While in academic research the standards for citations are strict and may involve a set format, in business research just listing a website or the name of a scholarly paper is often sufficient.

The first factor in deciding how to include citations is the audience, but another factor is industry norms. If it’s customary at your organization or in your industry to cite sources in a particular way, then follow those norms. At the very least, citations should be informative enough that someone who wants to follow up could find the original source on the first or second try of an internet search.
And as a reminder, use only as many sources as you need, and no more.

section.title: ASOEC: A Process for Audience-First Research
section.para: In this section we’ve outlined ASOEC, an audience-first research process. ASOEC is iterative, which means that we repeat it as we gain more information. Beginning with the audience, we search for and organize information and then evaluate what we’ve found. This process of discovery will yield new insights, and with the new information about our audience’s expectations, we can revisit the research process to refine and prepare compelling messages in many different formats.

section.title: Crafting Messages with Original Research: Framing
section.para: The “C” in the ASOEC process stands for craft. Once we reach this stage, most of our research is probably done, we’ve organized our results and evaluated our sources, and we’re ready to communicate them to our audience. To do that we must craft, or construct, the message containing our research.

The key questions for the crafting stage of research are: How do I frame my findings? How do I use my findings to accomplish my goals? And how do my findings augment my message? We’ll say more about these questions below.

As a proficient researcher and expert communicator, it’s important to remember that you are the expert. To be fair, you may not be the world’s foremost authority on the topic you’ve researched. But if you’ve followed the research process correctly, then you know enough to speak authoritatively about that topic to your audience. And if you’ve found quality sources, then you are an expert who will use other expert sources in your presentation. You’re an authority on the issue, using other authorities to communicate your findings powerfully and persuasively.

The reason we make this point here is that many communicators, even after an effective research process, face the temptation to hide behind their sources in delivering their messages or presentations. They put all the weight of their message on their expert sources rather than using their own voice to convey the strength of the claim the sources are supposed to support. For example, if someone asks a question, they might just repeat the words of the expert source, rather than trying to explain why the source is correct in the first place. The reason for this temptation is fear: fear of taking a bold stand, fear of being wrong, and fear of coming across as a pretender or fraud.

Falling to this temptation and yielding to this fear is a mistake for two reasons. The first is that you sell yourself short as a competent, knowledgeable communicator in your own right. Believe in the research process and your ideas, and in your ability to communicate them effectively. The second is that, by abandoning your own authoritative voice, you make it much less likely that you’ll persuade anyone of anything. Confidence is its own persuasive power, and selling yourself as an expert among experts communicates confidence.
Now, crafting messages.

The most important part of crafting messages with original research is to choose the correct frame. Every communication, no matter the message or the medium, has a frame. The frameHow we say what we want to say; the way we present our research or how we talk about what we want to persuade our audiences of. for a communication is how we say what we want to say—it’s the way we present our research or how we talk about what we want to persuade our audiences of. The frame is more than just the content of the message or the meaning we intend to convey. The frame is how we express that content and what shape we give to the meaning. The frame isn’t what we say; it’s how we say it.

We may think of the frame for a message or presentation as the packaging used to deliver it. We can deliver a package in many different ways: in a gift bag, wrapped like a present, or just thrown at the recipient. All these methods of delivering a package eventually accomplish the same purpose—they get the package to its intended recipient—but they all do so in very different ways. Our choice of one way over the others says something about our attitude toward the gift, its recipient, and the whole gift-giving process.

Likewise, the way we present a message says something about our attitude toward the message and the audience we intend to receive it. Even simple choices like what font to use or how to organize a document reflect specific decisions that can affect how an audience views the message.

Let’s think about frames in the context of crafting a message with our original research, then. In using research, we write as an authority who uses other authorities to make or support a certain point. Our voice as communicators should never be subordinate to the research; in other words, we’re in control.

This means that the most important part of framing our research is to cast ourselves as authorities who rely on other authorities. The research is therefore not the focal point of the message we craft—the information we wish to communicate is the focal point, and our research is a supplement to that. To put this in terms of frames—we begin by establishing what we want to accomplish by our communication. Our purpose isn’t just to share some nice facts we discovered, it’s to persuade people of our view and to commit them to action. We use the framing of our message to control the context of our communication and to encourage our audience to see the message the way we want them to see it, rather than the other way around.

Sometimes the research that required hours to do might only take up a single slide in a business presentation or report. That’s fine. It might take up more. That’s fine too. As always, the audience plays the decisive role: the best way to frame something is whatever way will make the most powerful impact on the audience.

The most important factor in choosing one frame for a message over another is our audience. Each piece of writing—each email, each paper, each story, each journal entry—has an audience, even if that audience is just ourselves. The way our audience thinks and understands our communications with them is determined by things like their identity, their background and education level, their expectations, and their previous relationship with us. All these considerations and more affect how we want to frame what we write. Choosing the correct frame for a certain audience will make the audience more receptive to our message and more likely to act as we want.

Do we want our message to create feelings of energy and excitement and make people believe that something significant is about to happen? Then we will want to choose words that are upbeat and positive. Do we want our message to make people pause and consider their own lives in light of what they are reading? Then we will want to choose precise words that express important questions at the right moments.

Many of these points may appear obvious, but they can actually be very difficult to accomplish in our writing. Much of the struggle in writing comes in trying to produce the first draft. Sometimes a half-baked draft can be enough to fulfill the requirements of an assignment, but in other cases, we will have to put much more precision and effort into our writing.

In our model of communication, nonverbal messages and other aspects of the model can be included in the framing as well. Ideally, we enter the research process with clear objectives for what we want to accomplish. If the nonverbal aspects help us reach those objectives, then they belong. If not, then they don’t.

In many situations, how something is said can be just as important as or even more important than what is said. The what is the content, the research, the message; the how is the frame. Learning to control the framing requires us to think beyond what we want to say in order to pay attention to the ways we will say it. Those ways often seem less important than the content of our message, but they aren’t—they often make the difference between successful and unsuccessful communication. As we observed previously in discussing emotional literacy and the other fundamentals of interpersonal communication, so much of human interaction happens beneath the surface, below the words and the sentences we spend so much time composing.
Crafting effective messages is about controlling the framing to present our audience with the information we need them to receive, delivered in the way best suited to allow them to receive it.
We’ll continue to discuss framing in future topics.

section.title: Crafting with AI: The Pitfalls of Artificial Tone
section.para: We’ve seen that once you have analyzed your audience, searched for information, and organized your data, you arrive at the Craft stage. In modern workplaces, it is becoming common to use generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, to help with this step. You might paste your research notes into one of these tools, for example, and ask it to use that information in order to “write a persuasive email.”

There is nothing inherently wrong with this practice. While AI is excellent at grammar and structure, though, it often struggles with the concept of frame, in the many ways we’ve discussed it. This is because AI lacks the social context to know if your relationship with the reader or audience is formal, friendly, tense, or collaborative. As a result, AI-generated drafts often suffer from “tone drift,” or messaging that sounds overly robotic, aggressively demanding, or unnaturally enthusiastic.

section.title: Identifying and Revising AI Tone Mistakes
section.para: Let’s see an example. Imagine you need to ask your supervisor for additional software licenses to finish a project. You paste your research and data into an AI tool, and it generates the following draft:

sidebar.para: Subject: Urgent Requisition for Software Capital
Dear Management,

It is imperative that we immediately acquire five additional licenses for the design software. The current lack of resources is a catastrophic bottleneck that is impeding our workflow optimization. To facilitate the synergistic outcome of the project paradigm, we require an immediate injection of funds to procure these assets.
We are thrilled to announce that without these licenses, the project will fail to meet the deadline. Please process this payment by end of day to ensure we can continue our journey toward excellence.
Sincerely,
The Design Team

section.para: What tone issues or other problems do you notice in this message? Take a moment to think to yourself.

First, note how the AI frames the request as a demand (“imperative,” “immediate injection”). It uses hollow buzzwords (“synergistic outcome,” “paradigm”) that obscure the communication’s meaning. Worst of all, it pairs “thrilled to announce” with the threat that the “project will fail.” It is a framing disaster.

How could we use a human touch to create a better frame and craft a more effective piece of communication? Here’s one possible revision, which focuses on solutions and benefits instead of demands and buzzwords:

sidebar.para: Subject: Resource Request—Ensuring On-Time Project Delivery
Hi Deena,
To make sure we meet the final deadline for the website launch next Friday, the design team needs five temporary software licenses.

The reason why is that all our current licenses are fully booked. This means that two designers have a lot of downtime. By purchasing these licenses, a $500 total cost, we will be able to double our output speed this week. That way we can meet the deadline for the launch.
Please let me know if you approve this expense so we can stay on schedule. We’re looking forward to wrapping this up!

section.para: The lesson here is that while AI is great for generating text, it cannot generate judgment. As the communicator, you are responsible for the final output. Do not just view AI-generated drafts as finished products. See them instead as raw material requiring your refinement. It’s up to you to craft an appropriate frame and to establish a suitable human tone. Considering frame and tone will make it much more likely that a message actually serves its purpose.

section.title: Practice with Sentence Tone
section.para: To help you develop a sense for tone issues, let’s look at three specific AI-generated sentences where the framing went wrong. Then we’ll see how we could fix them.

listitem.para: Flawed: “It is requested that the recipient of this correspondence acknowledge receipt immediately to facilitate record maintenance.”

section.para: This sounds like a legal summons, not a business email. Can we make it more human? How about this?

listitem.para: Revised: “Please reply to confirm you received this email. Thanks!”

section.para: Most of the time, simple is best.
Here’s a second sentence:

listitem.para: Flawed: “I am delighted to inform you that your application for the loan has been rejected due to insufficient credit history, but we wish you the best!”

section.para: Here we see a common problem—AI often tries to be “polite” by adding happy introductory phrases (“delighted to inform you”) as a preface to bad news. But for a person this framing is confusing and insulting. Here’s a possible revision:

listitem.para: Revised: “Thank you for applying. Unfortunately, we cannot approve your loan at this time due to . . .”

section.para: The bad news is the same, but it’s delivered more respectfully.
Now take a look at this last sentence:

listitem.para: Flawed: “We are leveraging key learnings to pivot our ideation toward a more value-added ecosystem.”

section.para: The word choice in this sentence frames the writer as someone trying to sound smart without saying anything. Simplification will help:

listitem.para: Revised: “We are using the survey results to improve our product features.”

section.para: Once again, simple is usually best. We’re communicating with people, not robots.

As you gain experience with AI-generated text, continue to consider how you can revise tone issues and other problems in order to craft better messages. A later topic will examine how to plan your communication strategy specifically for AI prompting. For now, just remember that you own the frame, not the AI.

section.title: Clarity and Written Communication
section.para: To finish this topic, we’ll add a few points about clarity in written communication. We’ll have a chance to discuss clarity in verbal presentations later.

There are lots of ways to write effectively, but since this isn’t a writing course, we can’t adequately cover all or even many of them. You have your own style, and the best way to develop it and strengthen your voice as a communicator in written media is to practice. Try different approaches and get feedback from others on what works best and why.

The best general advice for improving written communication is to write simplyTo use normal language and uncomplicated sentences. and directlyTo say clearly what you mean without fluff.. To write simply means to use normal language and uncomplicated sentences. To write directly means to say clearly what you mean without fluffWriting that adds nothing to the purpose of a communication other than to make it longer and seem more intelligent, often by using fancy words and complicated sentences.. Fluff is writing that adds nothing to the purpose of a communication other than to make it longer and seem more intelligent, often by using fancy words and complicated sentences.

Business communicators are especially susceptible to fluff and other bad writing habits. They think they will fit in with the crowd by using words like “leverage” and “synergize” as part of long, flowery sentences. Perhaps, they think, they can dazzle the reader with the marvelous ability of going many lines without using a period. They can be forgiven for thinking so, since many of the authors they read fill their writing with that sort of nonsense.

The reality is, however, that the exact opposite is true: you will stand out from the crowd as an expert communicator by not writing that way. Simple and direct writing, especially in business, will shine as crystal-clear messaging, accessible to all audiences. It will mark you as an authority to be taken seriously. It is powerful, interesting, and persuasive. Do whatever you can to avoid the indulgent excesses of your colleagues, and write more simply and directly.

Just as we wish to control the context of communication, so we also wish to control the sentences we craft. A well-crafted sentence can leave a lasting impact on both author and reader. We can begin crafting and controlling our writing by asking ourselves, What purpose does my next sentence need to accomplish? Then we write a sentence that accomplishes that purpose. After that, we ask the same question about the next sentence and write another one. We do the same again and again. Before we know it, we’ll have a group of sentences that, by achieving small purposes individually, can achieve much larger purposes together.

Another strategy for constructing simple, direct sentences is to consider how you would use plain language to explain the issue to a friend who didn’t know anything about the topic. The words that come to mind will probably be simple, direct ways to express the idea. Then you just write those words. They may not be perfect, but they’ll be a start.

After you’ve completed a piece of writing, try reading it out loud to yourself. Make sure to pause where you have commas, use a questioning tone when you read a question, and so on. You’ll find that this technique will catch many of your problems for you. Troubling spots will not sound natural or will trip you up as you try to read them. When things don’t sound natural to you as the author, you can bet they won’t sound natural to anyone else, either.

Clarity in written communication takes practice. As we present our research and learn how to frame it correctly for our audiences, we’ll become communicators who can share their expertise and craft compelling, purpose-driven messages.

section.title: Persuasion: A Criterion of Success in Business Communication
section.para: At its most basic level, persuasionThe process of getting people to believe or do what you want them to believe or do. is the process of getting people to believe or do what you want them to believe or do. You might try to persuade someone that a certain benefits package is in their best interest, for example, or that they should dine at one restaurant rather than another. Persuasion is also a skill: there are principles for doing it well, and we can improve by practicing.

Most professions involve persuasion in some way, but it’s an absolutely essential part of business and business communication in particular. Management, client relations, customer service, and human resources are just a few of the fields where persuasion is not only part of the job but, to a great extent, is the job. And that group doesn’t even include sales, where virtually the only standard of success is whether you were able to persuade someone to buy a product or service. For the human side of business at least, persuasion is fundamental.

Persuasion also fits into our model of communication as one of the overarching purposes for which we communicate in the first place. One such purpose is to informCommunicating in order to share information with someone.: we communicate in order to share information with someone. Another is to understandCommunicating in order to receive information from others and appreciate their point of view.: we communicate in order to receive information from others and appreciate their point of view. Persuasion is a third overarching purpose: we communicate to get others to believe or do what we want.

As one of the broad purposes behind communication in general, then, persuasion becomes one of the most important criteria by which we judge our success. A criterion of successThe standard or measuring-stick we use to evaluate whether we’ve been successful at something. is the standard or measuring-stick we use to evaluate whether we’ve been successful at something. We use a criterion of success to figure out whether we accomplished a goal. So, say our goal in sending a message to a job recruiter is to persuade them to give us an interview. The purpose of our communication is to persuade, and that becomes our criterion—whether we succeed depends on whether we got an interview or not. If we did, that’s success. If not, something about our communication didn’t work.

In addition, as we saw in the previous topic, persuasion is one of the primary goals of original research and crafting messages around that research. In many research and presentation situations, the goal is not merely to inform an audience but also to persuade them to act. If the research for our environmental impact report reveals that constructing a new building would do catastrophic damage to a local ecosystem, then the purpose of our report isn’t just to tell people about that—it’s to convince them to construct the building somewhere else. And we’ll know we’ve been successful if that’s what they end up doing.

Persuasion brings together many of the points from the previous topic about our audience. We don’t persuade in a vacuum—that is, we can’t talk of persuading without talking about who we want to persuade and what we want them to do. We’re trying to persuade people, a particular audience, and throughout this topic we’ll always have them in mind, either explicitly or implicitly.

In line with the previous topic, in fact, we might say that our approach to persuasion will be audience-first, just like our approach to research. But it may sound funny to put it that way, since any attempt at persuasion that doesn’t put the audience first isn’t likely to be very effective. It might not be obvious that our audience is the first concern in research, but it’s clear that the audience must come first in persuasion.
With that in mind, everything we said in the previous topic about the primacy of the audience applies here as well.
But there’s more to say, and it may help here to explain the “across channels” part of the topic title.

Every channel of communication, from snail mail to TikTok, has its best and worst practices. Some strategies for eliciting a response on Facebook are better than other strategies; some techniques for getting subscribers on YouTube are more effective than others. Customizing a message for these platforms involves understanding the best practices and putting them to work.

In addition to these platform-specific best practices, though, there are underlying principles that apply regardless of platform. These principles come not from the details of a technology but from the ways human beings think and interact with each other. Because it’s always a person using TikTok, Facebook, YouTube, or an office email, the underlying principles can help us be successful across channels, rather than just on a single one.

And that’s what we’ll learn here: principles of persuasion that aren’t limited to a particular channel, but apply widely, to all kinds of communication. The goal of our whole course is to become an effective communicator, and the next step is to become an effective persuader, since persuasion is so basic to business communication.

One note before getting started. Although the principles we’ll cover apply in all areas of business communication, here we are not primarily concerned with sales or sales techniques. Persuasion is the basic task of sales, and no doubt much of what we say will apply to those in sales professions. But we are not focusing on the sales profession. Instead, we’ll emphasize approaches that translate well to any industry, so that anyone can use them.

section.title: The Principles of Persuasion
section.para: In this section we’ll discuss four principles of persuasion. As mentioned in the previous section, these four principles range across channels of communication and so will be effective no matter the situation or means of message delivery. They arise not from the specifics of a particular context or goal but from the ways people think and interact with each other.
Here are the four principles of persuasion:

listitem.para: Adapt the message
Control the frame
Be what the audience needs
Remember that everything is persuasion

section.para: Let’s get into the details.

section.title: Principle #1: Adapt the Message
section.para: Without question, the most important principle of persuasion is message adaptationThe ability to customize a message to meet the needs of a particular audience and situation.: the ability to customize a message to meet the needs of a particular audience and situation. Indeed, near the beginning of a review of research literature on persuasion, communications studies professor Daniel O’Keefe wrote, “If there is one skill that is most fundamental to persuasive success, it is message adaptation—adapting or tailoring one’s persuasive efforts to the particular situation faced, the particular audience to be influenced.”O’Keefe, D. J. (2019). Persuasion. In O. Hargie (Ed.), The handbook of communication skills (4th ed.). Routledge, p. 319. Everything else depends on message adaptation, and our skill as persuaders is almost entirely determined by the creativity and insight with which we customize our message to a particular audience.

Adapting a message requires that we understand the audience and their needs. We want them to believe or do something—that’s the reason we’re communicating with them in the first place. But how do we get them to want what we want? The only way is to start from wherever our audience already is. In other words, we begin persuading on the basis of what our audience already believes and wants. From those starting points, we work toward what we want, adapting our message along the way so it takes the audience from where they are to where we want them to be.

Message adaptation also requires a willingness to break from the natural self-centeredness we talked about in the previous topic. Most of the time we’re so wrapped up in our own heads that we don’t pay attention to the signals others are sending us. But those signals are crucial for customizing our message toward a particular goal. Skilled communicators are able to step outside of themselves when necessary, to focus on what the audience needs.

If we see message adaptation as a way of getting our audience where we want them to go, we can also ask, why aren’t they already there? Persuasion experts Martin Fishbein and Icek Ajzen suggest a few reasons:

listitem.para: they have a negative attitude toward the behavior we want;
they believe other people have a negative attitude toward the behavior we want;
they may not have control over the behavior;
they think the behavior would be a good idea, but haven’t yet formed an intention to do it.Fishbein, M., & Ajzen, I. (2010). Predicting and changing behavior. Routledge.

section.para: The way we adapt our message will depend on which of these reasons explains why our audience isn’t already doing what we want them to. For example, if someone has a negative attitude about our message, then adapting it to overcome that challenge will push our adaptation in one direction; on the other hand, if our audience thinks they don’t have control over what we hope they’ll do, then our adaptation will have to go in a different direction.

And, of course, we can only know the correct direction if we’re paying attention to our audience. Even subtle changes in tone of voice or other nonverbal cues can suggest that we’re missing the mark. The better we’re able to discern those cues, the better we’ll be at adapting our message on the fly, even in the middle of a sentence.

Message adaptation is about more than just changing our words. It might involve slowing down, inviting others to speak, dropping a topic entirely, or even cutting off a bad communication before it gets worse. If the long-term goal is persuasion, then we must be willing to adapt in many different directions.

section.title: Principle #2: Control the Frame
section.para: The second principle of persuasion is frame controlManaging aspects of the communication frame, at least as much as one is able.. The frame for a message is how we communicate it. Frame includes things like level of detail and the logical development of a message, but it also includes parts of the context of communication, like who initiates a communication or where we’re meeting. Those may seem like insignificant aspects of an interaction, but they can have a major impact on whether we’re able to persuade. Frame control is managing those aspects of the communication frame, as least as much as we’re able.

Frame control is not totally independent of message adaptation. To see why, we can compare a persuasion-oriented communication opportunity with a realtor showing a house. The realtor has a goal: she wants to persuade the buyers to buy this house. So she invites them to a viewing and plans what she’ll show them—the living room first, followed by the playroom, then the kitchen and the bedrooms. During the visit she’ll also talk about the house and its features.

In this example, the circumstances and plan for the visit are the frame: the time of day, who else will be there, the order of the showing, and so on. The realtor has control over many of these things and so uses them to set the frame of her attempt to persuade. Message adaptation, on the other hand, is what she says and how she modifies her plan during the visit. Perhaps she discovers the couple has no intention of ever having children—why would she show them the playroom? She adapts her message as she goes to bring her audience to where she wants them to be.

Our frame is the way we see the world, and the frame for a communication is how we see the world in which that communication takes place. We control the frame by inviting our audience to step inside a world of our choosing. A little bit at a time, starting with their beliefs and desires, we invite them to see things differently. As with message adaptation, frame control requires knowledge of our audience and attention to how they’re receiving our message.

section.title: Principle #3: Be What the Audience Needs
section.para: The third principle of persuasion is to be what the audience needs. We can call it the “chameleonChameleons are lizards that change colors depending on their circumstances, to stick out or blend into the background. The chameleon principle emphasizes that we, as the communicators intending to persuade, are the one who must change first.” principle: chameleons are lizards that change colors depending on their circumstances, to stick out or blend into the background. The chameleon principle picks up where the first two principles leave off by emphasizing that we, as the communicators intending to persuade, are the ones who must change first. That is, if we hope the audience will change their behavior, then we must first change ours in order to make their change possible.

The image of a chameleon may suggest that we’re just puppets or that we’re grifters who will say whatever we think our audience wants to hear. But that isn’t the right way to understand this principle.
