Being what the audience needs means that we take our character and strengths and combine them with the information our audience gives us, to close the gap between where they are and where we want them to end up. We’re willing to change what we do to bring about a change in them, because we understand what’s still lacking in them.

Being what the audience needs calls on the fundamentals of interpersonal communication: reinforcing, reflecting, listening, explaining, self-disclosure, and all the rest. It’s a principle that demands skills in those fundamentals and vigilant monitoring of whether our current actions are working or not.
In a sense, persuasion puts to the test all the most important skills of business communication, from the beginning of our communication model to the end.

section.title: Principle #4: Remember That Everything Is Persuasion
section.para: The fourth and final principle of persuasion is that everything is persuasion. This principle calls back to an idea we introduced in the first topic—that everything is communication. That idea is that every part of our behavior and the context in which we interact is part of a communication. From where we meet to how we dress, everything communicates a message and offers information about us to anyone willing to listen.

And the same is true for persuasion: everything is persuasion in that every behavior and aspect of the context can make a difference in our ability to persuade. Humans are fickle decision-makers and sometimes make choices for the tiniest reasons. While we can’t control everything, we owe it to ourselves as communicators and persuaders to give ourselves the best chance of sending clear messages and getting others to buy in. With that expectation in mind, we should remember that everything is persuasion.

section.title: The Four Principles of Persuasion
section.para: The four principles of persuasion are general guides for how to communicate with others when we intend to persuade them. How we apply them to specific situations will depend on that situation’s specific details. But the principles all stem from a concern for our audience and where they’re at, and how we can take them somewhere else. Across different channels and means of communication, that concern always matters.
By its nature, business communication often ends up involving persuasion. Putting the principles of persuasion into practice calls on all our knowledge and skills as communicators.

section.title: Persuasion by Reasoning
section.para: As noted before, the principles of persuasion are general guides for how to communicate when we intend to persuade others. We can apply them in many situations, always keeping in mind our audience and what will best move them.

In addition to those principles, there are two general approaches we can take to persuasion, and in both we can apply one or more of the principles. The first general approach is persuasion by reasoning. The second is persuasion by emotion. We’ll cover the first here and the next in the next section.

Persuasion by reasoningAn attempt to persuade someone by using reason and evidence. is an attempt to persuade someone by using reason and evidence. Most attempts at persuasion by reasoning use argumentsAny set of statements where some of them, called the premises, support another, called the conclusion.. An argument is any set of statements where some of them, called the premises, support another, called the conclusion. A premiseA piece of evidence or reason in favor of a conclusion. is a piece of evidence or reason in favor of a conclusion. A conclusionThe point we want to persuade our audiences of. is the point we want to persuade our audiences of.
Here is a sample argument:

listitem.para: The new communications software will reduce customer service costs by 31%.
The new communications software will better organize internal messaging.
The new communications software will gather data and track useful patterns.
Therefore, we should adopt the new communications software.

section.para: In this argument, statements 1–3 are the premises, because they are the evidence in favor of the conclusion. The conclusion, statement 4, is what the argument is trying to persuade an audience about. The premises give the reasons why someone should believe the conclusion or take the action it suggests.

When we persuade by reason, we use arguments like that sample to summarize our evidence and show how it relates to our overall point. An argument is strong when it has more evidence and when the evidence more directly relates to the conclusion. For example, in the sample argument, each premise gives a good reason to adopt the new communications software. Now imagine another premise: “The new communications software will look good in our office because it has a cool box.” That statement isn’t relevant to the conclusion and so doesn’t offer any support. Including it as a premise in the argument would have made the argument weaker, and an argument whose only premise was that statement would be very weak.

There are many different types of arguments. Some of the more common ones in business communication include inductiveArguments that simply list the available evidence in support of a conclusion. arguments, which simply list the available evidence in support of a conclusion; generalizationsStatements that take information about a small sample and infer a conclusion about a larger group., which take information about a small sample and infer a conclusion about a larger group; arguments by analogyArguments that draw relationships of similarity between two things., which draw relationships of similarity between two things; and causal argumentsArguments that either reason about the cause of something on the basis of the effects it produces, or consider the effects of a proposed action., which either reason about the cause of something on the basis of the effects it produces, or consider the effects of a proposed action.

More important than memorizing the various argument types is understanding that, in persuasion by reasoning, arguments are better when they have more evidence and when that evidence more directly relates to the conclusion. And arguments are best when both the premises and the conclusion connect to the audience’s needs and interests.

The question of whether to use persuasion by reasoning is, as with everything else we’ve discussed, determined by what will best convince an audience. Generally speaking, audiences with more expert knowledge or stronger educational backgrounds will be more susceptible to persuasion by reasoning. The explanation for this isn’t that other people are too dumb; rather, audiences with experts or other highly-educated people are accustomed to the language of reasoning and argument, and meeting them at that level allows us to speak their language in our attempt to persuade.
Keeping a few other points in minds will help when working to persuade by reasoning.

First, good pieces of reasoning will present both sides of an argument, and may even acknowledge that the opposing side is strong. The fact that the opposing point of view has strong evidence does not mean our conclusion is incorrect; it merely means the issue we’re making an argument about is complex. Presenting both sides and acknowledging conflicting evidence suggests to your audience that you’re an authority on the issue, that you’re being honest, and that a fair evaluation of the evidence—which you’ve performed in your research—will lead to your conclusion. These are all valuable parts of persuasion by reasoning.

Second, good pieces of reasoning consider and respond to objections. An objectionA counter-argument, or an argument against our point of view. is a counter-argument, or an argument against our point of view. Beyond just acknowledging the strength of opposing evidence, we can also present the full argument against our view. Then we can respond to it, or explain why it’s not as strong as it seems. This feature of persuasion by reasoning demonstrates the same authority and honesty to our audience, which makes them more likely to take our conclusion seriously.

Third, it is best to present arguments by giving one part at a time, with adequate explanation for each part. In the sample argument, we would convince our audience of each premise by providing information backing up those statements. But some premises are more obviously true than others. Spend time supporting more complex premises and try to keep the information flow steady—not too little and not too much, in an amount adapted to the comprehension of the audience.

Fourth, audiences love arguments that involve examples or applications. An exampleA situation, real or imagined, that demonstrates the point we want to make. is a situation, real or imagined, that demonstrates the point we want to make. An applicationA way an argument matters or makes a difference in real life. is a way an argument matters or makes a difference in real life. Powerful examples might include striking visuals or interesting stories that illustrate an argument’s point. Powerful applications connect with what an audience wants to do, showing them the benefits of accepting a certain conclusion.

Finally, it isn’t always necessary to include everything we know about a topic in a particular argument. The best argument is the one that will best convince our audience. Even when we have information directly relevant to our conclusion, we might not include it if we determine it won’t connect with the needs or interests of our audience. This is also true for research. Spending hours on research is not by itself a reason to include the results of our research. Learn when to cut. Sometimes, leaving something out can make a greater impact than putting something in.

Persuasion by reasoning is a general approach to convincing others, where we use logic, evidence, and arguments. Any effective business communicator must master how to gather information and form an argument.
Sometimes, though, we’ll have to admit that arguments and reasoning aren’t the way to go. Fortunately, they aren’t the only approach.

section.title: Persuasion by Emotion
section.para: The second general approach is persuasion by emotionPersuasion by emotion leaves aside reason, evidence, and argument in favor of feelings.. Persuasion by emotion leaves aside reason, evidence, and argument in favor of feelings. The goal of this approach to persuasion is to induce a certain feeling in our audience, and then to connect that feeling to a certain conclusion or action.

Persuasion by emotion works through the process of dissonanceAny unsettling or otherwise upsetting feeling; a state our audience wants to get out of or eliminate. and resolutionEscaping or eliminating dissonance.. Dissonance here means any unsettling or otherwise upsetting feeling; it’s a state our audience wants to get out of or eliminate. Resolution is escaping or eliminating dissonance. For the purposes of persuasion, we usually want to offer a resolution in terms of what we’re trying to convince people to believe or do.

The process of dissonance and resolution could work with many emotions, though it often uses negative or unpleasant ones. There is a reason for this. Negative emotions tend to more effectively persuade people than positive ones. If we induce a positive emotional state in our audience, then we’ve already given them the reward, so to speak, without them needing to be convinced. On the other hand, negative emotions require resolution, and that’s where our message comes in.
The emotions we’ll discuss here are hypocrisy and guilt, fear, and anger.

Inducing emotions of hypocrisy or guilt in someone requires that we convince them they’ve done something wrong. This may be direct, such as when we offer evidence of their wrongdoing or negligence. It may also be more subtle, such as when we hint about people like our audience or give an example that hits uncomfortably close to home.

Persuading with hypocrisy or guilt also requires that we know a lot about our audience. Some people who have acted wrongly will simply not accept accusations about it. Others will be angry that we’ve called them out. Without great sensitivity to our audience, attempting to induce these emotions may just make our listeners angry at us. Anger toward us as communicators isn’t always a bad thing, but it does make our audience less likely to be convinced of our claims.

When these feelings are the dissonance, the resolution is a way to make up for the alleged wrong. In many cases this resolution will come by accepting a course of action we propose—the thing we were trying to convince our audience of in the first place.

The next emotion is fear. We induce fear in others by scaring them, often by discussing what might happen if they don’t follow our advice or otherwise make some change in their behavior. Fear is an effective motivator in many organisms and works for human beings as well. A more detailed knowledge of what people fear will make our messages even more convincing.
Anxiety and worry are closely related to fear and will act the same way in situations of persuasion.

We resolve a fear-based dissonance by showing how to eliminate the source of the fear. If our audience comes to adopt our point of view, for example, they’ll be able to avoid certain harmful consequences; if they follow our advice, they’ll get rid of what’s scaring them or causing anxiety.

The final emotion we’ll discuss here is anger. People feel anger when they perceive that someone has harmed them or someone they care about, or when they feel that they’ve been treated unfairly. There are many ways to induce anger, as most of the world learns anew each day as they spend time on the internet or social media.

One effective method is to argue that an individual or group deserves something, or has earned it or has a right to it. Not receiving what has been (allegedly) rightly earned tends to upset most people. Another effective method—one that’s even easier—is to show the audience opinions with which they disagree. Especially in polarized social and political climates, the mere consideration of opposing points of view often makes people angry.

Anger as dissonance leads to the resolution to do something about a perceived inequity or wrong. The action that amends the wrong will be what we wish to convince our audience of. The closer we can link the source of the anger to our proposed solution, the better we’ll be at persuading.

In this section we’ve been discussing ways to use emotion to persuade. Most people, at one time or another, have been on both sides of this communication: sometimes they’ve been the ones feeling the unpleasant emotions and looking to resolve them, and at other times they’ve been trying to get others to feel those things in order to spark some kind of change.

While these experiences are universal, it is worth considering the ethical dimension of persuasion by emotion. This approach to convincing others can be effective literally beyond the point of reason, in that when people are very emotional, they are no longer capable of reasoning. Persuasion by emotion is also the tool of effective communicators who have harmful intentions, since trying to persuade by reason would reveal either the weakness of their ideas or the immorality of their intentions.

But how to use a method of persuasion so unreasonably potent is something we ought to consider with care. In many cases of business communication, the possible harm from adopting a belief or course of action is minimal—most of the time, we aren’t debating life or death. But in other cases, our persuasion can have much more far-reaching effects, and there will be an ethical dimension to our communications decisions.

If part of being a good communicator is being skilled in persuasion by reason and by emotion, then another part is the wisdom to know when a certain mode is appropriate and when it isn’t. Individual business communicators are not responsible for the difficult moral situations created by societies, governments, and businesses. But they are responsible for their own actions, and whether and how to influence the behavior of others is an issue that should, at least some of the time, force us to stop and think.

section.title: Monroe’s Motivated Sequence Model
section.para: To complete our discussion of persuasive business communication across channels, we’ll offer a template for use in many different situations—the “motivated sequenceStages intended to motivate an audience: (1) attention, (2) need, (3) satisfaction, (4) visualization, and (5) call to action.,” created by Alan Monroe. We can customize this template for any persuasion-oriented situation of communication. Its different steps are stages we move through with our audience to help them reach the point we want them to accept.

The five stages of the motivated sequence are (1) attention, (2) need, (3) satisfaction, (4) visualization, and (5) call to action. Together the stages make up a sequence of stages intended to motivate an audience.

section.title: Attention
section.para: At the attention stage we grab our audience’s attention with a striking story or fact. The point here is to get them to listen to us and go with us to the next stage. As with everything else, the exact content we use at the attention stage depends on our audience and what they expect to hear from us. We can also ask ourselves, what would be interesting for us to hear? We should always prioritize what we know of the audience, however.

section.title: Need
section.para: The need stage is where we tell our audience what is wrong and why it’s wrong. Most of the time they’ll already know, and our discussion of the need is meant to prepare them for the next stage.

Remember that we must frame the need in ways that will best reach our audience. We should use terms and examples that they will understand and that will be meaningful to them. As best we’re able, we must step outside of ourselves in order to experience the need from their point of view, if possible. Remember, we aren’t trying to persuade ourselves—we’re already convinced of our message. The audience always comes first.
The need stage of the motivated sequence is a great place to showcase research we’ve gathered. This stage also corresponds roughly to dissonance in the process of persuasion by emotion.

section.title: Satisfaction
section.para: If we’ve captured our audience’s attention and managed to keep it long enough to demonstrate a certain need, then we’re ready for the satisfaction stage. Here we deliver our message, customized to our audience, in a way that shows how it will resolve their need. We may rely on more research here, but the key is to connect what we’re offering with what the audience lacks: how will we make up that lack? What changes for the better will our audience experience by adopting our point of view?

In the section on persuasion by reasoning, we emphasized that we don’t want to move too quickly in discussing an argument—we pace ourselves by making the flow of information match the difficulty of the material. A similar caution applies here. The satisfaction stage is crucial to the outcome of the motivated sequence—if we don’t make absolutely clear the connection between what the audience lacks and what we’re offering, then we won’t persuade them of anything. It’s worth taking time to make sure we do this properly in ways that connect with the audience’s knowledge and interest.

section.title: Visualization
section.para: At the visualization stage, we help the audience imagine what things would be like if they listened to us. What would be different? How would their need be resolved? What sorts of things could they expect to experience? Our goal is to get them to experience the answers to these questions with vivid descriptions of what might be.
On its own, the visualization stage sounds a bit unusual. Why would we take time for it? It may sound fun, but what’s the point of getting our audience to visualize?

To explain why visualization matters, we can return to the advice of Fishbein and Ajzen from a previous section. They outlined reasons our audience isn’t currently doing what we want them to. One of those reasons is that, while they may think the behavior is a good idea, they haven’t yet formed an intention to do it. The purpose of the visualization stage is to bridge that gap. We’ve already told them why our message is a good idea. Now we need to turn the good idea into a real intention to act, and we do it with an expressive, detailed picture of our audience’s possible future.

section.title: Call to Action
section.para: The final stage in the motivated sequence is the call to action. This stage is exactly what it sounds like: we call on our audience to act—according to the need we’ve identified, the satisfaction we’ve suggested, and the visualization we’ve painted.

In the call to action, we ask that our audience put all the pieces we’ve given them together. If we’ve done our job correctly, they won’t need anything else to see why we’ve offered them something useful and how to put it into practice. We will have persuaded them and motivated them to action.

section.title: Using the Motivated Sequence
section.para: Remember that, like many other models we’ve introduced in this course, the motivated sequence is just a model. This means that it’s a flexible tool we use in a specific context, for a specific purpose, and with a specific audience. As we understand our audience and the context for our communication with them, we should feel free to adjust the model to our needs. The point isn’t to see how perfectly we can follow the steps outlined in an article or book; it’s to bring about effective communication and persuasion by understanding useful methods. The motivated sequence is one of these, and it can help us communicate and persuade effectively in many different situations.

section.title: Persuasion in Business Communication
section.para: The general principles of persuasion cross the boundaries of different means of communication, and they can give us a concrete plan for action regardless of the channels we’re using to reach our audiences.

In any communication situation, we should establish what role persuasion will play. It isn’t always necessary to persuade—sometimes we’re speaking with someone else merely to inform or understand. But when we’re called on to convince someone, the ways we’ll do so have less to do with a particular social media platform or media type, and more to do with the connections between human belief, motivation, and action.
The principles of persuasion capture those connections and lead to successful persuasion in all areas of business communication.

chapter.label: Topic 8
chapter.title: Audience, Diversity in Communication, and Accessibility

section.title: Audience and Accessibility
section.para: For the past several topics we’ve been studying research, message-crafting, and persuasion. All of these skills are an integral part of effective business communication. Without them, we severely limit our ability to share information, regardless of our purpose.

Underlying these various subjects and uniting them all has been a focus on audiences. Our audience is our communication partner—they’re the ones we send our messages to, and they’re the ones whose understanding and actions determine whether we’ve been successful. They’re the starting point for research, persuasion, and other modes of communication.

There’s still more to learn about audiences, however, and that’s what we’ll be concerned with here. In this topic, we’ll learn new ways of thinking about how to bridge the gaps between ourselves and our audience. We’ll also explore the ways that the various identities of our audience create some of those gaps, and we’ll talk about diversity and sensitivity in communication. We’ll finish the topic by examining the two senses of accessibility, and how issues of accessibility ought to impact the methods we use to communicate.

The material in this topic will serve a double purpose. First, it will complete our discussion of the many ways audiences determine how we send and receive messages in business environments, as well as solidifying our knowledge of how to choose the correct communication channels. But second, the topic will also prepare us for what’s coming. The topic after this one will be about business presentations, and with so many important things to learn there, we won’t be able to talk about audiences in as much detail as we have here. But by the time we get there, we’ll have learned everything we need to know to jump right into presentations with a thorough appreciation for the role of audiences.

section.title: Audiences: Closing the Gaps
section.para: Let’s expand on how we’ve been thinking about audiences by thinking more about how we can unify what we want with what an audience already wants and believes.

In previous discussions on research and persuasion, we noted that our audience is always our starting point: without them, we have no reason to communicate in the first place; without them, we have no destination and so no goal in communicating. We begin by thinking about their view of the world: how do they perceive things? Then we consider how that perception will affect the way they receive our message: what is the clearest way, from their perspective, to put what we mean? What is the clearest way, from their perspective, to meet their needs?

These questions assume that we’re in a position to know some things about our audience—even if we don’t know who they are exactly, we often know what kind of people they’ll be, with certain backgrounds and reasons for paying attention to us. But other times we won’t have that knowledge—we might not know any of the people we’re expected to reach, for example, and we’ll have nothing to go on in making decisions about how to customize our message.

In reality, such situations are becoming less common—with the internet and social media, business communities are often so interconnected that the chances of going into a communication totally ignorant of the audience are pretty low. In addition, the extraordinary reach that technology gives us in communication, in terms of both broad audiences and very narrow ones, means that most of the time we’ll have at least something to go on.

But what do we do when we really don’t have anything? In those situations, while we may not have any knowledge about the audience, we still have knowledge of two other things: our message, and our communication skills. When we are ignorant of our audience, it becomes even more important to clearly understand what we want to say, so we can deliver that message as quickly and as accurately as possible. We must understand the business communication essentials, so that we can begin any communication with those. The skills we’ve discussed then allow us to enter a feedback loop with our audience as soon as we’re able to begin learning about them.

A situation where we’re ignorant of everything about our audience is on the extreme end of a spectrum, where the other end would be a situation with an audience we know everything about. In between are other audiences, distributed in terms of what we know and don’t know about them. Even if we hope to communicate the same message to all those audiences, the ways we do it will be different for each, depending on what we know.

A useful way to think about these differences is in terms of gapsAny difference between us and our audience.. In communication, a gap is any difference between us and our audience. Since there are countless such differences, of course, we’ll want to focus on three of the most important: gaps of knowledge, gaps of interest, and gaps of desire. Thinking in terms of gaps calls our attention to how we can bridge the gap: both to reach our audience more effectively, and to bring the audience over to our side.
Let’s take a brief look at each gap.

section.title: Gap of Knowledge
section.para: A gap of knowledgeA difference in the information available to us, compared to the information available to our audience. is a difference in the information available to us, compared to the information available to our audience. Gaps of knowledge are normal and are one of the primary reasons we communicate with people in the first place—other people know things that we don’t know, and we can discover those things by speaking with them. But from our perspective as communicators, a gap of knowledge means that there’s something crucial to our interaction that our audience doesn’t possess. Our job is to give it to them.

Sometimes we can bridge this gap easily, as when we’ve done some research and have key facts or figures to share with the audience. Other times the job won’t be so simple. We’ll sometimes need to think more abstractly, perhaps by asking ourselves questions like the following:

listitem.para: What would a novice in this area need to understand first in order to grasp what we want to tell them?
What is the most fundamental piece of information on which everything rests, or without which nothing else makes sense?
What is the most controversial part of the issue or message, and how can we work with that part to make it less controversial?

section.para: Remember, we ought to answer these questions with our audience in mind. A piece of information that’s fundamental to us, for example, may not be as fundamental to others, given what else they already know.

Awareness of knowledge gaps helps us combat a common problem in presenting information to others: the curse of knowledgethe assumption that, because something is easily known or understandable to us, that thing must therefore be easily known or understandable to others.. Everyone is susceptible to the curse of knowledge, but it most plagues those who are experts in something. The curse of knowledge is the assumption that, because something is easily known or understandable to us, that thing must therefore be easily known or understandable to others. If you’re an expert in construction management, for example, then you’ll know lots of things about planning and building that others won’t know. The curse of knowledge is to assume that your audience knows all those same things, and that you don’t need to explain any of them.

The curse of knowledge stems from the natural self-centeredness in communication that we’ve spoken about before. It’s a part of a larger assumption that our audience is more or less like us, and that we can count on those similarities in communicating.
That assumption is false. The gap of knowledge is always there, and we must be aware of it.

section.title: Gap of Interest
section.para: A gap of interestA difference in what we care about, compared to our audience. is a difference in what we care about, compared to our audience. It’s like a gap of knowledge, but for what matters to us. Once again, confusion about these gaps comes from assuming that our audience is pretty much like us. But why would they be? Why would they care about what we care about without our background and incentives?

Addressing a gap of interest requires more than just information: we must connect that information to what our audience does care about, whatever it is. This makes bridging a gap of interest different from bridging a gap of knowledge. For knowledge, the job is to give information; sometimes it may help to link that information to our audience’s existing beliefs, but it won’t always be necessary. Gaps of interest, in contrast, can only be crossed by taking something meaningful to our audience and framing our message in terms of the interest they have in it.

section.title: Gap of Desire
section.para: Bridging gaps of knowledge evens the field of information; bridging gaps of interest evens the field of value. We bridge the last gap, a gap of desireA difference between we want and what our audience wants., to finalize the connection to action.

A gap of desire is a difference between we want and what our audience wants. In most communications, we enter the interaction knowing what we want. Depending on the situation, we may assume that our audience shares our desire, but they may also be ambivalent or even actively not want what we do. Regardless, there’s almost always some kind of difference.

We distinguish between gaps of interest and gaps of desire because, for the purposes of action, an interest is not enough. There are many things we’re interested in, and many things we’d like to do, provided we had enough time and resources. But we only really desire a small number of things, exactly because we have such limited attention and resources. Of the things we’re interested in, we can only do a few.

To bridge a gap of desire, we must connect what the audience wants to what they will get from our interaction. One way to do that is to offer them what they want, or part of what they want, and persuade them to receive it. Another way is to persuade them to change what they want, so that our desire becomes theirs. In the first method we meet them in the middle. In the second we draw them across the bridge to our side.

In addition to the curse of knowledge, we could also recognize the curse of interestThe assumption that our audience cares about what we care about. and the curse of desireThe assumption that our audience wants what we want.. These are the assumptions that our audience cares about what we care about, and wants what we want. They are just as likely to be false as the assumption behind the curse of knowledge. Many boring or otherwise ineffective business communications are born of these curses. We should avoid them.

Of course, bridging gaps and avoiding curses may not be as easy as it seems. There are known gaps, or differences we know about, but also unknown gaps, or differences we don’t know about. Both are challenging, but at least the known ones we can plan for. The unknown gaps, on the other hand, will test our skills as communicators as we try to find them given the information our audience chooses to share with us.

In this way, becoming aware of gaps and attempting to bridge them are activities representative of all human communication. We’re all inherently different from each other in many ways, and so we can’t ever eliminate the gaps. But their existence, together with what we learn in crossing them, is what makes business communication such a rich and rewarding field to master.
In the next section we’ll continue thinking about gaps in communication, with an emphasis on differences emerging from identities and cultures.

section.title: Diversity and Communication
section.para: A gap is any difference between us and our audience. A major part of communication, and of persuasion in particular, is learning to bridge those gaps and minimize or even eliminate differences.

The differences behind the gaps exist for many reasons. The most common reason for them is that two people are simply on different sides of an agreement or business relationship—this explains some of the differences between a customer and a vendor, for example. One is hoping to buy and the other to sell, and those different goals form the gap they bridge with a sale.

Other differences run deeper, however, and stem not from business associations but from more fundamental identities. In this context, the term identitySomeone’s membership in various groups, such as a race, a gender, an ethnicity, a socioeconomic class, and so on. refers to someone’s membership in various groups, such as a race, a gender, an ethnicity, a socioeconomic class, and so on. In some of these groups, membership amounts to a self-selection process, while in others it doesn’t work that way. Given the powerful ways these groups can shape personalities and worldviews, they are the source of many gaps we’ll encounter in business communication.

In discussing these identities, it would be irresponsible not to admit that the way they are managed, and sometimes whether they’re even acknowledged at all, varies greatly from community to community. The social and ethical rules surrounding them change quickly and are sometimes not easily discernible. Much of the discourse about them gets worked out among academics or on the internet, with the results spilling into public view only as part of some controversy.
And yet, these identities matter for business communication. So what do we do?

Fortunately, we can sidestep many potentially troubling problems by accepting that, if we want to communicate effectively, these diverse identities are just a few of the many we’ll encounter and work with. For communication purposes, this makes them no different from whether someone likes a particular college football team or doesn’t want to go to a burger restaurant. Those are simply facts about individuals, which may become relevant at times depending on the context for communication.

With that principle in mind, we can discuss a few issues belonging to the topic of diversity and communication. DiversityA concept with multiple meanings, ranging from the simple acknowledgment of differences to the goal of creating an identity-rich community. has multiple meanings, ranging from the simple acknowledgment of differences to the goal of creating an identity-rich community. When we talk about diversity and communication, we’re talking about effective communication in a context where diversity- and identity-related issues are prominent.

One of the most pressing problems in diversity and communication is the gap between an individual’s identity, or the cultural views arising from that identity, and an organizational culture. It’s common to see this problem in clashes between management and employees at a business, or between customers and a business. Management may have particular ideas about the ways a company ought to communicate with its employees, for example, while some of those employees may feel that those ways are insensitive or even harmful to their identities.

Depending on the identities in question, some protections have become law. In the case Bostock v. Clayton County, decided in 2020, the Supreme Court ruled that “an employer who fires an individual merely for being gay or transgender defies the law,” the law being Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S.Ct. 1731, 1754 (2020). This ruling therefore extends support to individuals of certain identities, and may cover matters such as gendered bathrooms and pronoun use.

Partly in response to these challenges, many businesses are adopting specific norms and practices surrounding DEIAn acronym standing for “diversity, equity, and inclusion.”. DEI is an acronym standing for “diversity, equity, and inclusion.” We’ve talked about diversity already; equityEqual treatment. refers to fair treatment, and inclusionEmbracing many different cultures and identities so that all feel welcome. is embracing many different cultures and identities so that all feel welcome. In addition to involving these three individual components, the term DEI itself refers more generally to institutional-level attempts to address diversity- and identity-related problems.

We may have the opportunity to work on DEI-related initiatives in our capacity as communicators, but at the very least we’ll need to be sensitive to the issues involved in order to communicate effectively. The appropriate question usually isn’t whether we agree with someone’s political or social views. We’re often much better off merely asking how we can bridge gaps with a particular person here and now, whatever the source of those gaps.

And indeed, seeing things this way gives us a new view on DEI and its consequences for business communication. The most useful way of seeing it is as a new set of tools for bridging gaps that otherwise might be tricky or even impossible to cross. And DEI might even go beyond that: it may reveal gaps that we wouldn’t have even noticed were there in the first place. In other words, it helps provide the language to both appreciate and communicate about those gaps.

The underlying principle for diversity and communication is reasonable sensitivityThe sensitivity is our awareness of how different identities, backgrounds, and cultures shape a particular worldview, and how we ought to change the ways we communicate with others to take into account these important parts of their lives. The reasonable part acknowledges that we owe others a level of effort to understand them and travel to their side of the gap, but it maintains that this debt isn’t unlimited.. The idea of reasonable sensitivity has two parts. The sensitivity is our awareness of how different identities, backgrounds, and cultures shape a particular worldview, and how we ought to change the ways we communicate with others to take into account these important parts of their lives. The reasonable part acknowledges that we owe others a level of effort to understand them and travel to their side of the gap, but it maintains that this debt isn’t unlimited. In their communications with us, others owe us some effort of understanding as well.

In our communications, we put reasonable sensitivity into practice when we educate ourselves about diverse identities and cultures, then connect the dots to how we ought to communicate with individuals of those groups. We also make appropriate modifications to our means of communication when doing so would be a reasonable way to accommodate the identities of others. As mentioned before, probably the most visible result of reasonable sensitivity recently has been the addition of alternative pronoun options on things like government forms and other sources of demographic information. Since everything is communication, such modifications send the message that a plurality of identities is being recognized and included.

At its heart, business communication has always been about bridging gaps with other human beings. Whoever happens to be on the receiving end of our messages, the goal is the same: to understand, to be understood, and to allow each other to experience the mutual benefits of our communication.

section.title: Accessibility
section.para: AccessibilityWhether something is easily reachable. concerns whether something is easily reachable. Something can be inaccessible when it’s too high, too low, or too far away. Something can be accessible if we can get to it easily or many people have access to it.

The term also applies to communication, and in that case we’re talking about the messages and information we’re sending to others. An idea can be inaccessible when it’s written poorly or framed in the wrong way. It can be accessible for a broad audience if many people are able to connect with it.

In one sense, accessibility is the most obvious topic of all in communication—almost everything we’ve spoken about up to this point has been about how to make our ideas more accessible to others. Our model of communication, our skills in emotional intelligence, our model of audience-first research—the goal of all these things is to reach audiences in the ways most meaningful to them. That’s just accessibility.

In another sense, though, there are some less obvious things to say about accessibility and communication. The first we discussed previously in speaking about diversity. A big part of making our messages accessible to others is recognizing how diverse identities impact the ways people receive them. Savvy business communicators will understand that their efforts toward accessibility in this domain will bring results not only for their business and those they communicate with, but for themselves as well. We don’t just want to be good communicators for particular audiences; it is best to be good communicators in general, who are able to reach many different people.

The second, less obvious thing concerns the ADAAmericans with Disabilities Act: the set of laws governing how government, business, and other parts of public life in the US interact with people with disabilities., or Americans with Disabilities Act. The ADA is the set of laws governing how government, business, and other parts of public life in the US interact with people with disabilities. Since there are many different disabilities, and since they affect many different aspects of life, the ADA can have far-reaching implications for businesses.

We see some of these implications in business communication. For example, people who have communication disabilities, such as vision or hearing impairments, sometimes won’t be able to communicate with us through standard channels—someone who can’t see won’t be able to read emails or text messages, and someone who can’t hear wouldn’t be able to receive a phone call. Making our communications accessible to audiences like these may require some thought, and may even require consultation with human resources or accessibility professionals.

In considering these communications gaps, we must remember that we have two distinct obligations toward accessibility. The first is the obligation we have to anyone we communicate with, where we try to understand their beliefs and desires in order to frame our messages appropriately. We would do the same for individuals with disabilities. But in these situations, we also have an additional legal obligation toward accessibility. This obligation goes beyond the previous one, requiring us to make our messages accessible.

The good news is that making these communications-related accommodations is far easier in 2024 than it was in 1990. Computers have solved most of the problems for us: we can generate captions for videos automatically, we can translate written messages into American Sign Language, and we can quickly output the same information in many different formats to make it accessible to audiences of all abilities. These technologies are a boon to business communicators, but they benefit people with disabilities most of all.

However, we shouldn’t assume that technology has solved every accessibility problem. It’s still our responsibility to understand the requirements of the ADA and other communications-related legislation and augment our messages accordingly. The fact that we have powerful computers does not excuse us from the duties we have toward those we communicate with.

We must figure out how best to accommodate the many audiences we will interact with. As we mentioned before, we’ve been learning to do this for many topics already—remember, ADA- and diversity-compliant communication is just a small part of the larger project of human communication itself. But sometimes we need specialized knowledge and specialized approaches.

In the end, all human interaction involves either getting out of or inviting someone into our own heads. Either way we have to know our audiences: what do they expect to receive from us, and how can we best give it to them? Who are they, and how does that affect their behavior? What is the context most relevant to them? What are their knowledge, interests, and desires? How can we understand them and use them to make our communication successful?

The effectiveness of our business communication depends in large part on our ability to answer these questions without getting stuck inside our own heads—by stepping out of them, leaving ourselves behind, and seeing the world through the eyes of our audience.

chapter.title: Effective Business Presentations and Technology Use

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 4: Effective Business Presentations and Technology Use. This week we will cover the following topics:

listitem.para: : Planning Effective Business Presentations
: Creating and Delivering Effective Business Presentations
: Technology and the Future of Business Communication

section.title: Business Presentations
section.para: A business presentationAny kind of presentation you give in a business context. is any kind of presentation you give in a business context. The format, duration, and content of these presentations will vary widely, but we don’t need to worry about exact details: pretty much any situation where one person stands in front of a group to deliver a message counts as a business presentation.

Regardless of your role in an organization, giving effective presentations is a fundamental skill for any business professional. You probably already know that too. Think of poor presentations you’ve seen before, and then think of good ones. What impressions did the presentations leave you with? Would you want to hear those presentations again?

In many ways, mastery of this skill is a good metric for someone’s overall ability as a communicator. The task of giving a good presentation will involve facing many of the challenges we’ve discussed so far, and to overcome them, your execution will have to be razor-sharp. Whether someone can deliver a dynamite talk in front of an unfamiliar or even hostile group is a true test of ability.

The importance of business presentations is reflected in how business communications textbooks cover it. Every book has at least something to say about it, and one, Floyd and Cardon’s 2020 Business and Professional Communication, devotes four whole chapters to presentations! We won’t give it that much coverage, but that doesn’t mean we have to shortchange what we learn. We’ll still get into the basics and beyond to prepare you for giving effective presentations wherever you are.

It’s a bit unfortunate, then, that while business presentations are so important, for many people they’re also utterly terrifying. If they terrify you, you’re in good company: some surveys estimate that as many as 40 percent of Americans fear public speaking, and one poll showed that some people fear speaking in front of a group more than drowning.Brewer, G. (2001, March 19). Snakes top list of Americans’ fears. Gallup.

Why are so many people so scared of it? One reason is the fear of disaster, when you’re scared of the entire thing going horribly wrong; another reason is impostor syndromeThe fear that your audience will discover you don’t actually know as much as you pretend to., or the fear that your audience will discover you don’t actually know as much as you pretend to. You may dread the build-up to the speech as it weighs on you, day after day; or perhaps the speech’s aftermath is worse for you, as you agonize over perceived mistakes and what everyone must have thought. Then there’s the more basic fear of just standing in front of a group: you feel exposed, vulnerable, like everyone is rooting for you to fail. You want to run, hide, or do anything other than start to talk.

Business presentations can be scary, but there’s good news to share. For one thing, the fear is common, so the fact that you have it doesn’t mean there’s anything wrong with you. For another, there are concrete steps you can take to overcome your fear. The most important ones are those we’ll cover in this topic—they’ll help us plan and deliver a presentation that we won’t need to stew over, because we’ll be confident in our preparation and our speaking abilities, and we’ll walk away knowing we’ve done a good job.

We’ll begin the topic by learning how to plan effectively. We’ll learn to avoid common mistakes by taking an audience-first approach to presenting, just as we did with research. We’ll see the power of focusing on one key idea, and we’ll discover the principles behind designing effective slides. From there we’ll study how to deliver the presentation and how to request and receive useful feedback.

Before jumping in, let’s take a moment to see the difference between a business presentation and an academic presentation. An academic presentation is any presentation given in an academic setting. The two kinds of presentations share some features, but they are not the same, so we want to be clear about the differences.

Though the two presentations can both be given to inform or persuade, the primary difference between them is that academic presentations usually make an extended argument—and many times that argument has no connection to any choice or action the audience might take. That’s not the case for business presentations, which are almost always tied to some choice or action. They’re meant to persuade about a certain issue here and now—to initiate an action in the audience, here and now.

Another major difference is that an academic presentation requires a much stricter level of rigor. As discussed in a previous topic, rigor is the exactness with which we handle information. Since academic presentations are often given to audiences with PhDs who are experts in the field themselves, they expect a corresponding level of elite expertise. Business presentations may have this expectation, but it isn’t common.

To allow for this rigor, academic presentations also tend to be longer. Most standard business presentations last for fifteen or twenty minutes, but a full hour or even more wouldn’t be unusual for an academic presentation. Academic presentations tend to have question and answer (Q&A) sessions afterwards, and they may be more adversarial, or intentionally hostile, than business presentations.

There are other minor differences, but these are the most important ones. If you’re wondering what kind of presentation you’re giving, you may ask the person responsible for your event or consider your audience and their needs, but most business professionals won’t ever have to give academic presentations.

section.title: Planning an Effective Business Presentation
section.para: Let’s start thinking about how to give an effective business presentation. We’ll start with planning, and then move to slide design and delivery.

section.title: Common Presentation Mistakes
section.para: If our planning is going to make a difference, we want it to help us avoid common mistakes people make with presentations. The two most common mistakes also happen to be the ones that do the most damage: speaking for too long, and using slides with too much information. These two problems usually stem from a common cause: you’re trying to share too much. For example, have you ever seen a presentation where the speaker knew she was running out of time, so she rushes through her most important points? She speaks beyond her allotted time but doesn’t even end up saying what she wanted to say, and the audience is left wondering why she didn’t just begin with the important material. How could her slides have been filled with so many words, and yet she still couldn’t communicate her most crucial idea?

Another common mistake is giving information that simply isn’t relevant to the audience. A related problem is over-explaining details, whether relevant or not. These issues may also connect to the problem of badly organizing data or badly organizing slides, such that they don’t harmonize with what the speaker wants to accomplish.

There are other common mistakes, but these are the major ones. Fortunately, with proper planning and preparation, we can learn to avoid them. Just because you’re tasked with giving a presentation doesn’t mean the universe has fated you to bore people.

section.title: Audience-First Presentations
section.para: The solution to these common presentation mistakes, and the first principle of effective business presentations, is the same as our approach for effective research: we think of the audience first. Just as audience-first research highlights the audience and their needs and interests, audience-first presentationsPresentations that focus on the audience and how the content and manner of the presentation can impact them. focus on those who will see our presentations, and how what we say and do can have an impact on them.

To give effective business presentations, the absolutely most fundamental point is to think about the audience first. We have to ask ourselves: what will their experience of our presentation be like? What will they be thinking and feeling? What time of day will it be—might they be hungry or sleepy? How much do they already know about the topic? Do we know for sure they’re already interested? What are their opinions about the issues?

Note that taking an audience-first approach to presenting shows us immediately what’s gone wrong with many of the common mistakes. What normal human being wants to hear a presentation that goes longer than it’s supposed to? That’s right—no one. So why would we give a presentation that does that? Why wouldn’t we plan to hook our audience’s attention and deliver the most important content right away? Why don’t we think about what it will be like for our audience, and not for us, to stare at slides full of text walls on a topic they aren’t familiar with? Why don’t we think about what it will be like for them to hear hackneyed clichés and bad jokes?

On the other hand, we must admit that taking an audience-first approach in presenting is harder than it is in research. The reason is that, for most people, giving a public presentation is harder than reporting about research. If giving a presentation scares or unnerves us, we naturally approach it thinking about ourselves and what will make us feel better. And when we do that, we tend to do things like overprepare—we stuff our presentations full of information so that we will have plenty to say and can answer any possible objection. But by doing that we’ve only sought to make ourselves feel comfortable, and so we’ve already lost sight of our audience.

It’s somewhat of a paradoxical cycle. We get scared and so focus on ourselves rather than on our audience; we compensate by trying to address our concerns, but in doing that, we make the presentation worse for our audience.

But it doesn’t have to be that way. Our model of communication involves customizing a message based on the needs and desires of our audience, and giving a presentation is just a special case of that process. It’s a piece of communication intended to be listened to by our audience; it’s their experience of listening to it, rather than ours of giving it, that ought to occupy our attention.

The solution is to start by thinking about the audience and to think about them at each point in the process. Although we’ll not call attention to it each time, the principles we’ll discuss in this topic are designed with the audience in mind.

section.title: One Key Idea
section.para: The next principle for planning effective business presentations is about the presentation’s content. The principle helps us narrow our thoughts until we’ve identified the one thing, the one bit of information or argument we would want our audience to have over everything else. We call that bit of information our one key ideaThe one bit of information or argument we would want our audience to have over everything else.—the single most important part of our presentation.

Our goal in a good business presentation should be to communicate our one key idea as clearly as possible, while providing all the information necessary for our audience to understand it. Our goal should be to communicate that idea, and just that—nothing else.

So how do we identify our one key idea? Sometimes it will be obvious, as when we’re asked to present on our team’s quarterly numbers or on a particular aspect of leadership theory. In those cases we have specific guidance and so our one key idea will just be the most important information we could deliver about those topics. But other times our presentations may be more open-ended, where we’re given less direction or even none at all. In those cases it’s crucial that we ask ourselves: what is the one thing we want our audience to know and remember? What one message is more important than all the rest?

To make sure that we’ve really identified something narrow enough, we should be able to express our one key idea in a single sentence. If we can’t, we’re either including too much information, or we don’t yet have a good grasp on what the most important part of our message is.

But you also might ask, why only one idea? Why not more? There certainly can be business presentations that give more content. Presentations can do much more than that and still be effective. But as an introduction to presentations in a business environment, there are two big advantages to choosing one key idea.

The first is that such a narrow focus requires us to strip everything from our presentations that doesn’t support that one idea, which will streamline what we say. The second advantage is also about quantity of information. Most presenters underestimate how much work it will take to clearly explain an important idea, while simultaneously overestimating an audience’s ability to maintain an attention span and intake large amounts of information. The one key idea respects the effort required for clear explanations, while acknowledging that many audiences simply cannot handle or will tune out presentations that try to make multiple difficult points.

You may sometimes have to give presentations whose content cannot be distilled easily into a single key idea. When that happens, the ideal of one key idea can be a base on which to build a larger presentation. The principles we’ll discuss later will still apply, but your job will be to flesh out more than just one important message.
With our mind on our audience, then, the one key idea becomes our anchor: our goal is to communicate that message, along with whatever might be necessary to understand it.

section.title: Outlining with the One Key Idea
section.para: Once we’ve identified our one key idea, we’ll want to make an outline. An outlineA brief list of the topics we intend to cover in a presentation. is a brief list of the topics we intend to cover in a presentation.

Since we’ll be focusing on one key idea, we’ll build our outline around it. But we’ll be making a very specific kind of outline called the double-upAn outline that doubles up on the one key idea—it appears in two places on the outline, rather than just one. outline. We give it this name because we’ll double up on the one key idea—it will appear in two places on our outline, rather than just one:

listitem.para: We mention it near the beginning,
And we mention it again at the end or culmination of the outline.

section.para: Remember, an outline is just a plan for a presentation, so a double-up outline will lead to a double-up presentation: a presentation that highlights the one key idea twice.
Here is a sample outline with the double position of the key idea:

listitem.para: Title
Introduction
Frame-setting (hook, problem, approach)
ONE KEY IDEA
Background and motivation for one key idea
ONE KEY IDEA
Arguments and reasons in favor of one key idea
Implications of one key idea
Conclusion

section.para: We’ll talk about the other aspects of the outline shortly. For now it’s important only to see that our outline is built around not just one appearance of the key idea, but two.

It won’t surprise you to find out that the reason for the double-up outline comes from our audience. Many presenters wait until the end of their presentation to give the most important idea, if they get to it at all. In doing so they get things backward: they give the most important part last, and so the audience loses the chance to interpret everything else in terms of that important information. In contrast, presentations built on our outline fix this problem by giving the key idea first. By highlighting it at the beginning, the audience can then receive and interpret everything else we say in terms of the one key idea. This strengthens the frame of our communication and makes it clear why each point is relevant: it all traces back and forward to the one key idea.

The key idea also gives us a test to determine whether something belongs in our presentation or not. We can ask ourselves, does this information contribute to the presentation and comprehension of the key idea? If it doesn’t, we can cut it.
The one key idea gives structure to the outline, our presentation, and the message we want to deliver.

section.title: Components of the Outline
section.para: The rest of our presentation outline is built around the key idea. Let’s take a brief look at the other components of the outline—we’ll have more to say about them when we talk about creating an effective slide deck.

section.title: Title
section.para: The titleWhat you call your presentation. of our presentation is what we call it. Shorter, catchier titles are usually better, since if our presentation is advertised at all, it will usually only be described by its title. The title should therefore communicate something about the key idea and what angle we’ll take on that idea. There are many ways of creating useful titles, and they may appear as sentence fragments, complete sentences, or questions. Brainstorm some possibilities and run them by colleagues you trust for their feedback.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: In our outline, the “introduction” refers specifically to an introduction you give about yourself and your organization. Note that this introduction may not always be necessary. If you’re presenting to colleagues, you won’t need to introduce yourself at all; if someone else has introduced you, an introduction can be minimal.
The key to a good introduction is its brevity: make it as short as possible. Anything longer means you’re already boring your audience.

section.title: Frame-Setting (Hook, Problem, Approach)
section.para: “Frame-setting” refers to how we set the frame of our presentation: the level at which it’s pitched and the background assumptions we’ll be making. The frame sets the expectations for our communication, and we may be able to set those expectations with as little as a single sentence: something like “Let’s talk about viral marketing through TikTok dances” might be enough.

The frame-setting part of our outline is also where we want to capture our audience’s attention. A hookA brief point—a joke, a surprising statistic, a paradox or confusing problem—that can be expressed quickly to get an audience’s attention. can be useful here. A hook is a brief point—a joke, a surprising statistic, a paradox or confusing problem—that can be expressed quickly to get an audience’s attention.

Once you have the audience’s attention, you have a critical window in which to briefly explain the problem or topic you’ll be discussing, along with a quick note about the approach you’ll be taking to it.

Notice that we’ve used the words “brief” and “quick” many times so far. Do not delay in any of these steps. Most audiences will not feel you’ve truly started your presentation until you’ve identified the original idea or contribution you’ll make to the discussion. The longer it takes you to make this point, the more you are asking your audience to listen to you without giving them any payoff for their effort.

section.title: ONE KEY IDEA
section.para: After setting the frame, it’s time to deliver the one key idea. State it in at least a full sentence, though you may need more. But don’t go into details here. At this point in the outline we are giving the audience a taste of the idea, but not the whole thing. The goal is to interest them in the information we will give next while controlling how they interpret that information.

section.title: Background and Motivation for One Key Idea
section.para: After giving a taste of the idea, begin giving the information necessary to understand both the idea itself and why it’s important. Discuss the motivations behind the idea as well as what points led us to it and to an appreciation of its value.
In this section of the presentation, we should be giving our audience everything they need to understand the idea and see why it matters.

section.title: ONE KEY IDEA
section.para: Now that we’ve given the background and motivation to our important idea, we’re ready to state it in its fullness. Repeat the idea, and this time give more than a taste: give all the interesting details and flesh it out. We use the background we’ve built to explore the idea and how it solves a problem, breaks new ground, or changes the way we ought to see something.

section.title: Arguments and Reasons in Favor of One Key Idea
section.para: With the key idea and all its details on the table, we can offer the arguments and reasons in its favor. What evidence makes it so powerful? What reasons recommend it to our audience?
Note that not every presentation needs this section, and in some cases, these arguments and reasons may appear earlier, in discussing the background and motivation for the key idea.

section.title: Implications of One Key Idea
section.para: Next we follow the implications of the one key idea: what other ideas does it lead to? What possibilities? What changes and new visions will we adopt when we understand it?
We shouldn’t hold back here. If the idea is interesting, its implications will be too! This section cashes in on the work we’ve done before.

section.title: Conclusion
section.para: Finally, our outline finishes with a conclusion. We briefly summarize what we’ve talked about, and then we state again the one key idea and its most important implications. Then we close.

section.title: Outline Length and Timing
section.para: We’ll finish our section on planning with a comment about timing.

As we’ve seen, the most common mistake with presentations is that the speaker speaks for too long. Don’t do that. Never speak longer than the time you’ve been given. If you plan intelligently and understand your key idea, you won’t need to—and everyone in your audience will thank you for it.
Have a plan and keep track of time while you execute that plan. Then, when you’re done, be done.

section.title: Principles of Clear Slide Design
section.para: Many business presentations will involve using a presentation aid, such as a slide deck or hard copies of a presentation summary. By far the most common presentation aid is the slide deck, and that’s what we’ll cover here.

This topic will cover the most important principles for designing slides. We call these guidelines the principle of clear slide design, since the most important thing your slides should do is communicate your one key idea and other messages clearly.

section.title: Programs for Creating Slide Decks
section.para: The term slideA particular type of visual aid, mostly text-based but not exclusively so, shown on a screen or projector as part of a presentation. refers to a particular type of visual aid, mostly text-based but not exclusively so, shown on a screen or projector as part of a presentation. A slide deckA collection of slides. is a collection of those slides.

There are many software programs for creating slides. The most common is Microsoft’s PowerPoint, which dates back to 1987 and is so ubiquitous that slides and slide decks are sometimes just called “powerpoints.” Mac users probably know Keynote, a program substantially similar to PowerPoint for Apple’s operating systems. A third option is Google Slides, which belongs to the Google Docs suite of productivity apps.

PowerPoint appears on many Windows computers and is also available for free as part of Microsoft 365. The 365 version runs on any web browser. Keynote is available on most Apple devices, and Google Slides is free for anyone with a Google account.
In this topic we’ll focus on PowerPoint. Some of the specific how-to items will apply only to that software, but the principles of clear slide design are true regardless of which program you use.

If you don’t know how to do a particular thing in PowerPoint or another slide program, the easiest way to figure it out is to do an internet search for your question. There are many sites with slide tutorials, and YouTube has many demonstration videos.

section.title: Designing for Clarity
section.para: In any presentation, the most important thing your slides will do is help deliver or emphasize your message. This means that their fundamental purpose is to communicate: in their design and content, your slides send all sorts of messages to your audience.

Given this purpose, we ought to design our slides first and foremost so they communicate clearly—we want them to leave no doubt about our what we’re saying, including about our one key idea. We can have the most stylish slide deck in the world, with the most hand-curated colors and images, but if we fill that deck with walls of text and poorly worded descriptions, our presentation will fail. The visual side of our slides might make a positive impression, but in the end they will not have communicated to the audience what we wanted to communicate.

We therefore divide the principles of slide design into five parts: theme, organization and layout, style, visual aids, and slide mechanics. The goal of each part is clarity, and each has ways we can go both right and wrong. By following the principles outlined here, we guarantee that we’ll be going right a lot more often.

section.title: Slide Theme
section.para: A slide themeThe basic structure of a slide, along with a color palette and any associated background images. is the basic structure of a slide, along with a color palette and any associated background images. A theme sets the basic look for a slide deck and is kept constant from slide to slide.

shows a sample of standard themes available in a recent edition of PowerPoint. Glance through them to see what sticks out. Notice that some, like “Integer pillars” on the second row, have a lot of busy images that might distract viewers from your message. Others, like “Madison” (third row) and “Dividend” (bottom row), are simpler.

imagedata.alt: Several of the slide theme options available on PowerPoint.

section.para: In general, a simpler slide theme is better. You don’t necessarily need to choose the plain-white variant—that theme is the simplest and contains no frills to distract viewers, but it’s also so basic that it might be too boring.
Select a simple theme with softer colors whose look and standard fonts will stand out because of what you say with them, rather than because of how they appear on their own.

section.title: Organization and Layout
section.para: The next principle of slide design is organization and layout. This principle involves the way text, images, and other pieces of information are arranged on a slide.

There are many different facets of slide organization and layout. We’ll cover the most significant below, but when you make choices about your slide organization, remember that your goal is to communicate clearly. Any choice that takes away from that goal makes it more difficult for your audience to understand your message. Decisions about layout are some of the most important nonverbal means of communication in a business presentation.

Let’s first look at organization from a broad perspective. Figures 9.2–9.6 present the organization and layout of four different PowerPoint themes. Though there are many others, these four give some basic options. is simple, even spare, with nothing to either distract or entice an audience. has some color and an attractive look, though the standard font size is perhaps a bit small. has a strange color palette and, at least for the purposes of this presentation, should be considered unusable. isn’t as simple as , but doesn’t have too much going on, either. has a nice mix of features and allows the text to show clearly, as long as the colors are suitable for the occasion.

imagedata.alt: An example set of slides in a very simple style.
An example set of slides with a wood grain background.
And example set of slides. The background is a brick wall, and the text is bright red in an all caps style.
A sample set of slides with a relatively simple theme of neutral grays and clean lines.
A sample set of slides in a theme with an interesting teal background with red accents and white text.

section.para: As you evaluate these examples of organization, remember to take an audience-first approach. The question is not whether we like the organization, nor even whether our audience will like it. The question is whether it will contribute to the clarity of our message. It’s true that the visual appeal of a slide deck can help make that contribution, but visual appeal alone cannot successfully communicate a message in a business presentation.

Suppose we decide on the organization and layout of image . This arrangement doesn’t have any serious problems for clarity, and its colors have some appeal. While it may not be the best choice for a given presentation, we’ll use it to illustrate other parts of slide design below.

imagedata.alt: A sample set of slides with purple and magenta accents. The first slide shows the title slide, the next shows an example of a heading slide, and the last shows an example of a content slide with a bulleted list.

section.para: Next, let’s zoom in to take look at some lower-level organizational choices. Two prominent ones are line spacingThe amount of space between lines of text. and alignmentWhether text is aligned to the left, right, or center of the visible space.. Line spacing is the amount of space between lines of text, while alignment refers to whether text is aligned to the left, right, or center of the visible space.

For the most part, PowerPoint handles line spacing automatically and adjusts it depending on the amount of text in a particular place. Note how the line spacing and the text size have changed in and as we’ve added information. In most situations, it’s best to default to PowerPoint’s automatic suggestions for spacing between lines.

imagedata.alt: A slide with one bullet and three sub-bullets. The text remains large to fill the available space.
A slide with one bullet and six sub-bullets. The text is smaller to accommodate the additional content on the slide.

section.para: Outside of title slides, it would be uncommon to align text in a business presentation either in the center or on the right side of a textbox. Left alignment is preferable.

An appropriate amount of space between lines helps us prevent a wall of textA large amount of text, sometimes given in small type and usually presented with no line or paragraph breaks.. A wall of text is any large amount of text, sometimes given in small type, and usually presented with no line or paragraph breaks. shows a wall of text about climate change.

imagedata.alt: A slide with a wall of text on it. There is only one bullet point, but the text spans 14 lines and almost fills the entire slide with small, difficult-to-read text.

section.para: Walls of text are bad for many reasons. Their small font makes them harder to read, and the lack of line or paragraph breaks makes it easy to lose your place. Those two things mean that walls of text get in the way of clarity; but even beyond that, walls of text are just discouraging for audiences to see. They’ll think, “Is she going to read that? Even worse, am I expected to read it?”
That isn’t the reaction we want to provoke in our audiences. Keep things simple, and don’t lose control of the amount of text on a page.

Notice that an attractive slide organization contains a healthy amount of white spaceThe space within the viewable area that you’ve left blank.. White space, sometimes called negative space, is simply the place you’ve left blank. Depending on your slide theme, your white space may not actually be white, but that doesn’t matter.
