The key is separating elements on your slides from each other to allow the audience to identify each on its own and still grasp the relationship between them.

The final point to make about organization and layout is section breaks and headings. shows a section break slide, which is a special slide marking a new section of a presentation. A section break slide is something like the start of a chapter in a book: it marks a new phase in the story. Using section breaks helps an audience keep track of where you are in your presentation and communicates the relationship elements within a section have to each other.

imagedata.alt: A slide that serves as a section break. It has a heading for the next section of the presentation and a place for a short description, if necessary.

section.para: In , the heading is the label “Views on science” at the top of the slide. This heading describes the content in this slide and should be a description general enough to include whatever a slide contains. Once again, the emphasis is on the audience’s understanding. Slide headings organize the information on a slide and tell the audience that all the smaller points contribute to something larger. Headings shouldn’t be too long, however, since making the heading too long creates the layout problem illustrated in .

imagedata.alt: A slide with a heading at the top and some information related to the heading topic below it.
A slide that illustrates the formatting problem with a too-long heading. The heading bleeds over the section of the slide for the heading, making it difficult to read and cramped.

section.para: As with other parts of slide design, the most important part of organization and layout is clarity. If anything detracts from our audience’s ability to understand our slides as quickly as possible, we ought to think about making a change.

section.title: Style
section.para: In the context of business presentations, the term style can mean many things, and it isn’t entirely separate from organization and layout. Here we’ll restrict ourselves to three of the most significant style decisions for a presentation: font size and typeface, bullets, and headers and footers.

First, font size and typeface. A typefaceAlso called a font; the design of the letters on the screen. (also often called a font) is the design of the letters on the screen. Most people have played around with different typefaces in a word processor before, and so know that they aren’t all equally easy to read. You’ve seen the standard typeface in our sample presentation so far; now compare it to the examples in Figures 9.14–9.17. is an all-capitals typeface that is mostly readable but also gives the slide an unusual look. requires a magnifying glass to read and would be a catastrophe in a presentation. makes it seem as though the presenter was designing slides for a children’s birthday party. , on the other hand, might be a viable option, and it certainly offers a very formal feel.

imagedata.alt: A slide with a typeface using all capitals. The typeface is also quite decorative and difficult to read.
A slide featuring very small and decorative script handwriting that is very difficult to read.
A slide featuring a very silly-looking typeface.
A slide featuring a typical professional-looking serif font—an appropriate choice for a business presentation.

section.para: For your presentations, choose standard typefaces, and stick to PowerPoint’s standard options if necessary. Some presentations are challenging to understand, but if the reason for the challenge is a difficult typeface, the presentation is probably a failure.

Font sizeThe size of the letters on the screen. is the size of the letters on the screen. As we discussed in a previous section, PowerPoint scales font sizes automatically, depending on the amount of text in a particular location. As long as you aren’t creating walls of text, those default font sizes will work. No one should ever have to squint to read a slide or be overwhelmed by imposingly large letters.

BulletsA small image or letter that marks the beginning of a line or list; often used for setting up information on a slide. are a standard way of setting up information on a slide. A bullet is a small image or letter that marks the beginning of a line or list. In , the bullets are actually arrows, and there are two sizes of bullets: one larger and one smaller. In that slide, the line “Three categories:” is at one level, and it has three sub-levels, which are the three lines below it.

Bullets are instantly recognizable to audiences and clearly show the relationship between different pieces of information. There are other ways of setting up slides, but bullets are common and suitable for many purposes.

Note that PowerPoint allows the embedding of bullets at deeper and deeper levels. shows an example of this embedding down to the fifth level. In general, levels lower than the second should be avoided. That is, stick to the first and second levels of bullets.

imagedata.alt: A slide showing five layers of bullets. Each sub-bullet uses smaller text than the previous, illustrating that the text gets progressively more difficult to read.

section.para: The third and final aspect of slide style we’ll discuss here is headers and footers. A headerA line of text near the top of a slide, which appears as exactly the same or almost the same in each slide. is a line of text near the top of a slide, which appears as exactly the same or almost the same in each slide. A footerA line of text near the bottom of a slide, which appears as exactly the same or almost the same in each slide. is similar, except it appears at the bottom.

In many of PowerPoint’s themes, both headers and footers take up little space and already conform to a slide’s organization and layout. Depending on the theme, PowerPoint also offers different options for which pieces of information can go in a header and which can go in a footer.

Headers and footers offer many useful advantages for business presentations. If you’re presenting to an unfamiliar audience, headers and footers can remind them of your name, your organization, and your contact information, like an email address or social media account. Many headers can also display the number of the slide you’re currently on, which gives your presentation a sense of forward motion (and, just as importantly, an assurance to your audience that the presentation will eventually end).

section.title: Visual Aids
section.para: The fourth principle of slide design is visual aidsAny image, chart, graph, or other item that isn’t a line of text or textbox. . For business presentations, a visual aid is any image, chart, graph, or other item that isn’t a line of text or textbox.

Design principles involving visual aids go beyond what we’re able to cover here. The most important point for business presentations, however, is the same one we’ve made before: the purpose is to communicate clearly, and simple is better.

As such, your visual aids ought to be images or graphs that your audience can understand in seconds with a minimum of explanation. A funny or captivating image probably needs little explanation, of course, but charts and graphs may need more. For charts and graphs, include text to indicate what is important and what the most significant conclusions are. As part of your speech, make sure to thoroughly explain what each graph shows, what metrics or categories appear in each axis, and so on.

In business presentations, tables should be used with caution. While they are a useful way of organizing information, a clear understanding of most tables requires a viewer to read each cell in the table one at a time. In addition, relationships between figures in a table are not as easily or as quickly grasped as relationships displayed visually. When possible, avoid tables and use visual representations of information.

Even if you include a bar graph or other visual aid that’s easy to understand, remember that your audience will probably only have time and motivation to comprehend the gist of what you show them. If you want them to notice something, you must say it and draw attention to it in the slide itself.
For most business presentations, safe guidelines would be to use no more than one image per slide, unless you’re making a comparison. In those cases, don’t use more than two.
Do not use clipart, or anything that looks like it came from the 1990s. Your audience will not take you seriously if you do.

section.title: Slide Mechanics
section.para: Our final principle of clear slide design is slide mechanicsThe way text and images appear on the screen, such as by popping into place or by sliding across the screen. . Slide mechanics include the way text and images appear on the screen, such as by popping into place or by sliding across the screen. They also include sounds and methods for integrating video.

For a business presentation, slide animations should be simple. The two most basic options on PowerPoint are “Appear” and “Fade.” Use these. Anything fancier suggests to your audience that you just found out that morning how to make the words bounce on the screen, and you just couldn’t wait to show everybody. Remember that you are trying to leave them with a sense of your professionalism and credibility as a communicator, and not to impress your friends on the playground.
For most business presentations, sounds marking slide transitions or other events in your speech will not be necessary.

Use caution with videos. Sometimes they may be necessary and they can be useful, but longer videos will bore an audience and will make them wonder why you need to present when you could have just sent a link to the video instead.

section.title: Overview of Clear Slide Design Principles
section.para: Building clear slides is a skill that requires practice to master. You can speed up the development of your skills in this area, however, merely by simplifying your slides. No audience will complain about a brief slide deck that clearly communicates a key idea and its supporting evidence. No PowerPoint theme, font, visual aid, or other piece of information can make up for a jumbled mess of a message.

chapter.label: Topic 10
chapter.title: Creating and Delivering Effective Business Presentations

section.title: Creating an Effective Slide Deck
section.para: In the previous topic we introduced business presentations and discussed how to plan them with the audience in mind. The focus in our planning was “one key idea,” or the most important message we’d like our audience to have. We then covered the principles of clear slide design, where our focus was on the clarity with which our slides ought to communicate.

Now it’s time to put these different pieces together in order to produce an effective slide deck. That’s our subject here, and we’ll cover everything necessary. Then the next two sections will be on how to give your presentation to a real-life audience.

section.title: Each Presentation Tells a Story
section.para: Actually, a better name for this subsection might be, each good presentation tells a story. That is, each good presentation gives a beginning, a middle, and an end. The beginning tells us what the story will be about and sets the frame. The middle gives the details, and the end showcases the best part.
We can take the beginning-middle-end idea of a story and apply it to the outline we saw in a previous section. The outline looked like this:

listitem.para: Title
Introduction
Frame-setting (hook, problem, approach)
Background and motivation for one key idea
Arguments and reasons in favor of one key idea
Implications of one key idea
Conclusion

section.para: Now we can add a bit more structure to the outline in order to bring out the beginning, the middle, and the end:

listitem.para: Title
Introduction
Frame-setting (hook, problem, approach)
Background and motivation for one key idea
Arguments and reasons in favor of one key idea
Implications of one key idea
Conclusion

section.para: The beginning of our presentation consists of our title and introduction, the frame-setting, and the initial statement of the one key idea. The middle contains the background and motivation for the key idea, which often involves a discussion of the problems or conflicts the key idea will resolve. Then the end states the key idea again and proceeds to explore the details behind it and the implications it has for any problems or conflicts we’ve seen previously.

section.title: Allotting Slides and Time
section.para: We can see how the beginning-middle-end structure fits cleanly onto our outline. But we want our presentations to do more in respecting our audience-first approach and in giving the presentation’s central message. For those reasons, we need to understand the correct way to allot slides and time to each part of our presentation.

At first it may seem like the right way to do this follows from the three main divisions of the presentation. So suppose we’re planning a fifteen-minute presentation with fifteen slides: we might then think we should give five slides to the beginning, five to the middle, and five to the end, and we’d spend roughly five minutes speaking about each part.
But that is the wrong way to give a presentation. It’s the way most people would do it, true. But most people are doing it wrong, or at least poorly.

The mistake that most people make is that they spend far, far too much time on the beginning and middle of their presentation. That’s a mistake, and it gets worse when we understand that most people do not give their key idea or message near the beginning of their presentation at all; when it appears, it’s often at the end. The result is a presentation that spends 70% or more of its slides and time on things that are not the most important thing we want our audience to understand. That leaves us only 30% for what matters most.

But even that 30% makes this way of giving presentations sound better than it is, because in that 30% of your time and slides, you’re probably introducing the key idea for the first time. This means you’ll be using energy and time having your audience get to know the key idea before you are even able to talk about why it’s important. And even then, because you just introduced the most important part at the end of the presentation, you might also have to re-explain everything from the middle in terms of the key idea.
These are all mistakes. But we don’t have to make them.

We can avoid these problems by flipping this allotment around. Rather than spending two-thirds or so of our time and slides on the beginning and middle of our presentation, we want almost that amount to be spent on the end alone.
Thus the flipped, audience-first structure for a business presentation looks like this:

listitem.para: Beginning (20%)
Title
Introduction
Frame-setting (hook, problem, approach)
Middle (20%)
Background and motivation for one key idea
Arguments and reasons in favor of one key idea
Implications of one key idea
Conclusion

section.para: The 60% given to the end is crucial. That’s where the meat of the presentation is—our key idea, our important message. And we spend more than half the time on that, along with all the reasons for it and the implications it has for other issues.

Giving a business presentation with PowerPoint or other presentation software also gives us a powerful way to stick to this audience-first setup: we simply design our slides so that the correct number of slides corresponds to each part.

So suppose again that our job is to give a fifteen-minute presentation, and we plan to use fifteen slides. Let’s plug those values into our structured outline for both the number of slides and the time we’d want to take on them:

listitem.para: Beginning (20%; 3 slides, 3 minutes)
Title
Introduction
Frame-setting (hook, problem, approach)
Middle (20%; 3 slides, 3 minutes)
Background and motivation for one key idea
End (60%; 9 slides, 9 minutes)
Arguments and reasons in favor of one key idea
Implications of one key idea
Conclusion

section.para: The beauty of having only three slides in the beginning of our presentation is that, once we finish that third slide, we automatically move on to the middle! And then it happens again with the middle too—we do three slides, and after those slides, we’ve set the stage for what really matters. And then we move on to it. In other words, by sticking to this outline and strictly following the allotted number of slides, we make it very difficult for ourselves to give an unbalanced presentation. There just aren’t enough slides in either the beginning or the middle to make it unbalanced in the first place. We do a few slides in each of those parts, and then move on.

Notice also that this structure gives the majority of our slides and time to the one key idea. This allows us to give that idea its due: we have enough time to present it, argue for it, explore it, and sell it to our audience. That idea is the whole point of the story, after all, and the reason we’re up there giving a presentation. If we aren’t going to give that idea the attention it deserves, then what’s the point?

In the remainder of this section, we’ll walk through each part of the outline. The numbers we’ll discuss for slides and times are somewhat flexible, but don’t get carried away. If you aren’t spending at least half your time on whatever is most important in your presentation, then you’re losing sight of your message and the needs of your audience.

section.title: Slides for the Beginning (20%)
section.para: Let’s consider how to set up slides for the beginning of a fifteen-minute, fifteen-slide presentation. Note that our focus here is on the content of these slides, rather than the slide design; we covered slide design in the previous section.
Our goal will be to spend three slides in the beginning of our presentation. Fortunately, the beginning won’t cover material that requires us to have any more slides. We can set things up like this:

listitem.para: Title (1 slide)
Introduction and frame-setting (1 slide)
First statement of ONE KEY IDEA (1 slide)

section.para: This structure is simple, but it will take some thought to carry out. On the title slide, for example, we can put our name, contact information, title of the presentation, and other basic information. But since we have only a single slide for the introduction and frame-setting, we’ll have to carefully consider what text to add for the second slide. We’ll probably end up with several bullet points that prompt a bit of explanation, but that’s what the speaker notes in a presentation are for. We’ll cover speaker notes in the next section.
In many cases, the second slide will involve a hook and a statement of the problem we’re facing.

The third slide will then have our first statement of the one key idea. Remember that this statement will introduce that idea, and make brief reference to how it follows up on the hook and resolves the problem we mentioned on the slide before.

The advantage of including the key idea in the beginning is that, from this point forward, our audience will already know the most important thing we want them to have, at least in a basic form. This means that they’ll be interpreting the middle part of our presentation through the lens of the key idea. They’re therefore much more likely to understand our main point, understand its connections to other issues, and be ready for a more detailed explanation later on.

section.title: Slides for the Middle (20%)
section.para: The middle of our presentation will contain the next 20% of our slides, which in our example is the next three. The purpose of the middle is to give the background and motivation behind the one key idea.

Depending on what that idea is and what it’s intended for, the middle might fulfill this purpose in various ways. For example, it might present three problems in detail, one on each slide, which the key idea will fix. Or if we’re presenting on a new product idea, we might spend a slide or two talking about the development process and how it led us to this exciting new point. Or it might do something completely different. How exactly the middle will give the background and motivation will depend on our circumstances.
Still, we shouldn’t have more than 20% of our slides or use more than 20% of our time here. So for our sample presentation, our slides might look like this:

listitem.para: Problem #1 (1 slide)
Here we may follow up on a problem we mentioned in the frame-setting earlier in the presentation.
Problem #2 (1 slide)
Here we may also follow up on a problem we’ve mentioned before.
Discussion of what the problems have in common and what a solution would need to look like (1 slide)

section.para: As we said, this is just an example, and the slides for the middle of our presentation can be allotted in different ways. Note, though, that everything is oriented toward the key idea we’ll be presenting later. Everything looks in that direction and sets the stage for the end.

section.title: Slides for the End (60%)
section.para: By the time we reach the ending portion of our presentation, we should still have more than half our time remaining. That time will allow us to explore the key idea in appropriate depth.
As with the middle, the end can develop in many ways, and there are lots of possibilities for setting it up. Here’s one way it might look:

listitem.para: Second statement of ONE KEY IDEA (1 slide)
More detailed explanation of ONE KEY IDEA (1 slide)
Arguments in favor of ONE KEY IDEA or comparisons of its advantages over other ideas (2–3 slides)
Implications or expected results of ONE KEY IDEA—in resolving the problems we’ve mentioned, in promoting growth, etc. (2–3 slides)
Acknowledge and respond to potential concerns about ONE KEY IDEA (1 slide)
Summary and conclusion (1 slide)

section.para: This setup for the end of our presentation is very general, but for any presentation we could make it much more specific. As always, though, the emphasis is focused on the key idea, the most important message we want our audience to receive. Everything else is subordinate to that.

You may feel as though this setup for our ending, as well as for the beginning and middle, doesn’t offer enough slides. This is intentional. Using fewer slides makes our presentations more likely to be shorter, which is good—but more importantly, using fewer slides requires us to be much more thoughtful about what is important and what we are going to say. If we know that we can’t use more than a single slide to address potential concerns about our key idea, for example, then we’ll make sure that we only talk about the most important concerns while leaving out everything else. Deliberately restricting the number of slides is a healthy way to trim the fat from a presentation.

The end of our presentation will probably also contain many of the elements of effective communication that we’ve discussed elsewhere in this topic and in this course. We’ll probably include research, and we may spend a little time offering important definitions. Depending on our key idea and what it means, we’ll probably have some attempts at different kinds of persuasion and we may include a call to action. We haven’t included these communication techniques in our outlines because they’re specific to certain kinds of presentations or topics, but the end may be the best place for them, when they do apply.

section.title: Effective Slide Decks
section.para: Let’s summarize what we’ve learned here about effective slide decks.

In conjunction with the principles of clear slide design, effective slide decks are built around one key idea (or more than one, depending on the presentation). Effective slide decks give audiences everything they need to understand that key idea and what it means for them: they set the frame for discussing it, they state it clearly at the beginning of the presentation, they explain why it matters. After doing these things, effective slide decks then explore the key idea in detail and talk about its implications for problems or other issues the audience cares about.

The emphasis here is always on the key idea, but we only have that emphasis because of the audience. An audience-first approach to business presentations foregrounds the needs of those listening to us, tailors a message to them, and then gives them that message in the clearest and most interesting way possible.
We can combine the slide setups from the different parts of our presentation into one more comprehensive guide:

listitem.para: Title (1 slide)
Introduction and frame-setting (1 slide)
First statement of ONE KEY IDEA (1 slide)
Problem #1 (1 slide)
Here we may follow up on a problem we mentioned in the frame-setting earlier in the presentation.
Problem #2 (1 slide)
Here we may also follow up on a problem we’ve mentioned before.
Discussion of what the problems have in common and what a solution would need to look like (1 slide)
Second statement of ONE KEY IDEA (1 slide)
More detailed explanation of ONE KEY IDEA (1 slide)
Arguments in favor of ONE KEY IDEA or comparisons of its advantages over other ideas (2–3 slides)
Implications or expected results of ONE KEY IDEA—in resolving the problems we’ve mentioned, in promoting growth, and so on (2–3 slides)
Summary and conclusion (1 slide)

section.para: This is a powerful way of setting up a slide deck and of organizing a business presentation. It’s also flexible and can be adapted for many different kinds of presentations in many different circumstances. Everything centers around the audience and our most important message for them.

section.title: Using Speaker Notes and Citations in Business Presentations
section.para: In the section following this one we’ll cover how to deliver an effective business presentation, once it’s finally planned and created. But before that there are two more tools to cover: speaker notes and citations.

section.title: Speaker Notes
section.para: As noted in the principles of clear slide design, we want to avoid filling our slides with too much text. Slides with too much text are hard to read and tend to discourage audiences, so shorter slides with more white space are preferable.

But that creates a problem. In the end of our presentation, for example, we’ll want to flesh out the details of our key idea. But doing so will clearly take more than a few basic statements! So how do we keep track of all the information we need to share in our presentation, without making our slides a disaster?

The answer is speaker notesNotes that only the speaker can see. . In PowerPoint and other presentation software, speaker notes are notes that only the speaker can see—they don’t appear in the version of the presentation that the rest of the audience sees. And we can fill our speaker notes with all the talking points required to communicate our key idea without our audience ever seeing all of that extra text.

shows an example of how to use speaker notes. The image shows what a presenter will see on her screen—but while she sees all of this helpful information, the audience will only see the title slide on the left. The speaker notes for a particular slide will be in the box on the right. As noted in the image, the notes can include bulleted or numbered lists and styled text. It’s here that we’ll be able to keep track of all the additional information we want to share with our audience, but don’t want to include on the slides themselves.

imagedata.alt: The view of speaker notes in Microsoft PowerPoint. The speaker sees the present slide, the slide up next in the presentation, any notes the speaker has made for the current slide, the time, and how long the presentation has been going, along with a few other tools.

section.para: also shows a few other advantages of presenting this way. The small slide on the right at the top is the next slide, which means the presenter will know what she has to talk about next and can transition cleanly. At the top of the current slide, the screen also shows the current time (on the right, 2:52 PM) and a timer tracking how long the presentation has lasted so far (on the left, four seconds). Note that switching out of this presenter view in PowerPoint resets the timer.
Creating speaker notes in PowerPoint is easy. In the main slide editor, the speaker note box is just below the current slide, as shown in .

imagedata.alt: The screen within Microsoft PowerPoint where you can make and edit speaker notes.

section.para: It’s probably best to create speaker notes after you’ve finalized your slides. You’ll want to make sure that your notes talk only about things that are actually in the slides or topics you want the audience to know about. If you write speaker notes first but then end up cutting something out of the slides themselves, you may be left with confusing or incorrect talking points.
Should you use speaker notes? Yes, absolutely. They’re an integral part of effective business presentations. You’ll set yourself up for far more success by learning how to use them well.

section.title: Citations in Business Presentations
section.para: The last point to cover before talking about presentation delivery is citations. We previously discussed citations in , where we said that they are references to the original source for some piece of information. Since many business presentations will involve original research, it’s important to properly credit sources as well as to allow your audience to track the sources down for themselves.

The most common way to cite sources in a presentation is to give the source information in a textbox at the bottom of the slide. shows how a slide looks with the citation. In this example, the reference is to a paper by Halinski and other authors (“et al.” is a Latin abbreviation meaning “and others,” and is common in citations with multiple authors). This citation doesn’t include all the bibliographic information, but it does have enough for an audience member to write it down quickly or to Google keywords (Googling “halinski creativity during threat” brings up this paper as the first result).

imagedata.alt: A slide featuring a short-form citation. The citation reads “Halinski et al., ‘Creativity During Threat to Organizational Survival,’ Journal of Management, 2023”.

section.para: Usually a short-form citation such as the one in is sufficient, since it’s more than enough information for anyone in the audience to know your sources. Depending on the circumstances you might include more, though, such as we see in , which contains a complete bibliographic entry for the article. A complete entry like this one is overkill for most business presentations, but if you need to be more specific, you can include a simple note in the textbox, as we see in , referring viewers to a particular section of an article.

imagedata.alt: A slide featuring a complete citation entry. The citation reads “Halinski, M., Boekhorst, J. A., Allen, D., & Good, J. R. L. (2003). Creativity During Threat to Organizational Survival: The Influence of Employee Creativity on Downsizing Survival Selection. In Journal of Management. SAGE Publications. https://doi.org/10.1177/01492063231216691”.
A slide featuring a citation plus a note. The citation reads “Halinski et al., ‘Creativity During Threat to Organizational Survival,’ Journal of Management, 2023; see especially study #1.”

section.para: We can cite websites and other forms of media in the same way. shows a citation to a website, and while it lacks all the information in a complete bibliographic entry, it has enough for someone else to find the original source.

imagedata.alt: A slide featuring a citation to a website. The citation reads “Vice, ‘The best holiday movies for your zodiac sign,’ December 15 2023”.

section.para: Be sure to cite your sources in business presentations. The guidance given here is enough for most situations, but pay attention to citation norms in your field or among presenters in your industry.

section.title: Delivering an Effective Business Presentation
section.para: So you’ve planned your presentation, studied the principles of clear slide design, and built your slide deck according to the principles. You’ve got all your content ready and you know what you want to say about your one key idea. Now it’s time to deliver your presentation!
But what’s the best way to do it?

Well, it turns out that we’ve already learned most of the techniques for effectively delivering a business presentation. Those techniques are the same as those of business communication more generally; giving a presentation is just an instance of person-to-group communication, and so everything we’ve said about that communication before now applies to presentations. Desires, needs, audience, tone, eye contact, gestures, everything else: good presentations involve all of it.

Because presentations are such a common occurrence, though, there’s more we can say about delivering them here. You’ll notice that there will be a bit of repetition, but that isn’t bad. The only way to get better at business communication is to learn and relearn the principles through practice.

section.title: Presenting with a Sense of Play
section.para: Given how difficult many people find public speaking, it might be hard to believe that giving a presentation could be fun. But when you understand your audience and your message, and understand the materials you’ve prepared, it can be exactly that—and when it is, your audience will notice. Your audience will see that you’re having a good time telling your story, and your attitude will be infectious. You’ll draw them into your frame and you’ll be able to lead them where you want them to go. You’ll have the special experience of connecting with an audience over interesting, worthwhile topics that you’re an authority on, and your audience members will see you that way.
Business communication experts Kelly Quintanilla and Shawn Wahl describe this sort of attitude as presenting with a “sense of play”:

blockquote.para: After teaching public speaking for a combined 30 years and listening to thousands of speeches, we can say with certainty that the most important thing you can do to handle the anxiety created by public speaking is to treat the experience with a sense of play. Let’s look at the reality of the situation. Typically, you’ll speak to an audience for between 5 and 30 minutes. Is 30 minutes really worth all that worrying? What if you faint? What if you accidentally flash the audience? What if you spill your drink on your notes? What if you bump the table over and the podium hits you in the head, knocking you to the ground? Chances are none of these things will happen. Instead, any problems you face will be minor.

But truth be told, all these things have happened to us, and we still continue to love speaking in public. Why? Are we deranged? No, we have learned to treat public speaking with a sense of play. If something small doesn’t go according to plan, we realize that, for the most part, no one but us will notice. If we make a bigger mistake, such as spilling a drink, we acknowledge it, laugh it off, and then move forward. Yes, we are embarrassed, but that’s life, and it has little impact on the audience. Quintanilla, K. M., & Whal, S. T. (2019), Business and professional communication (4th ed.). Sage, p. 325.

section.para: Yes, stuff sometimes happens during a presentation. I once gave an academic presentation with the zipper on my pants down; when I realized later what had happened, I returned to the room I spoke in and gave the podium a hug, since I stood behind it most of the time. When considering the many wild things that can happen when we present, it’s crucial to realize that we, as the speakers, are almost entirely in control of how our audience reacts to them. That is, our audience will take their cues about potentially embarrassing events from us, and will follow our lead.

For example, let’s say you get up to the lectern and knock over your water bottle. That could be embarrassing, and it might be someone’s worst nightmare. But how we react to it will determine how the audience reacts. If we roll our eyes at ourselves and say, “I guess I better not get thirsty,” then our audience will laugh, move on, and forget about it. But if we get flustered and make a big deal of it, our audience will think it’s a big deal too, until eventually they start to think, “Wow, this presentation really is a disaster.”

The idea of a “sense of play” aptly describes the demeanor we ought to have when presenting. If we are there to share and learn interesting things, our audience will feel the same way. This isn’t to say that developing this demeanor is easy. For many people it might take hundreds of hours of practice. But if a positive demeanor is our intent, the right attitude will come and the behavior will follow.
We owe it to ourselves to present this way. As Quintanilla and Wahl put it:

blockquote.para: Public speaking is an extremely valuable skill and one you should work to master. Prior to giving any speech, you should do your research, design an audience-centered message, and practice. In the moment when you are delivering the speech, you have to learn to roll with it. The adrenaline rush will affect you in some way, shape, or form. Begin to determine your responses to the rush, and develop strategies to overcome or accept those responses. Never give public speaking more power over your life than it deserves. It’s okay if it makes you a little nervous, but never let it stand between you and an opportunity to express yourself as a leader.Quintanilla, K. M., & Whal, S. T. (2019). Business and professional communication (4th ed.). Sage, p. 325.

section.para: As effective business communicators, we are leaders. And we can show that leadership in our presentations.

section.title: Practice Your Presentation
section.para: There is no substitute for practicing your presentation. Live practices with real audiences are best. The more you practice, the more you’ll know your material, and the better you can react when things change.
Time yourself during practices. Know the structure of your presentation so that, if you’re going long, you can cut some material at the end but keep the most important points.

Academics, business professionals, and many other speakers practice their presentations all the time. The fact that you also need to practice says nothing about your skill as a communicator. You will improve through practice and will be a stronger presenter.

section.title: Open Strong
section.para: With the idea of a sense of play in the background, let’s look at a few more specifics, starting with our opening.

Effective beginnings often cut immediately to your hook. You don’t even need to say who you are or where you come from; you may launch immediately to something that grabs your audience’s attention. Once you’ve interested them, you can repeat your name and integrate your introduction into your plan for the presentation. Remember, an audience-first presentation begins with something that will interest them. Right away we must answer the question, why should they listen to me? “Because it will be entertaining!” is a perfectly good answer, and so is “Because they’ll learn something” and “Because they’ll get to know a new opportunity.” But we have to give the audience a reason to believe those answers in the first place.

Regardless of whether you skip straight to the hook, don’t undercut yourself by talking about how nervous you are or how your topic is boring. Your audience will believe you and those remarks set your message in opposition to your audience.

Especially when opening but also throughout your presentation, don’t just read the material on the slides. Use your speaker notes to cue your memory so that you can speak without looking at the slides, and look at your audience as you move your eyes over the room. Meet each person’s glance. Speak slowly and assertively. As with every moment of communication, part of what you are communicating is you. Show them your value.
This kind of slow, deliberate, but interesting opening marks you immediately as someone to be listened to, and you’ll have your audience right where you want them.

section.title: Continue Strong
section.para: As your presentation continues, resist the temptation to dwell on minor details. Trust your slides, your notes, and your speaker plan. Confidently move into the one key idea and allow your audience to feel the excitement you have for it.

Use verbal transitions as you move from slide to slide and section to section in your presentation. Pause between each section and allow your audience to understand and appreciate that you’re moving to a new topic. Use signpostsLanguage that describes where you are in your presentation and what you are currently doing. , or language that describes where you are in your presentation and what you are currently doing: “I’ve just spoken about why our new laptops will allow us to work more comfortably. Now I’d like to tell you what that comfort means for you.” These statements don’t deliver your message to your audience, but instead allow your audience to locate where you’re currently at in delivering that message.

Sometimes you may notice that your audience isn’t understanding or isn’t interested in what you’re saying. With practice and preparation you can adjust your material mid-presentation to adapt to what the audience is communicating back to you. This adaptation requires a clear understanding of your message and your reasons for wanting to give that message to your audience.

Extemporaneous and off-the-cuff changes to a presentation may seem like the province of the unprepared, but doing them effectively actually requires even greater preparation. It is one thing to ready yourself to present something; it’s another to know your message so well that you can go off the planned track to meet the audience in another location entirely, while still delivering that same message.

Humor is helpful, but groan-inducing puns or other jokes often are not. The audience may offer some pity laughs but those attempts at humor do not endear you to your listeners. When in doubt, ask for honest feedback about jokes.

section.title: Finish Strong
section.para: When the time comes to finish your presentation, finish. Slow your speech and alter your tone of voice at the very end of your talk in order to communicate that you are in fact done speaking. Saying your final line, pausing and looking around, and then saying “Thank you” is a clear way to communicate that your remarks have come to an end.

Make sure your final lines are reiterations of your one key idea and its implications or value for your audience. Just as we can undercut our message by a weak beginning, we can also do so by a weak ending, which often involves just trailing your voice off until you’re quiet, speaking about things that don’t matter, or asking forgiveness for how bad the presentation was. Do none of those things.
Never false close, or seem as though you’re about to finish but then continue to speak. People will hate you for it. When you are done, be done. Don’t get people’s hopes up and then destroy them.

section.title: Nonverbal and Other Behaviors for Presenting
section.para: We’ll cover just a few other behaviors important for presenting. See our previous topics, especially , for more detailed discussions.

As always, everything is communication, and this is even more true when all eyes in a room are on you. Speak slowly and deliberately. Look people in the eye and maintain eye contact. Pause when you need to remind yourself of what to say next, and then return to the audience. Alternate your intonation to add emphasis and anticipation to what you say.

Use appropriate hand gestures. Keep your hands from engaging in tics like playing with your hair or fiddling with your tie. Use your arms and hands to emphasize important points and to mark transitions from one topic to the next.
Smile and engage your audience with your facial expressions. Raise your eyebrows or use playful expressions like fake glowers or sarcastic pouting, when appropriate. Be expressive, in positive ways.

Move around, if you’re able, but only if you don’t need your speaker notes. Stay close to the notes when necessary, and don’t get caught on the opposite side of the room when it’s time to transition and you can’t remember what to say next.

Your personal appearance when presenting matters. Dress professionally in a way that gives you confidence and communicates your status both as an effective communicator and as an authority on the topic you’re speaking about.

section.title: Questions, Answers, and Dealing with Hostility
section.para: We’ll finish this section on delivering presentations with two more points: questions and answers, and hostile audiences.

Some presentations may include time for audience questions at the end (in some fields, it may also be customary for audience members to ask questions during a presentation; learn the norms for your field). Academic-oriented presentations, for example, almost always have a Q&A period.
If you do take questions after your presentation while still speaking to the group, a few pointers will help you handle things well.

First, listen carefully to the question. After the person asking is done speaking, repeat the question back to them, or a shortened version of it, to make sure you’ve understood. Thank them for the question, and then give a brief answer. When you’re done answering, you may ask them whether your remark has responded to their question, but this isn’t necessary. If you do ask and they say you didn’t respond, either clarify what they’d like to know, or say that you’ll be happy to talk about it later. Don’t spend too much time on any one question.

If a question is totally irrelevant to your presentation, thank the person asking for an interesting question, and then say that you’ll have to think about it more, because you haven’t yet considered that angle.

If you don’t know the answer to a question, “I don’t know” is a fine response in many circumstances. You can also add that you’re interested in learning more about that issue and how it relates to what you presented on.

When you’re cornered by a difficult, relevant question that you don’t have an answer for, and you’re being pressed for one anyway, acknowledge that the question is important and that you’ll have to address it in the future.

Handling a question-and-answer session is a matter of mastering certain stock responses (“That’s interesting, I hadn’t considered that before,” “I’ll have to think about that further,” and so on) and speaking confidently. As with handling mishaps during presentations, your audience will follow your lead; if they see that you’ve been mentally devastated by a difficult question, they’ll think you’ve failed. But if you acknowledge a difficult situation and that there is more to work on, then you’re just admitting that you don’t have every answer, which the audience already knew anyway.

Sometimes you may have to present to audiences who are openly hostile to you, your organization, or your ideas. When this happens there may not be much you can do either to sway them to your side or even to calm them down.

Whatever the situation, the best response to hostility is to acknowledge that a situation is difficult or frustrating, and then to calmly stick to the facts. If you as the speaker become overly defensive or emotional in front of a hostile audience, you’ll be throwing gas on a fire. Reiterate your message and its value, and don’t let your audience take over the frame of your presentation.
Presentations to a hostile audience are an extreme test of your business communication skills. Remaining calm will cover many other mistakes.

section.title: Debriefing and Receiving Feedback
section.para: The final section in this topic is on debriefing and receiving feedback.

To debriefTo talk about how a presentation went with a trusted group of colleagues. after a presentation is to talk about how it went with a trusted group of colleagues. The ideal group is one that will be supportive but also honest about what went well and what didn’t. Listen to their thoughts, and pay close attention to points brought up by more than one person. If multiple people noticed an issue with an idea or your speaking style during a presentation, they are probably on to something.

When you receive feedback, remember that your value as a person is not connected to your ability as a presenter. Try to distance yourself from negative remarks by simply seeing them as things you’ll do differently next time. You’re always learning as a communicator and as a presenter. Allow yourself to make mistakes and grow.

Not everyone will tell you the truth about how a presentation went. People who will give you their honest opinion in measured words are your best allies here, and you should cultivate relationships with them. They will help you become better communicators.

Business presentations can be dynamic, exciting, and even fun. They can also be the professional equivalent of watching dry paint get even drier. Where our presentations will fall on this continuum is mostly up to us.

chapter.label: Topic 11
chapter.title: Technology and the Future of Business Communication

section.title: Technology and Business Communication
section.para: In 1860, the fastest way for information to travel from cities in the eastern United States to California was to send it by the Pony Express. The Pony Express was a mail service that operated between April 1860 and October 1861. While it wasn’t around long, the Express could deliver mail from one side of the continent to another in an average of ten days, with the record being under eight, when news of Abraham Lincoln’s inaugural address reached California in that time from the eastern states.

Eight days is glacially slow by our standards, of course, but back then it was blazing fast, especially when one of the only other options was to send your message in a boat that traveled around the southern tip of South America and back up to the United States’ west coast. The Pony Express was able to send communications quickly by building rest stations along a trail that crossed the country and stocking the stations with horses. Riders would push their horses to a sprint for twenty or twenty-five miles, and when they reached a new station, they’d pick up a fresh horse and continue. This relay-race method of carrying letters meant that horses were at a constant gallop and could make the trip without stopping to rest.

Though groundbreaking, the Pony Express wasn’t profitable. And yet, what ended it wasn’t a lack of money or people willing to make the journey. It died because of the telegraph, an entirely different system of communication. Using electricity and Morse code, telegraph operators could send messages from New York to San Francisco in just minutes, forever closing the gap between the cities.

The rise and sudden end of the Pony Express illustrates the beginning of a pattern that has continued since then: wherever there are new communications technologies, major changes to businesses and the ways they operate are sure to follow. It happened with the telephone, radio, television, computer, internet, cell phone, and social media. And it will happen again. Whatever the communications technology, we can be certain that it will have major impacts on the possibilities for doing business, and it may create completely new industries that couldn’t have existed before. It’s impossible to predict exactly what the impacts will be, but we know they’ll come.

It is in this relationship between technology and business communication that we begin to glimpse the importance of something we read about way back in the first topic of this course: the idea that the purpose of business communication is business success. The field of business communication exists in order to contribute to a business’s successful operation, but the point goes even beyond that—new means or channels of business communication often open new ways that businesses can be successful in the first place. The telegraph did this, and so did the phone and all the other technologies we mentioned before. These were new means of communication, which invented new ways for businesses to operate and interact with the public.

Thus it’s a bit redundant to say that business communication ought to play a leading role in how an organization functions and how it explores business opportunities. It’s redundant because business communication already does play this role, whether or not we acknowledge it and whether or not we’re prepared to make it work for us. It’s already happening right now, as new technologies create new audiences and new audiences create new segments of a market for us to communicate with. The integral role of technology and communication in business success will always exist. The only question is, what will we do about it?

In this topic and the three following, we deal with that question and others like it. Here we consider the role of new media and digital literacy in business communication, along with the possibility of future-proofing our means of communication. In the next topic we cover cross-cultural communication in business, a more pressing problem than ever before because of—again—new technologies. then continues that theme with a discussion of ethical concerns in business communication, and , the final topic, deepens the relationship between communication success and business success.

Technological changes drive changes in communication, which in turn drive new opportunities for businesses to succeed. Effective business communicators have a chance to harness this power and direct these changes both for their own good and for the good of their organizations and society as a whole.
Let’s see how.

section.title: New Media
section.para: In the context of business communication, the term new mediaAny novel way of sharing information; in a business communication context, technological innovations that transform a business’s ability to communicate internally or externally. refers to any novel way of sharing information. This definition is intentionally broad and could include things as different as virtual-reality goggles to newly-coined words. Humans are constantly inventing new means for exchanging ideas, and whatever they come up with belongs to new media.

In the context of technology and business communication, however, “new media” refers primarily to technological innovations that transform a business’s ability to communicate internally or externally. The telegraph was once an example of new media, as were the phone and other inventions mentioned in the previous section. Those and other technologies transformed or even created whole industries and, in some cases, made fundamental changes to how businesses work.

It is not always obvious what impact new media will have on business communication, however. In 2013, for example, Google released a wearable technology called Google Glass. Google Glass was an eyeglass frame that had no lenses, but that had a small screen on the side that a user could look at. A person with the Google Glass and a Wi-Fi connection could access the internet and bring the power of a computer right before their eyes.

Google marketed the wearable technology as a generational shift in technology access, and it’s certainly easy to imagine how it might have impacted business communication. The most obvious way would be by an increased and highly customized ad presence that’s literally in front of the customer’s eyes all the time. But there could be other ways too, including new opportunities for things like filming, surveying, teaching, and other activities.

Unfortunately for Google, there was already a well-known product that could access the internet and bring the power of a computer before the eyes of customers. That product was a smartphone, and when the Glass premiered in early 2013, most people already had smartphones. And if you did have a smartphone, what was the point of buying Glass? Why not just use your phone? People asked themselves those exact questions back in 2013, and they answered that there was no point. Google stopped selling Glass in March of the same year it debuted and stopped supporting it entirely that September.

The story of Google Glass has many lessons to teach concerning new media. One is that, in order to be successful, new media shouldn’t make its users look like they’re wearing last year’s failed robot cosplay. But a more important lesson is that, when it comes to business communication, we can’t know the effects of new media in advance. We can guess at those effects, and we can dress our guesses up as “predictions” or “forecasts” to make them sound more official. But since the landscape of business communication is so large and varied, and the number of factors impacting it so enormous, it simply isn’t possible for anyone to tell with certainty or even much confidence what things will be like after the arrival of a new form of media.

From a communications perspective, we therefore find ourselves in the following position with respect to new media: we can know for sure that some new media will change the landscape of business communication, but we cannot know exactly which cases of new media will do so, nor how they will do it. And while this is a position characterized primarily by ignorance, we can draw out some guidance for how effective business communicators relate to and use new media in their professional lives.

The first piece of guidance is that effective business communicators are always trying to get the lay of the land in which they’re working. They’re noting who’s using what means of communication and how they’re doing it. They’re paying attention to trends they read about and, more importantly, trends they notice themselves: are clients picking up a new technology? Are people buzzing about a new way of reaching customers? In order for us to interact well with new media, we first have to know about new media. And that happens as we keep our eyes open and stay aware of what’s happening and what changes we’re noticing in those we communicate with.

The second piece of guidance is that effective business communicators are early adopters. An early adopterA person who begins to use that technology very early on in its lifecycle, perhaps even as one of the first people to do so. of some technology is a person who begins to use that technology very early on in its lifecycle, perhaps even as one of the first people to do so. Early adopters might be early adopters because they’re well-connected, but most of the time they start using a product before others simply because they find out about it and take the initiative to involve themselves.

Gmail is an example. It’s now the world’s most popular email service, but for the first few years of its existence it was available as an invite-only beta service. Those who knew about it had the chance to train themselves on a communications technology that would in fact change the way businesses operate.

Being an early adopter is an important part of the third piece of guidance, which is to establish individual and brand identity in new media as soon as possible. The less business-speak way of saying this is that it’s a good idea to carve out a niche for yourself and for your organization, as soon as possible, in new media. Most of the time this might be as simple as creating an account and staking a claim on usernames or web addresses. Being an early adopter doesn’t automatically mean you’re an early user, after all; and as we said before, we don’t always know what the impact of a certain new media will be. The next big thing could have a Gmail-sized impact on the business world, or it could be Google Glass. Effective business communicators will be prepared to react in either direction.

To be clear, all of this is easier said than done, and sometimes we have to make choices about new technologies on the basis of almost no information. But at the very least we can keep an open mind—not just by being willing to consider new ideas, but by remembering that arrogance about our ability to foresee the future is often just a mask for ignorance and fear.

We’ll close this section with an example of that arrogance. In the previous topic we discussed how the completion of the transcontinental telegraph line ended the Pony Express. Just a few years after that line began to operate, William Orton took over its management as the president of Western Union Telegraph Company. Orton had years of experience in the industry and knew the landscape.

But when faced with new media and a powerful new way to communicate—the telephone—Orton refused to consider its strengths and focused only on how the technology failed to match up with his preconceived idea of what communication ought to look like. “This ‘telephone’ has too many shortcomings to be seriously considered as a means of communication,” Orton reportedly said when its inventor, Alexander Graham Bell, offered him the chance to buy the patents.Szczerba, R. J. (2015, January 5). 15 worst tech predictions of all time. Forbes.

Orton had reasons to oppose the telephone: the new media was rough, and it would require infrastructure changes. It was a direct competitor to the telegraph. But his refusal to appreciate new possibilities seems also to have stemmed from the fact that those possibilities challenged the way he was comfortable doing business. Rather than see the challenge as an opportunity for growth, it was for him something to be ridiculed and discarded.

Some new media perhaps deserve to be ridiculed (here we’re looking at you, Google Glass, with computer-unenhanced eyes). But since we don’t know beforehand what impact they’ll have, effective business communicators err on the side of acceptance and lean into trends in order to contribute to the future possibilities of their organizations.

section.title: Digital Literacy
section.para: In we introduced the idea of emotional literacy. Emotional literacy refers to a person’s ability to understand and use affective information, or information about the feelings and emotions of the people around them. More generally, the term “literacy” is a familiarity and proficiency we have with a certain field—we could have automotive literacy, for example, which would be a familiarity with how cars work; or we could have culinary literacy, which would mean we’re a good cook.

Another literacy, this one more relevant to business communication, is digital literacyOne's ability to use computer technology in all its forms, from managing a personal computer to coding a video game to running financial databases. . Digital literacy is our ability to use computer technology in all its forms, from managing a personal computer to coding a video game to running financial databases. Since digital literacy includes so many different things, we’ll want to focus specifically on those aspects of digital literacy that concern business communication.

Many topics we’ve covered so far deal with digital literacy. discussed email, spoke about organizational culture and communication, the internet and social media, presentation software. Each of these fits into digital literacy as a system we could have a particular ability with. That ability, together with our skills as business communicators, would then determine how well we’re able to use each of these systems to interact with others effectively.

First and foremost, expert business communicators must push themselves to achieve high levels of digital literacy. Depending on your background and day-to-day responsibilities, this may not be easy, since you may lack experience or even awareness of different technologies and their capabilities. As we’ve seen, interaction with new media and keeping our eyes open for trends can help us with the awareness part. But the experience part can only come from us. The only way we can understand how different technological tools may be used for communication is to use them ourselves. Business communications is a field that changes quickly and requires its practitioners to grow accordingly.

Beyond our own skills, however, the development of digital literacy in others may be a major part of our role in an organization. Digital literacy training has no natural home in many companies; some parts fall to human resources, others to information technology, and others simply to the unspoken expectation that employees will already have the requisite digital literacy upon beginning their employment. This situation—where digital literacy is essential to an organization, but doesn’t fit cleanly into a certain department—gives experts in business communication an opportunity to make a valuable contribution.

Group trainings in certain aspects of communications technologies are the most obvious way of addressing shortcomings in digital literacy. The simplest examples of these trainings are the kind done at public libraries or other community centers, where people can learn to use email or find information on the internet. We’ll probably be able to count on colleagues at our organizations having more knowledge than that—but how much more? And how do we find out how much knowledge our colleagues have?

In your efforts at enhancing digital literacy, a good place to start is with colleagues whose job titles or descriptions don’t name a specific skill or domain of communication technology. This isn’t to say that other people won’t need training, but someone hired to be a social media manager is much more likely than other people in an organization to already possess communication technology skills. On the other hand, titles like “product manager” are much vaguer, and the corresponding job descriptions may be vague as well; people in those roles may lack knowledge that others take for granted.

As a general rule, digital literacy trainings are better when they are individualized, and better when they are about a specific topic and can treat that topic from beginning to end. This means that the most effective literacy trainings are one-on-one consultations in order to train someone with a particular tool or piece of software. These trainings also happen to be the most time-consuming, however. The proper balance of individual consultations with group meetings depends on your organization and its needs.

In working with the digital literacy of others, our training as an effective communicator reminds us to take an audience-first approach. It may be difficult for us, but we must try to imagine what it would be like not to have some bit of knowledge; what would it be like for us to not know, say, how to access files on Slack, or send a group message. From that imagined perspective, it will be easier to be sympathetic and reframe someone’s lack of digital literacy as an opportunity to learn.

You don’t need to go overboard here, though. When I was a customer support representative for a software company, an angry customer once emailed needing help. At the end of his message he said, “And do NOT just send me to another website!” This gentleman was tired of support staff sending him links that he had to open and read to find a solution to his problem. That’s fair. But it was also still true that the solution to his problem was clearly explained at a different website. So I responded by copying and pasting the directions from the website into the email I sent him. He felt he was getting an individualized treatment, which was true in a sense, and he received the information he needed.

Addressing digital literacy needs, including our own, often puts us at risk for the curse of knowledge. In we learned that the curse of knowledge is the assumption that, because something is easily understandable for us, it must therefore be easily understandable to others, and so requires little explanation. But we’re discussing digital literacy precisely because shortcomings in knowledge do exist, so we can’t assume that others know what we do.

Incorrect assumptions about what others know and don’t know can lead to the rundown problemBeing expected to know or do something that you don't know, but feeling unable to ask for help with what you don't know. , an issue common in many areas of business communication. In the American TV show The Office, in an episode called “Michael Scott Paper Company,” Jim is asked by his boss Charles to prepare a “rundown” of his sales clients. Jim doesn’t know what a rundown is, but he’s already made an unfavorable impression on Charles, so he doesn’t feel he can ask. He spends the day trying to figure out how to make a rundown, and even after he completes it, he still isn’t sure whether he’s done it right. Daniels, G. (Writer), Spitzer, J. (Writer), Gervais, R. (Writer), Stupnitsky, G. (Director) & Eisenberg, L. (Director). (2009, April 9). Michael Scott Paper Company (Season 5, Episode 21) [TV series episode]. In G. Daniels, R. Gervais, S. Merchant, B. Silverman, H. Klein, & P. Lieberstein (Executive Producers), The Office. Reveille Productions; NBC Universal Television; 3 Arts Entertainment; Deedle-Dee Productions.

Even seasoned business communicators will sometimes face rundowns of their own—topics, skills, and other aspects of digital literacy they aren’t familiar with. For our own rundowns we ought to just ask, and we can be proactive in helping others enhance their skills as well. If we’re going to be experts in open lines of communication, we should take advantage of that openness.
Every organization faces problems of digital literacy. Effective business communicators can be some of the people best suited to overcoming those problems.

section.title: Artificial Intelligence and Business Communication
section.para: Previous topics have covered the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in various ways, but it’s time to cover this important issue in more detail. We’ll do that both here and in the next section.

The term “artificial intelligence” is just a way of saying “computers that are trained to learn and then alter their response based on what they learn.” Businesses have been using AI for many years and for many reasons, such as planning delivery routes for drivers or chatting with customers online about common problems.

But innovations in the last several years, especially programs trained with data from human language, introduce new challenges and new opportunities. ChatGPT is one such innovation, as are other forms of generative AI, including Gemini (Google) and Claude (Anthropic). Various versions of these programs are available on the internet and within apps, in both free and paid tiers. It’s common for businesses and other organizations to have enterprise accounts with one or more AI service, and you have probably already used them yourself.

We call these services “generative” AI because their primary function is to generate text, images, music, and other objects. They do this by receiving instructions written in normal human language instead of computer code. Their immense generative range, along with the ease of giving them instructions, make many forms of generative AI extremely powerful.

For example, here’s a paragraph that a recent version of ChatGPT produced in response to the prompt, “Please write a medium-length paragraph on how to effectively address an organization’s digital literacy needs”:

blockquote.para: Effectively addressing an organization’s digital literacy needs begins with a clear, realistic assessment of current skills across roles rather than assuming a uniform baseline. Digital literacy should be framed not as a one-time training initiative but as an ongoing capacity that supports the organization’s strategic goals, daily workflows, and decision-making. Successful approaches combine targeted, role-specific training with opportunities for hands-on practice, allowing employees to apply new tools and concepts directly to their work. Leadership support is crucial: when managers model digital competence and openly engage in learning, it signals that skill development is valued rather than remedial. Finally, organizations should build in mechanisms for continuous improvement—such as peer mentoring, accessible support resources, and periodic reassessment—so that digital literacy evolves alongside changing technologies instead of lagging behind them.

section.para: Given that the AI produced that text in less than three seconds, the potential of generative AI is not hard to see.

In addition, and as we have seen in previous sections, AI can also help modify text that already exists, for purpose or tone or any other aspect of a message. This next bit of text was generated by giving the AI the paragraph it just wrote, and then providing the additional prompt, “Can you re-write it using the slang of different ’90s and early 2000s TV shows that millennials would recognize?”

blockquote.para: Effectively addressing an organization’s digital literacy needs starts with doing a legit reality check—because assuming everyone has the same skill level is a real “we were on a break!” moment waiting to happen. Digital literacy shouldn’t be treated like a one-and-done training montage; it’s more of a long-running series that needs to support the org’s big plans, day-to-day grind, and “what are we even doing here?” decisions. The strongest approach is a solid mix of role-specific training and hands-on practice, so people can actually try the thing instead of just nodding along like it’s a bad PowerPoint episode. Leadership matters a lot here: when managers jump in, learn out loud, and admit they don’t know everything, it sends a clear signal that growing skills is cool—not a punishment. And to keep the whole thing from going full dial-up, organizations need ongoing support systems—peer help, easy resources, and regular check-ins—so digital literacy stays fresh, current, and definitely not stuck in reruns.

section.para: I don’t know when you would need to change the tone of a message to include references to Saved By the Bell or Friends, but with generative AI, you can. Other AI programs take similar text prompts to create images, logos, music, sound effects, and so on.

This is not the place to discuss the various ethical issues surrounding the use of generative AI in different media. As far as business communication is concerned, the following are the two most important points we can more confidently make right now:

listitem.para: No one knows the long-term impact the technology will actually have. Specific things said about these services can be obsolete in months or even weeks. It is clear that many things are changing in many industries and positions. What the end state of these changes will be, we cannot say.

The choice about using generative AI services for business communication, whether to create text or other objects, depends on industry- and field-specific norms. It is not possible to give generally applicable guidance about what is desirable or ethical in AI use.

section.para: We are not yet to the point where whole industries are producing nothing but AI-generated media. Each field and profession is currently working out what they see as the appropriate way to use AI services. It’s common in writing boilerplateStandardized text used in contracts or orientations. of all kinds, for example, which is standardized text used in contracts or orientations. But in other places, AI is a much more direct threat to human work, and that’s where the battles are being fought.

We’ve seen one such battle in the last few years in the 2023 strike of Hollywood screenwriters. One of the major issues in the strike was the use of AI. Writers wanted strict rules about the role AI could play in producing scripts, of course, along with protections about pay and credits for human writers when AI is involved. The issue swung in different directions, and the agreement that ended the strike gave writers those protections. But it also allowed studios to train AI on material that currently exists, which will only make it better at mimicking human writing. Richardson, D. (2023, October 16). Hollywood’s AI issues are far from settled after writers’ labor deal with studios. CNBC.

This conflict, however, was just a first big argument in an ongoing debate over the use of AI. The debate will last years, and given the history of business development in the United States, it is likely that more and more business functions will be turned over to AI.

There is reason for optimism, though. Even now, several years after ChatGPT erupted into the public consciousness, paid-tier generative AI systems still often produce bland, lifeless text with no lasting appeal. And it definitely cannot replicate most of what an effective human communicator can offer—it can produce the words, but not the eye contact, the gestures, and the sincere understanding that humans show to each other in moments of connection. We should insist on making those elements of human interaction part of our regular communications. These skills of empathy and emotional intelligence could become far more valuable business assets in an AI-saturated future.

section.title: Message Planning with Artificial Intelligence
section.para: As discussed in the previous section, generative AI is powerful, but it lacks the sincere understanding and genuine human empathy required for effective business connection. This does not mean, however, that we should ignore these tools. What we ought to do is shift how we view them. They may not be able to effectively author messages all by themselves, but they can be tools for planning and execution.

In the planning stage of the communication process, for example, AI can act as a brainstorming assistant. It can suggest possible channels for communication you might have missed, or draft key messages for you to refine. But because AI often defaults to generic, low-stakes responses, it is always important that you review its output to refine it and make it fit the context in which you’re communicating.
To illustrate these points, let’s look at how to structure a communication plan, and then compare a plan created by a human against one generated by AI.

section.title: The Communication Plan Template
section.para: Whether you are sketching on a notepad or prompting an AI, every effective communication plan must answer four questions. You can use this simple template to structure your strategy:

listitem.para: Audience: Who specifically needs to hear this message?
Purpose: Why are we communicating, and what is the desired outcome?
Channel: What is the most effective medium (email, instant message, face-to-face, etc.)?
Key messages: What are the 1–3 most critical points the audience must understand?

section.para: Let’s suppose that you are an IT manager at a mid-sized logistics company. A server crashed last night and caused a four-hour email outage for the sales team. The server is now fixed, but some emails sent during that window may be lost. You need to inform the team immediately.

Below are two plans. Plan A was created by a human manager using the template above. Plan B was generated by an AI tool with the prompt: “Write a communication plan for a server crash at our company.”

listitem.para: Audience: The sales team (primary); executive leadership (secondary)
