Purpose: To inform sales that the system is back online and to give instructions on how to check for lost client messages.
Channels: Slack/Teams message: for immediate notification. Follow-up email containing detailed technical instructions.

Key messages: Email service is fully restored as of 8:00 AM. If you sent a client email between 2:00 AM and 6:00 AM, check your “Sent” folder to make sure it went through. IT support is on standby to help verify client receipt or solve other problems.
Audience: All staff, customers, shareholders, and social media followers
Purpose: To apologize for the inconvenience, to maintain transparency, and to uphold brand reputation.
Channel: Company website banner, posts on Facebook, Instagram, and X, all-hands emails, press releases.

Key messages: We experienced a temporary disruption in our digital infrastructure. Our technical team worked tirelessly to resolve the issue with maximum efficiency. We value your patience and understanding as we continue our commitment to excellence.

section.title: Analyzing the Difference
section.para: If you compare these two plans, the limitations of the AI approach become clear. Let’s look at a few contrasts.

First, the human plan correctly isolates the sales team as the only group that truly needs to know. The AI plan suggests alerting customers and audiences on social media, which is both unnecessary and perhaps risky. It is probably better not to publicly announce an internal glitch if you don’t have to; doing so might worry clients unnecessarily.

The human plan includes the specific technical instruction to “check your Sent folder.” This is the most useful piece of information for the employee, because it shows whether sales emails were actually sent or not. The AI plan misses this entirely and instead offers instead a generic apology about a “commitment to excellence.”

The human plan uses a fast channel for communication (Slack) because sales reps are often on their phones. The AI suggests a press release, which is a slow, formal channel inappropriate for a minor internal IT ticket, and may be outdated in some industries besides.

Given these contrasts, and the advantages of the human plan, the implications are clear. AI tools are excellent at following the structure of a plan—ours gave us all the categories we needed, after all—but they often fail at the logic and reality of an actual business context. If you had followed the AI’s plan with no thought about your audience or the real demands of the situation, you might have caused a public relations issue over a minor server glitch.

To use AI effectively in the planning stage, you must actively manage the output. The fact that an AI produced it is a reason to be more skeptical of its usefulness, at least initially, rather than less. Start by feeding the specific template into your prompt; explicitly asking the tool to categorize its answer by things like “Audience, Purpose, Channel, and Key Messages” forces it to organize its output into a usable business structure and not a generic block of text. Once the AI generates a draft, your role shifts to quality control. You must check the output to make sure that the proposed channel actually reaches the intended audience, and that it does so with the correct tone and context. Remember that AI is best at providing only the skeleton of a plan. It is up to you to add the most meaningful content, such as the specific dates, times, names, and technical instructions that turn a generic strategy into an actionable solution. Doing all of that with a human sensitivity and refinement is a powerful strategy for effective business communication.

section.title: Future-Proofing Business Communication
section.para: Since we don’t know what new technology will mean for business communication, we may be concerned with how to future-proofTo make something immune from future changes, or otherwise unsusceptible to interruption by what is new. our communication. To future-proof something means to make it immune from future changes, or otherwise unsusceptible to interruption by what is new.

Is it possible to future-proof business communication? Not entirely. The lesson of William Orton, the telegraph, and the telephone will be learned time and again, and new technologies will continue to introduce new means of communication. Coming technologies will be implemented whether or not they seem like good ideas, if only for the promise they seem to present.

There are a few things to say on future-proofing, however. Clear communication, regardless of the means or channel, will always be valuable; jargon and business- and academic-speak tend to age fast and badly. This means that good writing is uncommonly resistant to future changes, AI services notwithstanding. In addition, the more aware of future changes we are, the better we’ll be able to control our messaging on new means and channels. We should look to expand to other platforms to establish our identity there, even if those platforms don’t end up as key parts of our organizations. Collaborating with others is one of the best ways to stay current on future changes and what they mean for communication.

But more important by far than future-proofing business communication is future-proofing ourselves as business communicators. Effective human communication will always be a valuable skill—and so it will always be in demand. Technology is changing much faster than human nature, and so while the technological means for communication will no doubt differ in the future, the basic techniques for clear, compassionate, and sensitive communication will not. The best future-proofing we can do is to arm ourselves with useful skills, especially ones that machines cannot easily duplicate. Regardless of what Silicon Valley tells us, the place of greatest importance for the future of meaningful business communication is not in technology, but in people.

chapter.label: Week 5
chapter.title: Cross-Cultural and Ethical Issues in Business Communication

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 5: Cross-Cultural and Ethical Issues in Business Communication. This week we will cover the following topics:

listitem.para: : Cross-Cultural Communication in Business
: Ethical Concerns in Local and Multinational Communication
: Communication Success and Business Success

section.title: Cultural Differences in Business Communication
section.para: Our previous topic dealt with technology and the future of business communication, and so we extended our thinking forward in time. For this topic and the next, we’ll instead push ourselves to extend our thinking in the present, in order to consider a larger group of people and societies in the possible audiences for our communications.

Considering more people and more societies requires us to think about cross-cultural communication in business. That phrase is a bit of a mouthful, so let’s break it down and put it in the context of what we’ve learned so far about communication.

section.title: Culture
section.para: First, culture. In we discussed the idea of an organizational culture, which we defined like this:

blockquote.para: An organization’s ways of being and doing things, together with the values and principles supposedly behind those ways, are its culture. Organizational cultures determine what it’s like to be a member in an organization, what it’s like to associate with them, and what channels of communication are likely to be most successful.

section.para: Since this was a definition of organizational culture, we meant it to apply to business-related organizations such as companies, corporations, teams, and other groups. This very same definition, however, can also apply to organizations that don’t have anything to do with business, and so we can also use it as a definition of culture more broadly.

CultureThe way of being and doing things related to any group, together with the values and principles supposedly behind those ways. is the way of being and doing things related to any group, together with the values and principles supposedly behind those ways. Cultures determine what it’s like to be a member of that group, what it’s like for others to associate with the group, and what channels of communication are likely to be most successful. Culture is such a broad notion, in fact, that it includes things like whether a group even thinks of itself as having a culture, or whether a group includes the kind of people who tend to define things. That’s right—the fact that I’m giving a definition of culture, and that the definition makes some sense to you, are aspects of our shared culture.

Cultures can be divided on the basis of many factors, including geographical area, political unit, and time period. And within any culture there will be many subculturesCultures embedded in a larger culture. , or cultures embedded in a larger culture. Subcultures can also be divided in many ways, and need not respect the boundaries of the larger cultures within which they’re embedded. We can consider the United States to be a culture, for example—one which has many different subcultures. One of those subcultures might be everyone who enjoys watching soccer. That’s a subculture united by a common interest, and obviously that subculture extends beyond the United States and into many other places in the world.

In addition to interests, common lines of division for subcultures include religion, race, gender, sexual orientation, attitude toward certain political issues, and others. You can think of the many subcultures you belong to and interact with; there are too many divisions to name here.

section.title: Cross-Cultural Communication and Cultural Difference
section.para: With this background understanding of a culture, we can now define cross-cultural communication. Cross-cultural communicationAny communication where there are major cultural differences between you and your audience, or between the sender and receiver of the message. is any communication where there are major cultural differences between you and your audience, or between the sender and receiver of the message. Of course, the important part of this definition is “major cultural differences,” because any person-to-person communication might be considered “cross-cultural” in the sense that two people don’t share every aspect of their culture. We therefore need to specify what a major cultural difference amounts to. From there we’ll be able to consider cross-cultural communication for business in particular.

Cultures differ along many different dimensions, but one influential way of understanding the differences is based on the social theories of Dutch researcher Geert Hofstede. Hofstede proposed the “6-D” model of national culture, or the idea that major differences between cultures could be identified along six different dimensions.Hofstede, G. (n.d.). The 6-D model of national culture. Retrieved January 25, 2024, from Here are Hofstede’s six dimensions of cultural difference, along with his explanation for the meaning of each difference:

listitem.para: IndividualismThe extent to which people feel independent, as opposed to being interdependent as members of larger wholes. . Individualism is the extent to which people feel independent, as opposed to being interdependent as members of larger wholes.

Power DistanceThe extent to which the less powerful members of organizations and institutions (like the family) accept and expect that power is distributed unequally. . Power distance is the extent to which the less powerful members of organizations and institutions (like the family) accept and expect that power is distributed unequally.
MasculinityThe extent to which the use of force is endorsed socially. . Masculinity is the extent to which the use of force is endorsed socially.
Uncertainty AvoidanceA society’s level of tolerance for uncertainty and ambiguity. . Uncertainty avoidance deals with a society’s tolerance for uncertainty and ambiguity.
Long-Term OrientationHow a society deals with change and preparation for change. . Long-term orientation deals with change and preparation for change.
IndulgenceHow people and individuals perviece the good things in life and manage their impulses. . Indulgence is about the good things in life and how people and individuals manage their impulses.

section.para: Hofstede meant for his six dimensions of cultural difference to apply to whole countries, but it’s clear that they can apply to subcultures as well. Certain religious groups may have high uncertainty avoidance along with high long-term orientation; a scientific society may be more comfortable with uncertainty but also have a long-term orientation and high individualism. These dimensions may even apply at the level of families and individuals.

While Hofstede’s work is useful, we ought to be cautious in how we use it. Cultures and subcultures can and do shift along these six axes, but they differ in other ways as well, and it isn’t clear whether all or even most cultural differences reduce to these six measures. In addition, the language used to categorize the measures is an aspect of culture itself, and shows a clear bias for Western ways of organizing and classifying people. Just as the acceptance of definitions is an aspect of culture, so is our way of thinking about culture; just because we think about culture a certain way does not mean that way is the most helpful. We will return to this point later.

For now, we can simply appreciate better our definition of cross-cultural communication. It’s any communication where the sender and receiver of a message differ in major cultural features, of the kind identified by Hofstede. Two people liking different music or having different opinions about a TV show might indicate differences in subculture, but they are not major differences. Cross-cultural communication involves major differences.

section.title: Norms, Communication, and Cultural Difference
section.para: A company’s organizational culture affects the way its employees communicate, and a group’s culture similarly affects its methods for communication. We can call these methods, and the expectations associated with them, a culture’s normsRules that govern how people interact with each other, such as the tone of voice, patterns of deference to someone in authority, personal space, and so on. for communication. A communication norm is a rule that governs how people interact with each other, such as the tone of voice, patterns of deference to someone in authority, personal space, and so on. We often don’t notice such norms in our own culture, since they’re just the basic ways people get along. We may become more sensitive to them when visiting a different culture, however.

One important norm is the language two people will use to communicate. In the United States we generally expect that we’ll be communicating in English, and using that language is a communication norm. But that norm can change depending on the context. Social services in different cities or counties may have Spanish-speaking staff in order to serve more residents in that area. In those places, the language norm would be different.

Both minor and major cultural differences impact communication and the norms for communication cross-culturally. I lived in Chile for several years soon after graduating from high school, for example, and quickly learned that this South American culture was very different from the one I was used to. When visiting someone’s home in Chile, it’s customary to stand in the street or on the road and shout “Hallo!” to request that they come to the door and let you in. In the United States we would just knock, but that isn’t done there. In Chile more people have a religious background as well, or at least claim a religious affiliation, which affects what is and isn’t appropriate in certain kinds of communication.

There are other differences too. Chile is a much less individualistic culture, meaning it’s more collectivist; there’s a greater sense of belonging to a single people united by more than just citizenship in a country. This cultural feature makes it far more acceptable to approach strangers in the street and speak to them—more acceptable than this action would be in a place like Boston, for example, where doing that is a good way to get yelled at. Cultural differences in Chile and other Spanish-speaking countries are even baked into the language itself, as a Spanish speaker must choose different verb conjugations when addressing someone directly, depending on their relationship. The tú verb conjugations are considered less formal and perhaps more intimate, while the usted conjugations set some distance between a speaker and a conversation partner.

section.title: Cross-Cultural Differences for Business Communication
section.para: As we’ve seen, major shifts in culture between places and groups bring with them differences in norms for communication. This is true for business communication as well. The norms for business communication in a particular culture derive from the general norms for communication in that culture. But the unique details of this derivation, and how business communication works in a certain place, are not always immediately obvious. More often than not, familiarizing ourselves with appropriate cross-cultural practices for business communication will require some study and effort.
We’ll see an example in the next section.

section.title: Business Communication in Japanese Culture
section.para: In the previous section we saw a few cultural differences between the United States and Chile. These cultural differences do impact business communication practices, and the norms for business communication in Chile will not be identical to those in America. However, Chile has still taken many of its communication norms from American and European culture, and so it won’t be as different as other cultures might be.
To see an example of how major cultural differences lead to major differences in norms for business communication, let’s consider Japan and Japanese culture.

section.title: Japanese Culture and Business Communication
section.para: On Hofstede’s dimensions of cultural difference, Japan scores in the middle for individualism, medium-high for power distance, at the top of the scale for masculinity, very high for uncertainty avoidance, tends to take a very long-term orientation, and tends far more toward restraint than indulgence. Put in more common terms, and with the understanding that many individuals and subcultures in Japan will not follow these patterns, we can say that Japan is more collectivist, more accepting of authority and more deferential to it, more accepting of force or forceful ways of behaving, more averse to uncertainty, and takes a longer-term view involving restraint of impulses, as compared to the United States.
Those are definitely major cultural differences. How might they affect cross-cultural business communication with a Japanese audience? Here are a few ways.

First, silence. Americans and other Western groups, especially upon meeting for the first time, tend to talk a lot in order to get to know each other. The exchange of ideas in meetings and other interactions is also thought to be a good way of working. This is not true in Japan, where it’s not customary for people to fill verbal space all the time.

Second, teams. As a more collectivist culture, Japanese business communication often involves praising an entire group or team, even when it’s known that a single individual made the crucial contribution.

Third, rank. Rank and seniority play a role in business life in the United States, but they’re often in the background. Not so in Japan. Clear and meaningful deference is shown to those with superior rank in Japan, and rank is often associated with age. The proper way to interact with someone of high status is different from how you’d interact with someone else.

Fourth, aggression. In keeping with the more subdued approach to business interactions between business organizations, aggressive sales or negotiating tactics will fail in Japan, even though more forceful ways of acting between individuals in an authority structure would be acceptable elsewhere. Some people in the United States would find aggressive approaches distasteful, but Japan has a more wholesale rejection of those ways of doing business.

Fifth, meishi. A meishi is a Japanese business card. Many business professionals in America have cards, but these items are much more important in Japan and are accompanied by special rituals for their exchange. In meeting someone for the first time in a business context, it’s not only customary but expected that you will exchange business cards. This is done with the lower-ranking person offering their card first. They extend the card to the recipient with both hands. After a moment the recipient will then extend their card, which you are expected to receive with both hands. You’re then expected to review the card, noting the rank and title. If a meeting follows this exchange, you do not put the card away but instead place it on the table between you and your conversation partner. If you receive more than one card, you are to arrange them in a certain order on the table, preserving the rank relationships among the people you’re speaking to.

Sixth, bowing. Outside of curtain calls at the end of performances, Americans almost never bow. But bowing is an important part of greeting and showing deference to authority in Japanese culture, and shows an awareness of the power differences between two people.

These are only six aspects of Japanese business culture; there are others. But these are enough to get an idea for how different the communication norms will be when dealing with Japanese audiences. Someone without thorough knowledge of these differences and norms would almost immediately offend Japanese communication partners and torpedo any chance of success with them. Successful business communication in this situation would require both awareness of the cross-cultural differences and a willingness to adapt to another way of doing things.

In reality, though, that willingness is no different from the attitude we take to our audience in other contexts. We’re always customizing our message and its presentation for the benefit of our audience. Sometimes that means we use an example involving video games because it will connect with our audience; sometimes that means we learn a Japanese ritual for exchanging business cards. The only difference is in the details.

section.title: Ethnocentrism
section.para: When it comes to cross-cultural business communication, effective communicators understand that our own way is not necessarily the best way. For us it seems to be the best way, but that’s because we’re most familiar with it and we’re already comfortable governing our behavior by those norms. We naturally assume that whatever way we do things now is the best way of doing them, or even the best way we could be doing them.

This bias is called ethnocentrismThe belief that our own culture and cultural practices should be the benchmark by which we judge other cultures and practices. . Ethnocentrism is the fancy name for the belief that our own culture and cultural practices should be the benchmark by which we judge other cultures and practices. An ethnocentric view might look at norms for Japanese business communication and think, “That’s dumb. Why are they so deferential? Why do you need a special ritual for business cards?” But this criticism would be both misplaced and misguided. In reality, there are many different ways of organizing the rules for communication in business, and different cultures come to different solutions about how to do it. The United States does it one way, and that way has certain advantages and disadvantages, relative to certain ends. Japan does it another way, and Chile does it a third way. While these different means of communication might be superior to others in certain respects, it isn’t the case that one is superior in general. They’re just different.

An important part of effective business communication across cultures is understanding our tendency to ethnocentrism. This tendency isn’t a moral failing, nor does it make us bad people; it’s natural to use what we know as a standard for judging what we don’t. But we’ll be more effective communicators when we recognize this bias in ourselves and take action to prevent it from impairing our exchanges with others.

Our job as cross-cultural communicators is the same as it’s always been in the other topics of this book: to understand our audience and to modify our communication to work with their expectations and needs. We do this not just by customizing the content of a message or the delivery of a presentation, but also in conforming our behavior to different norms for interaction in business settings.
Everything is communication, and cross-cultural issues in business really bring out the truth of this principle.

section.title: Meeting the Expectations of Your Audience
section.para: The most important principle for cross-cultural communication in business is to regulate your behavior according to the norms the audience believes are appropriate. As we’ve noted before, this principle is just a special case of the idea that we must work with the audience’s beliefs and expectations in order to communicate successfully. Cross-cultural success might require more of us, or more to get started, but it’s not really that different from leaving out certain jokes from your presentation because some audience members might find them offensive.

Understanding and meeting the norms an English audience believes are appropriate will not take much work, at least for those from the United States. But to do so with a Japanese audience will likely take real effort. If you have the task of communicating with a Japanese audience, take your preparation seriously. You will find useful principles in this book, but you also need detailed instruction from someone with real experience.

The same is true for anyone communicating with other cultures, especially those very different from what you are used to personally. Even when your audience seems to come from a culture similar to yours, don’t assume that the norms for business communication are therefore similar to those you know. Ask trusted advisers or find out whether your organization has a cultural training program for those working with cross-cultural audiences. You may be surprised to learn how different norms can be even when two cultures don’t have the major differences we discussed earlier. If you don’t know the norms, you can’t meet the expectations of your audience.

Most of the time, cultural differences don’t indicate anything more than different ways of doing things, or different ways of regulating behavior in certain interactions. Thus they don’t usually involve questions of the morality of cultural beliefs or practices.

This may not always be the case, however. For example, what if your job is to arrange communications with clients who come from a misogynistic culture or subculture? If the expectation of our audience is that we subordinate or even ignore the contributions women make to a discussion, should we follow along and meet those expectations? Should we regulate our behavior in a way that isn’t just different, but might actually be discriminatory? We’ll discuss this issue and give examples in the next topic.
When the expectations of our audience just reflect cultural differences, it’s our job to learn them and put them into practice. Our field guide for how to do this is next.

section.title: A Field Guide to Cross-Cultural Communication
section.para: Our job as effective cross-cultural communicators is to meet the expectations of our audience. So how do we do that? Each culture and subculture is different, and so each set of expectations is different. But we can give some general guidance for how to approach the problem of business communication across cultures.

section.title: Let Go of Stereotypes
section.para: Our minds are full of pre-formed beliefs about different cultures and about the people who come from them. We may call these beliefs stereotypesA stock belief about an individual or group of individuals based on assumptions about their behavior and way of life. —a stereotype is a stock belief about an individual or group of individuals based on assumptions about their behavior and way of life. Some of the stereotypes we hold will be more true and others more false, but all will be inaccurate in the sense that they’re just generalizations made on the basis of our experience. Generalizations are almost always false of at least some of the people they’re meant to apply to.

That’s why the first point in our field guide to cross-cultural communication is to let go of stereotypes. We already know our stereotypes can be inaccurate at best, so our goal should be to adopt the most correct beliefs possible about a culture and about individuals within that culture. Doing so demands that we drop our pre-formed beliefs and let ourselves learn. We can’t assume that we already know the correct norms for an interaction, or that we can understand the correct norms simply by examining what we already believe.

section.title: Do Your Homework
section.para: Once we clear our minds, it’s time to learn, and that means we need to do some homework. We need to find sources that teach us about the culture we wish to communicate with and that help us understand how that culture’s features give rise to its norms for communication.

Speaking directly to someone with hands-on experience is best here, but organizations may also provide cultural training. The expansion of international business has also created an industry around cultural training and consulting, with specialties for different places and peoples. Depending on the role you expect to take in communication, the homework you’ll have to do may be extensive.

You’ll want to make sure you know a few key norms in particular. First, what will the language of business communication be? Could it be a language other than English? If it is English, how much of the language can you expect that your audience will know? What buzzwords or other colloquialisms will you need to eliminate from your conversation in order to make sure that your audience understands your meaning?

Second, what is the pattern of authority and deference in the culture you’ll be communicating with? American organizations with a flat leadership structure, where most or all of the employees share authority and there isn’t a hierarchy, are obviously very different from traditional Japanese businesses. We can consider these two examples as the ends of a spectrum that other cultures and organizations may fall between. How much must you be aware of power differences, and what rituals or behaviors must you perform in response to them?

Third, what are the most significant ways that people fail in communicating with this culture? In other words, what are the biggest mistakes people make? Not all mistakes in cross-cultural communication are created equal; some are minor social faux pas, while others are dealbreakers and relationship-enders. Find out the most serious no-no’s and don’t do them. Pay close attention to those involving personal touch, which is acceptable in some cultures but discouraged or forbidden in others.

section.title: Practice
section.para: Learning about cultural differences and new norms is one thing, but actually changing your behavior is another. Once you’ve got some knowledge, make it real by practicing with mock conversations or meetings. If you’re going to meet a Japanese audience, practice the meishi business-card ritual until you can perform it without thinking. Know what you’re supposed to do, and get experience doing it.

It might sound strange to practice the exchange of business cards, but it’s no different from practicing a business presentation. If you want to succeed best, you have to know your audience and what they expect you to do. Sometimes those expectations will push you to act in entirely new ways, and doing so well will take time and practice.

section.title: Expect to Make Mistakes
section.para: You won’t be perfect in your cross-cultural communication, especially at the beginning. Expect to make mistakes and, when they come, learn from them. Don’t get discouraged when you do or say something embarrassing. As with business presentations, most audiences will judge you not on the mistake, but on how you react to the mistake.

Just as you expect others to treat your mistakes with grace and kindness, do the same for them. If someone offends you or crosses a cultural line, be forgiving where appropriate. They are probably in the same situation you are. You do not need to tolerate harmful or discriminatory treatment, but the norms of your business culture may be just as difficult for someone else to learn as those in Japan are for us.

section.title: Learn to Work within Constraints, Not against Them
section.para: We face constraints in every area of business communication, since there are always things that would be inappropriate or wrong to do or say. Effective communicators learn these constraints and then modify their behavior to work with them, not against them.

For example, if your normal approach to contract negotiations won’t work in another culture, you may need to learn a new way of doing things. While cultural constraints do block certain paths, they also open us up to others, and they can be inspirations for creative solutions to cross-cultural communication problems.

section.title: Be Prepared for Change
section.para: Many cultures and subcultures change slowly, but sometimes things can happen quickly. In the COVID-19 pandemic, many businesses, universities, and other institutions went from normal functioning to suspended or remote operation in less than a week, even overnight. That change created a new landscape to navigate in business communication.

The same can happen for cultures. Even established cultures can change quickly, and international events have an impact on how we should act when communicating. Be aware of what’s happening and how current events in the world influence the culture you wish to work with.

section.title: Push for Institutional Awareness
section.para: Effective business communicators can set an example of cultural awareness and sensitivity for others to follow. Their example doesn’t require that they devalue or renounce their own culture, but they can be models of how to modify behavior for a particular audience.

As you take this field guide and work through the obstacles of cross-cultural communication, try where appropriate to make cultural training a part of your organization. That training is simply a way of understanding new audiences and opening new channels for communication. The more we can learn, the better.

Cross-cultural communication in business presents us with special challenges, but also promises special rewards. We will be successful as we try to understand cultural differences and customize our communications to the norms of our audience.

chapter.label: Topic 13
chapter.title: Ethical Concerns in Local and Multinational Communication

section.title: Ethics and Ethical Problems
section.para: In our previous topic on cross-cultural communication, we considered a hypothetical situation in which we’re communicating with clients who come from a misogynistic culture. Our general principle for cross-cultural communication was to meet the expectations of the audience, but in a situation like this one, we may feel our audience’s expectations are immoral or otherwise impossible for us to meet. What is the correct thing to do here? What is our responsibility as communicators, and does that responsibility supersede other kinds of responsibilities, such as those we have toward individual human beings?

This hypothetical is an example of an ethical problem. EthicsThe area of thought that concerns right and wrong, good and bad, morality and immorality. is the area of thought that concerns right and wrong, good and bad, morality and immorality. An ethical problem is a situation like the one we described, where we experience competing pressures and don’t know how to choose an action: on the one hand, we have a responsibility to our company to make a sincere effort in doing business. On the other we may have moral objections to some of the actions we’re asked to take. What is the right thing to do? How do we balance these different commitments? This is an example of an ethical problem, and ethics studies problems like that one and the principles behind them.

Note that ethics is not about what people already do; it is about what people should or ought to do. When we consider a situation from an ethical perspective, we’re not so much worried about what people usually do in that situation—our focus is instead on what people ought to do, or what the ideal thing to do would be, whether or not anyone in fact makes that choice.
Here’s another ethical problem you might have heard before:

important.title: The Trolley Problem
important.para: A trolley has lost its brakes, and it’s barreling down the track, unable to stop. Five people happen to be tied up and laid across the tracks ahead, meaning that if the trolley continues its course, it will kill those five people. But there’s a lever you can pull that will divert the trolley to a second track and save those five people. On that second track, however, there’s a single person tied up, and if you divert the trolley it will kill that one person. You don’t know any of the six people. What is the right thing to do? To let the trolley continue as it would have, or to pull the lever and divert it? Why?

section.para: Ethics concerns right and wrong in all aspects of life, but there are branches of ethics that concentrate on particular areas of human experience: engineering ethics deals with ethical problems in the engineering profession, relationship ethics deals with ethical problems in relationships, and so on. For our purposes, we’re most interested in business ethicsThe branch devoted to the ethical problems and principles arising in business contexts. , which is the branch devoted to the ethical problems and principles arising in business contexts.
Here’s a business ethics problem. Unlike the trolley, these events are real, and you might be familiar with them.Craig v. Masterpiece Cake Shop, Inc., 2015 COA 115, ¶¶ 3–7.

important.title: Masterpiece Cake Shop
important.para: Jack Phillips owned a bakery, Masterpiece Cakeshop, in Lakewood, Colorado. In July 2012, Charlie Craig and David Mullins visited Masterpiece to ask Phillips about designing their wedding cake. Craig and Mullins planned to marry in Massachusetts, a state where same-sex marriages were legal; at the time, the state of Colorado prohibited same-sex marriages. In the summer of 2015, the Supreme Court’s decision in Obergefell v. Hodges made same-sex marriages legal throughout the United States. Colorado itself made same-sex marriage legal in late 2014 when Attorney General John Suthers ordered the state’s county clerks to issue licenses for same-sex marriages just as they would for traditional heterosexual marriages. 576 U.S. 644 (2015), synopsis available at: for the Supreme Court’s decision, and for more information about Suther’s order in Colorado. They meant to return to Colorado later for a party with Phillips’s cake.

Phillips refused to make a wedding cake for Craig and Mullins, telling them that to do so would violate his religious beliefs. He said he would sell them other baked goods but not a cake. The couple left. In a phone call the next day with Craig’s mother, Deborah Munn, Phillips said that Masterpiece Cakeshop did not make wedding cakes for any same-sex marriages. During this call he mentioned his religious beliefs again and noted that Colorado did not recognize same-sex marriages.

According to court documents, a lower court found that “Phillips has been a Christian for approximately thirty-five years and believes in Jesus Christ as his Lord and savior. Phillips believes that decorating cakes is a form of art, that he can honor God through his artistic talents, and that he would displease God by creating cakes for same-sex marriages.”Craig v. Masterpiece Cake Shop, Inc., 2015 COA 115, ¶ 4.

Some time later, Craig and Mullins filed a discrimination charge against Masterpiece Bakery. They claimed that Phillips was refusing their request for a cake because of their sexual orientation, and Phillips later admitted that this was true. When the Colorado Civil Rights Division found the discrimination allegations credible, Craig and Mullins filed a formal complaint in court, arguing that “Masterpiece had discriminated against them in a place of public accommodation because of their sexual orientation.”Craig v. Masterpiece Cake Shop, Inc., 2015 COA 115, ¶ 4.

section.para: What is the right thing to do in this situation? How should it be handled?

The Masterpiece case is an example of an ethical problem in business: the people involved might have a business relationship, but they hold conflicting values that in their minds make a successful business relationship impossible. Business ethics focuses on cases like these, and tries to determine the principles we ought to follow in resolving them.

This case also shows that business ethics is about more than just being honest, or “doing the right thing,” since it isn’t always clear what the “right thing” is. The deeper questions of business ethics involve the morality of whole economic systems and whether established ways of doing business are good for human lives. For example, a previous topic in this course covers internet and social media communication, but that topic takes the use of those tools as givens, or as the default way people behave. But business ethics could ask about whether it’s desirable in general for people to use social media to communicate. Is it good for individuals, families, and societies to conduct so much of their interaction online, in forums run by corporations and designed to generate profit? Why or why not?

A full treatment of business ethics goes far beyond what we’re able to cover here. Business ethics courses are common in business degrees, MBA programs, and other places, however, so you can learn more by taking one of those courses. In the remainder of this topic, we’ll confine our attention to ethical concerns surrounding business communication.

warning.title: Note
warning.para: Much of the content for this topic is drawn from Bryce Gessell’s book Business Ethics: A Practical Approach, with additional commentary.

section.title: Ethical Concerns and Confidentiality in Business Communication
section.para: Within business ethics we find a group of ethical problems involving business communication. The Masterpiece Cakeshop case in the previous section might be one of these; certain parts of the case do involve communication. But consider this next case, which deals with communication more directly.

important.title: Wilbur and Safety First Insurance
important.para: Wilbur was an insurance underwriter for Safety First Insurance. He reported for work at 8 a.m. and worked until noon each business day. Then he took an hour for lunch and returned at 1 p.m. to work until 5 p.m. He usually went out for lunch to local restaurants.

One day Wilbur didn’t feel like going out to eat, so he brought food from home for lunch. At noon he left his the first-floor offices of Safety First and sat outside at a picnic table to eat. While he ate he watched videos on his phone, including a few with content he understood was against company policy. But Wilbur knew that the grounds outside the office and the picnic table were not company property, and so he felt confident he was doing nothing wrong. He returned to work after eating and finished the workday.

Without Wilbur realizing it, however, the picnic table was close enough to the office that his phone was still connected to Safety First’s office Wi-Fi network while he watched the videos. Wilbur assumed he’d gone far enough away to disconnect and join a wireless network, but he hadn’t. Safety First’s internet monitoring software automatically reported his internet activities to his supervisor.

A few days later Wilbur’s supervisor asked for a meeting. He explained what the monitoring software had discovered and asked Wilbur to explain. Wilbur said he didn’t realize he was on the company’s Wi-Fi, and he apologized for what he’d done. He promised to be more careful in the future. But the supervisor pointed out that Wilbur’s actions were a serious violation of company policy. The next day, in a decision supported by all the company’s executives, Safety First terminated Wilbur’s employment. They gave him no severance package, arguing that his termination was with cause.

section.para: Wilbur’s case raises several ethical questions:

listitem.para: Given that Wilbur wasn’t on company property when he watched the videos, did he actually violate company policy?
Did the executives of Wilbur’s company have legitimate cause to terminate his employment without severance?

Should a company be allowed to monitor its employees’ internet communication? If a company can monitor which videos employees watch, can it also monitor emails from their private accounts, or texts to their spouses?

section.para: In the background of all these questions is perhaps the most important ethical issue in all of business communication: confidentialityThe privacy of certain pieces of information, and efforts to preserve that privacy. . Confidentiality refers to the privacy of certain pieces of information, and efforts to preserve that privacy. The very idea of business communication, and even of human communication itself, is built on the exchange of information. But confidentiality demands that we restrict which pieces of information we share, suggesting that some are not appropriate to share in certain circumstances. Wilbur’s case features this kind of concern—should his off-time, off-property internet communication be confidential, even if he happened to be on the company’s network? Why or why not?

Ethical issues of confidentiality appear in much more mundane situations as well. We saw one in , in our discussion of groups and group communication. There we considered the case of Maura, who sent an email to her supervisor, Helen, complaining about the behavior of a coworker. The information in the email was sensitive, and Maura expected that Helen would maintain confidentiality. Maura was happy to see that Helen sent her response only to Maura. Maura responded again, and the two carried on an email communication about the coworker’s behavior, with Maura believing that she was communicating about the issue with just a single person.

But digital communication makes it very difficult to know whether someone is preserving confidentiality, and without Maura’s knowledge, Helen had been blind-copying some of her colleagues on her responses, including the coworker whose behavior was being discussed. In other words, Maura had, without realizing it, actually been communicating with an entire group of people. They could all see her complaints and monitor the entire communication.

In , our discussion of this case centered on how Maura might change her behavior if she knew she was communicating with many people, rather than just with Helen. That knowledge would certainly change the context: to that larger audience Maura would probably choose to say nothing at all.

But we can now also consider the ethical dimensions of this example. Is what Helen did ethical? What responsibility does she have to Maura to maintain confidentiality? If she believes it’s in the best interest of the company to breach confidentiality and share Maura’s thoughts with others, is she obligated to do so? Can Maura face professional repercussions because of her communication? All of these are ethical questions, and they all arise in response to a situation we’ve probably encountered before.

Another common instance of communication with confidentiality concerns is the sharing of medical information. The relationship between a doctor and patient is a fiduciaryA relationship where one party has a responsibility to elevate the other party’s interests above any possible competing interests. one, which is a legal term for a relationship where one party—in this case, the doctor—has a responsibility to elevate the other party’s interest above any possible competing interests. The fiduciary loyalty of a doctor to a patient therefore involves confidentiality, in that whatever a patient tells a doctor is supposed to stay between them.

In reality, however, dozens or even hundreds of people have almost unfettered access to a patient’s medical records at most hospitals. The patient will know few or none of these people, and they don’t have the same fiduciary relationship that the doctor does. So why are they allowed access to the records? Are they obligated not to share what they learn about a patient’s health or medical care? What sense can we make of the “confidentiality” of medical records, when hundreds of people can look up those records at will?

Because human communication is predicated on exchanging information, confidentiality and the judicious sharing of certain pieces of information will always be an ethical issue. As a business communicator, you must learn to be aware of this ethical concern and learn to navigate what it means for your day-to-day interactions. Some information would be unwise to share, but some would be illegal or immoral to share, and seasoned communication professionals learn to tell the difference.

section.title: Conflicts of Local and Multinational Communication Norms
section.para: Cross-cultural communication in business presents special ethical challenges. As communication norms differ from place to place, and business practices around those norms differ as well, we may find ourselves communicating with people whose norms seem to us inappropriate or wrong. We may also be faced with conflicts between values we hold and corporate imperatives, such as increasing shareholder value. Such conflicts also emerge in situations where we are able to exploit the norms of other cultures to give ourselves or our organization an advantage. These issues may sound distant to you, but with the increasing globalization of business and business communication, there is a good chance you will confront one or more of them in your career.
Let’s take a look at some ethical conflicts between local and multinational norms.

important.title: Activision Blizzard
important.para: Activision Blizzard is one of America’s largest gaming companies. They produce titles such as Call of Duty, World of Warcraft, Diablo, Overwatch, and Candy Crush Saga, among many others. In the fiscal year from 2021 to 2022, they had over $7.6 billion in revenue, which was a decrease from over $8 billion the year previous.

One of the company’s most successful games is Hearthstone, a computer-based collectible card game with an adventure theme. In 2018, Hearthstone had over 100 million registered users all over the world, with many local and regional tournaments in addition to the Hearthstone Grandmasters, the worldwide championship.

Chung Ng Wai, a gamer better known by his moniker “Blitzchung,” was an elite Hearthstone player who had advanced to the Grandmasters tournament in October 2019.Beauchamp, Z. (2019, October 8). One of America’s biggest gaming companies is acting as China’s censor. Vox. At the time, many pro-democracy protests were happening in Hong Kong, a country whose government operates under the supervision of China’s. Blitzchung himself is from Hong Kong, and after winning a Grandmasters match, he gave an interview in which he said “Liberate Hong Kong, revolution of our time,” repeating a slogan popular among the protesters.

Activision Blizzard wasted no time in laying down punishments. They determined that Blitzchung’s comment amounted to “engaging in any act that, in Blizzard’s sole discretion, brings you into public disrepute, offends a portion or group of the public, or otherwise damages Blizzard image.”Blizzard Entertainment. (2019, October 8). Hearthstone grandmasters Asia-Pacific ruling. The company banned Blitzchung from competing for a year, stripped him of the prize money he had earned, and fired the commentators who had run the interview. The end of the company’s official statement read, “While we stand by one’s right to express individual thoughts and opinions, players and other participants that elect to participate in our esports competitions must abide by the official competition rules.”

Although China accounted for only a small percentage of Hearthstone’s userbase and revenue,Clement, J. (2023, February 9). Net revenue generated by Activision Blizzard from 2007 to 2022, by region. Statista. . many in the gaming community felt that Activision Blizzard was capitulating to Chinese interests in order to protect its expansion into that country. Rather than stand against the oppression and injustice that Hong Kong citizens were protesting, many gamers felt as though the company was acting as a bully mouthpiece for the Chinese government in its crackdown on the unrest.

section.para: In this case, the cross-cultural differences in norms of communication are on full display. They raise issues about justice and the role that American companies have in the international community. Did Blizzard respond appropriately? How do the norms of the country it’s based in interact with those where it does business?
Here’s another cross-cultural case.

important.title: Nestlé and Infant Formula in Developing Countries
important.para: In the 1960s, commercial powder-based baby formulas began to replace formula made with evaporated milk. Brands such as Similac and Enfamil sold their powder-based formulas to western markets, and their parent companies began to take the industry to third-world countries. One of these companies was Nestlé. Nestlé wished to expand its market share and began an aggressive advertising campaign aimed at selling formula in the developing world.

The advertising campaign had several components.For more background, see Akhter, S. H. (1994). Multinational corporations and the impact of public advocacy on corporate strategy: Nestlé and the infant formula controversy. Journal of International Business Studies, 25(3), 658–660, and Muller, M. (1974). The baby killer. War on Want. They distributed print media which suggested that baby formula was healthier than breastmilk and would make babies happier and more content. Many advertisements also contained giveaway offers for free samples and bottles to encourage new mothers to make other purchases. Nestlé was also allowed to place company representatives in hospitals, who dressed as nurses and spoke to mothers as though they weren’t salespeople but medical professionals. The “milk-nurses” would speak to families about the benefits of formula feeding and offer samples. Many new mothers also received deliveries of feeding supplies at their homes after giving birth to convince them to switch from breastfeeding.

The consequences of Nestlé’s marketing campaign were disastrous. In countries such as Jamaica, Chile, and Nigeria, many mothers chose to formula feed but ran into immediate, serious problems. Baby formula requires clean water, and if none is available, the liquid formula isn’t safe to drink. Because it’s so expensive, many families were only able to purchase a small amount of it. But when their formula supply ran out, the mother had often stopped breastfeeding for long enough that she was no longer able to produce any milk herself, which meant she had nothing to give her baby. Babies were hungry and malnourished, and many perished.

Despite this, representatives of formula companies refused to stop their campaign, apparently because to do so would have resulted in more harm. “What would the result be [of stopping their business activities in these areas]?” one representative said. “It would be the deaths of thousands of children because there are tens of thousands of mothers in these countries who have got to have some substitute for their milk in order to feed their babies.”Muller, M. (1974). The baby killer. War on Want, p. 6.

As word spread of Nestlé’s tactics, people in the developed world took action and organized an international boycott of Nestlé products in 1977. Nestlé fired back itself, suing an organization that had written about its activities. The company won the suit on the basis that its actions could not be directly connected to the deaths of infants.

section.para: In this case, Nestlé seems to have exploited the communication norms of the countries in which it was operating in order to change the behavior of women and families. Should they have been allowed to place representatives in hospitals, for example, and should those representatives have been allowed to pose as medical professionals? After creating the problem, do they owe anything to help solve it? What would have been the right thing to do? How could multinational companies avoid creating these sorts of problems in the first place?
This last case involves cross-cultural differences as well as serious breakdowns in corporate communication.

important.title: Cheryl Eckard and GlaxoSmithKline
important.para: Cheryl Eckard was a quality control manager at a GlaxoSmithKline manufacturing facility in Puerto Rico. The facility made medicine for children and others, and Eckard noticed many problems with the manufacturing processes over the course of many years. Some of these problems involved violations of industry and government standards, including pills that contained either more or less than the proper amount of medicine in each dose as well as bacteria-contaminated baby cream. Eckard reported her observations to her company on a number of occasions, but they ignored her warnings. GlaxoSmithKline’s own internal compliance department found that her complaints were “unsubstantiated” by their own findings. The company fired her in 2003.

Eckard then filed reports with multiple government agencies, which led to FDA-backed search warrants for the Puerto Rico facility. The violations were discovered across several months and, at the time, the FDA’s seizure of the medicine was the largest it had ever carried out for drug products.

A court case followed in which many groups were involved, both government and non-government. GlaxoSmithKline was found liable for its violations and ordered to pay hundreds of millions of dollars in fines and accrued interest. In addition, because of a part in the False Claims Act known as the qui tam provision, Eckard was able to be a plaintiff in the government’s case against GlaxoSmithKline. The terms of the settlement required that 22% of the payout, or just short of 100 million dollars, go to Eckard herself.Wearden, G. (2010, October 27). GlaxoSmithKline whistleblower awarded $96m payout. The Guardian.

section.para: Did Eckard do the right thing? Did Eckard’s company? What could have caused this breakdown in corporate communication? Are financial penalties the right kinds of penalties for these sorts of ethical violations? Why?

In this section and the previous one, we’ve seen the ethical problems that arise when different norms for communication come into conflict. This conflict commonly happens when our norms for communication differ from those of the audience we’re communicating with, but ethical issues can happen at the local level as well, including with confidentiality. As with other areas of business, business communication is a place we should expect to encounter ethical problems.

section.title: Ethical Business Communication
section.para: If we should expect to encounter ethical problems in business communication, what should we do about them? And just what is “ethical communication,” anyway? Let’s take a look at some answers to these questions.

First, know that we as business communicators will eventually run into ethical problems in our work. This knowledge ought to make us more sensitive to the ethical dimensions of communication. Since communication involves people, those ethical dimensions aren’t ever far below the surface. The more we can become familiar with them, the better we’ll be able to spot them and react appropriately.

Second, cultivate an attitude of considering the ethical dimensions of your work. Even when you aren’t facing a real ethical problem, your work will always be touching issues of confidentiality and other ethical values. As you become aware of these issues and values, you’ll be better attuned to proper courses of action.

Third, recognize that the context of communication is often much bigger than you assume. In previous topics we’ve spoken about how the context of communication includes things like the place we’re communicating in and the clothing we wear. But in modern business communication, and especially for cross-cultural work, the context is probably a lot bigger even than that, and probably includes cultural norms and practices that we don’t know or don’t understand. We ought to make an effort to respect those norms and practices, with the understanding that our interactions with them won’t always be free of the conflicts we’ve seen in this topic.

Fourth, be a good member of the community. As a business communicator, you belong to a community of people whose professional specialization is exchanging information. You therefore have a responsibility to do so wisely, with an awareness for how information impacts human lives. You should expect the other members of your community to exercise the same wisdom.
Fifth and finally, when you see something wrong, say something. Effective communicators understand that timing matters, and timely communication about pressing issues can make a big difference.

In the end, ethical business communication is about more than just being honest and following the law. It’s about being sensitive to human needs, and about being aware of how information and its uses affect human lives. Just as we’re sensitive to the needs of our audience in giving a presentation, we ought to be aware of how the sharing of information in local and global contexts can change human behavior both for good and for bad.

section.title: Context and Communication
section.para: We’ve done it: we’ve reached the final topic in our course on business communication. In the previous 13 topics we’ve seen ideas, definitions, examples, applications, and strategies covering all aspects of business communication, from the more theoretical (our model of communication) to the very practical (the iron laws of internet communication for business). Throughout these topics our focus has been to give guidance grounded in the way people really work and communicate, so that you can have the best chance for success wherever you implement your business communication skills.

In this short final topic, we’ll step back to look at some of the most important principles we’ve covered. Reading this topic isn’t a substitute for working your way through the rest of the material, but it should serve as high-level map for where we’ve been and where we hope to go.

Way back in our first topic, we defined business communication as the sending and interpreting of information in a business-related context. We commented on the breadth of this definition at the time, but we’re now in a much better position to appreciate how broad each term in this statement really is. We send information both overtly and subtly, consciously and unconsciously; something as simple as our clothing or a raised eyebrow can communicate massive amounts of information. Similarly, those around us, both those we think of as our audiences and those we don’t, are constantly receiving and interpreting the information we send. Their interpretation involves the meaning we hope they’ll receive, but it also depends on their own needs, beliefs, and desires, and so we don’t have complete control over the meanings other people end up drawing from our messages.

The definition of business communication also mentions “business-related contexts.” Again, we’re now in a much better position to appreciate how broad the term “context” really is here: from day-to-day water cooler interactions, to formal presentations, to social media planning sessions, contexts involving business are as varied as human beings themselves. One of the most important lessons we can take away from our course is that communication always goes far beyond things like email and LinkedIn posts. Each of us is communicating all the time, in whatever we do, and we’re always doing it from a particular cultural background, relying on assumptions about what others already understand and want.

In a sense, all business functions change depending on context, at least to some extent. For example, the accounting needs of a very small business will probably be minor; the business owner or a friend could do the books for such a company on their own time without too much trouble. But the accounting needs for a company with thousands of employees, millions of dollars in sales, and thousands of clients are very different, and would require whole teams of accountants and auditors to track. The accounting function, like all other business functions, changes for an organization as the context changes.

Communication stands out from other business functions, however, for how much of it depends on context, and how quickly communication needs can change in response to context. As our definition suggests, the proper way to communicate in a given situation depends almost entirely on context—there are fundamental principles applicable to all circumstances, and we’ve seen many of those. But the application of those principles in a particular situation is not always straightforward, and it’s the application that ends up making the difference in communication details. Likewise, communication needs can change from minute to minute and even second to second, as new sources of information change our understanding of what needs to be communicated and why. Perhaps more than any other business function, communication depends on context and can be a wild ride.

We’ve suggested this point in various ways in previous topics, but it’s worth noting more explicitly here. Success in business communication has a great deal to do with how flexible we are willing to be, and how flexible we are able to be. The separation between willingness and ability is intentional here, since they are not necessarily related—someone can be very willing to change how they communicate, but lack the tools to do so, while someone else can know exactly how they ought to shift their approach to an interaction and yet be unwilling to do it. Combining a willingness to meet audiences where they are with the ability to read them and make proper course corrections is the union of skills we’re going for, and the one you’re well on your way to developing with this course.
The context for communication determines how we need to communicate, but the rest is up to us. Our success depends on how willing and able we are to respond to different contexts.

section.title: Communication Success and Business Success
section.para: Our first topic noted that the ultimate purpose of business communication is to drive the success of individual professionals as well as of companies. Put in slogan form, the idea is that communication success is business success. Communicating successfully—with employees, management, clients, contractors, and everyone else—makes success in other areas of business much more likely, and sometimes even assured.

The reason for this assurance is that communication success is so fundamental to business success that, in many contexts, the two can’t be separated from each other. This is obvious in domains like sales, where closing a deal depends on the clarity with which you match your product’s benefits to the needs and desires of the customer. But it’s also true in most other areas of business. We see it in marketing and customer outreach, where the goal is to communicate a view of a product and its relationship to potential consumers; we see it in human resources, where one goal is the fluid transmission of clear policy; we see it in training and onboarding, where the goal is to standardize a knowledge base and levels of employee performance. We see it too in customer service, product management, facilities, information technology, and every other major domain of modern business organizations. All rely on effective communication, and successful communication goes a long way toward carrying out their most essential functions.

In short, communication success precedes most other forms of business success; if we aren’t communicating successfully, it will be difficult to make anything else happen. Failure in communication means that many other business functions won’t happen very effectively, or may not even happen at all.

For this reason alone, the skills you’ve gained as a business communicator are valuable no matter your role in an organization. If you can communicate effectively, in a wide range of contexts and with diverse audiences, then you possess skills that translate to many jobs and are not likely to go obsolete. Communication is a human practice, and as long as business involves humans, effective business communication will be indispensable.

section.title: The Principles of Business Communication
section.para: In the previous section we mentioned a few of the principles we’ve seen in our course. Next let’s see some of the other principles and themes that have emerged from our discussions.

listitem.para: Business communication is the sending and interpreting of information in a business context. We’re always sending, we’re always interpreting, and contexts are everywhere.

Everything is communication. From our clothing, to our tone of voice, to our facial expressions, to whether we work with our office door shut, everything we do is communication. The idea can frighten us, or it can inspire us to think about how to communicate better.
You are part of the message. Your image, reputation, and credibility are crucial parts of whatever you communicate. Those parts can take many years to build, but the wrong choices can destroy them.

You never have complete control of your messages. As the iron laws of internet communication for business suggest, even the best intentions and plans can wither before audiences who want you to fail. You don’t have full control; accept it.

Put the audience first. Efforts in research, persuasion, accessibility, presentations, and other purposes of communication depend on our understanding of the audience. Begin with the audience, don’t lose sight of them, and end with them. Remember, success in communication isn’t about whether you think you succeeded—it’s about whether the audience does.

You can’t predict the future, but fundamental principles always apply. We don’t know what new technologies lie beyond the horizon, nor what changes they’ll introduce to the landscape of business. But as long as communication involves human beings, we can count on certain principles. The only question will be how to apply them.

Culture is part of context—and yours isn’t necessarily best. The place people live and the norms that govern their interactions form part of the context for communication. Our tendency is to assume that the way we do things is best, but that’s just a bias of familiarity. Put the audience first, and make their culture and context yours.

section.para: For business communication it’s hard to do better than these principles. We’ll be more effective business communicators—and more effective human communicators—as we make them part of our lives.

section.title: Your Future as a Business Communicator
section.para: As we’ve said, skills in business communication are valuable for any role you occupy in any organization. As cultures and audiences continue to change, these skills will only become more valuable.

Going forward, your job as an effective business communicator will be twofold. First, begin as soon as possible to apply the things you’ve learned in this course. You can do so at a small level, in individual interactions, and with bigger projects like reports or presentations. You’ll see benefits immediately. At first those benefits may be small, such as an increased clarity with which you’re able to express yourself, or the ability to connect with an audience that you couldn’t reach before. But over time the benefits will accumulate and turn into something bigger.

Second, practice. Even experienced business communicators practice sales pitches, presentations, client calls, and other interactions. Because each task is so different, they all require something different from us. Look at the specifics of your audience and your situation, work out what you need to do, and practice.

Many people misunderstand this aspect of skill. We see highly skilled individuals, whether in the conference room or on the basketball court, and think to ourselves that such people must never need to practice—they’re already so good! What would they need practice for? But what we’re seeing when we watch highly skilled performers is not someone who doesn’t need to practice, but someone who has already practiced so much that the performance of their skill has become second nature. On social media in particular, it’s tempting to focus on the end product of a development process, but that focus stops us from seeing how the development process actually occurred.

In reality, skills and knowledge don’t mean you don’t have to practice. Looking backward, skills and knowledge mean you have already practiced a lot; looking forward, skills and knowledge mean that your practice will be more effective, and that you’ll be better able to handle a situation where things don’t go your way and your original plan isn’t working.

Think of it like this: imagine that we train an inexperienced communicator to give an effective presentation, but our training consists only in teaching that person to mimic exactly a presentation that another person has given. Our inexperienced communicator will come out of this training process with the ability to give that presentation, true. But that’s all they’ll be able to do, and they’ll only be able to do it as long as absolutely nothing goes wrong. If someone asks a question they haven’t heard before—if they forget a line or a gesture—if they can’t remember what a particular graph means—then it’s over.

On the other hand, someone with experience will be able to handle new situations with ease. They give a good presentation because they practiced that presentation. But when the context changes and they have to think on their feet, they know what to do then, too—not because of their practice for that presentation, but because of the many hours of practice and training in communication that took place long before.
Apply what you learn as soon as possible, and practice. Results won’t be far behind.

section.title: Everything Is Communication
section.para: We’ll end our course by reiterating one of our main themes: everything is communication. In business communication, everything we do shares information and sends a message.
If everything is communication, then what information do we want to share? What messages do we want to send?
The choice is ours.
